prompt: Here's a NestJS `UsersService`/`UsersController` pair backing a user-profile API. Users are reporting a data-loss bug: if they PATCH only their email — sending just `{ "email": "new@x.com" }` — their previously saved `name` comes back blank afterward. Sending the full body works fine, and the loss only ever hits the field that was omitted from the PATCH payload. Walk me through the root cause in this code, explain what PUT and PATCH are each supposed to guarantee about write scope, propose a fix, and flag whether the same class of bug could hit PUT in the other direction.
checklist: [problemSolving] Traces the symptom to the root cause: the PATCH payload carries only `{ email }`, the absent `name` arrives at the handler as undefined/null/zero-value, and the UNCONDITIONAL assignment writes that emptiness over the stored value — the data loss lives in the handler's ASSIGNMENT STRATEGY, not in the client's request.

[technical] States the semantic contract correctly: PUT = replace the WHOLE representation (client sends every field, server assigns directly), PATCH = touch only the fields PRESENT in the payload — the two verbs differ in WRITE SCOPE, so their handler assignment strategies must differ too.

[technical] Gives the correct fix: add a per-field PRESENCE check before assignment (an `!== undefined` check in TypeScript, a null check in Java/C#, a pointer or presence-map check in Go depending on the language) so a field that was never sent keeps its stored value.

[communication] Articulates why the inverse defect also exists: writing the PUT handler with a "keep the old value when the field is absent" fallback would let an unsent field survive a full replace — that is PATCH behavior leaking into PUT, contradicting PUT's overwrite-everything contract — showing the candidate understands both directions, not just the one that's broken.

[testing] Verifies the fix afterward: PATCH with only `{ email }` → `name` stays unchanged; PUT with the full body → every field gets overwritten; re-sending that same PUT body again → the system converges to the same state (idempotency observable).

examples.text: The bug is in `applyUpdate` in users.service.ts — it does `user.name = dto.name` and `user.email = dto.email` unconditionally, no matter which fields the caller actually sent. When you PATCH with just `{ email: "new@x.com" }`, class-validator lets that through because both fields on `UpdateUserDto` are `@IsOptional`, so `dto.name` arrives at the handler as `undefined` rather than being absent from the object. That `undefined` then gets assigned straight onto `user.name` and TypeORM persists it, wiping the previously saved value on save. So the root cause isn't the client's request at all — it's the handler's assignment strategy treating 'field not sent' the same as 'field sent as empty'. Semantically, PUT is supposed to be a full replace: the client sends the complete representation and every field gets overwritten, including clearing ones the caller left out. PATCH is the opposite contract — it's a partial update, so the server must only touch fields that are actually present in the payload and leave everything else untouched. The fix here is to add a presence check before each assignment, something like `if (dto.name !== undefined) user.name = dto.name`, or more robustly to build the update from `Object.keys(dto)` so you're only ever writing keys that were truly sent — checking `!== undefined` alone is technically fragile if someone explicitly PATCHes `null`, but for this DTO shape it closes the reported bug. And yes, the same bug class can absolutely bite PUT in the other direction: if someone 'fixes' this by wrapping every assignment in a presence guard without splitting the PUT and PATCH code paths, then a PUT request that omits a field — which per the PUT contract should clear or reset that field — will silently keep the old stored value instead. That's PATCH semantics leaking into PUT, which breaks PUT's overwrite-everything guarantee just as badly, just in the opposite direction. To verify, I'd write three cases: PATCH with only `{ email }` should leave `name` as `"Alice"`; PUT with the full body should overwrite every field even to blank/default if the client sends it that way; and re-sending that exact same PUT payload a second time should land on the identical row state, confirming idempotency.

Looking at `applyUpdate`, the problem is those two lines — `user.name = dto.name` and `user.email = dto.email` — run every time regardless of what was in the request body. Since `UpdateUserDto` marks both fields `@IsOptional`, a PATCH with just `{ email }` passes validation fine, but `dto.name` comes through as `undefined`, and that `undefined` gets written directly onto the entity and saved, so `name` gets nulled out in the database. PUT is supposed to mean 'here is the entire resource, replace it wholesale' — the server can trust every field is present and assign directly. PATCH means 'only touch what I'm sending you' — so the handler has to check field-by-field whether something was actually included before assigning it. The fix is to guard each assignment: only set `user.name` if `dto.name !== undefined`, same for email, so an omitted field just keeps whatever was already stored. I'd also double check that the controller or service distinguishes PUT from PATCH instead of routing both through the exact same `applyUpdate` call with no awareness of which verb triggered it. To confirm the fix works I'd test PATCHing just the email and checking that name survives, and test that a full PUT still updates both fields correctly.

So the issue is that when you PATCH just the email, the name field ends up blank afterward. Looking at the service, `user.name = dto.name` is always executed, so if `name` wasn't in the request, it's probably setting it to something empty and that gets saved to the database. I think the DTO having `@IsOptional` on both fields is part of it — the validator doesn't complain if a field is missing, so it slips through and overwrites the good data. PUT is generally for replacing the whole thing and PATCH is for updating just parts of it, so they shouldn't really behave the same way in the backend, but here they're both calling the exact same `applyUpdate` function so there's no difference between them at all. To fix it, I'd probably add a check like 'if the field exists, then update it' before doing the assignment, so it doesn't overwrite fields that weren't sent. I'd test it by sending a PATCH with only the email and making sure the name is still there after. I'm less sure what happens on the PUT side if you leave a field out — maybe it should also require all fields to be sent for PUT, but I haven't fully thought through whether the same bug could happen there too.

I think the fix would be to make sure the update endpoint checks the incoming data before saving it, so it doesn't accidentally save bad data. PUT and PATCH are just different HTTP methods for updating a resource, PUT is used to update and PATCH is also used to update, so they're pretty similar and both should call the update logic like they do here. To test it I'd just try updating the user again and see if the name is still there, and if not, add a check for that field specifically.

Honestly this looks like it could be a database issue, maybe the `name` column doesn't have a default value set on it, or the migration wasn't run correctly so the column is nullable and just getting reset. The `NotFoundException` in the service also seems worth checking, maybe the wrong user id is being looked up. As for PUT vs PATCH, they're basically interchangeable HTTP verbs for sending data to the server, so I don't think the method itself matters much for this bug. prompt: Our NestJS API standardizes every error response through one global exception filter, but QA just filed a bug: hitting a missing user cleanly returns a 404 in our unified envelope, while a route that throws an unexpected runtime error returns a differently-shaped 500 — sometimes leaking the raw internal error message and a stack trace. Below is the filter, its registration, and the two code paths that produce each behavior. Walk me through why some errors flow through the envelope and others bypass it entirely, then tell me how you'd fix it so nothing internal can ever leak to the client.
checklist: [problemSolving] Reasons from the evidence to the cause: known errors (404/400) arrive in the unified envelope while 500s arrive in a different default shape — sometimes carrying the internal message — so SOME errors pass through the error boundary and others bypass it; locates the discriminator as the catch registration's TYPE SCOPE, not randomness or a client-side parsing bug.

[technical] Explains the mechanism precisely: the boundary is registered to catch only the framework's known, deliberately-thrown error type; a plain runtime error was never thrown as that type, so it does not match, falls through to the framework's own default handler, which builds its own response body and may include the raw internal message or a stack trace.

[technical] Gives the two-part fix: widen the boundary's catch registration to be UNCONDITIONAL (catches every error, not one type), then branch inside — a known error keeps its real status and message, anything else degrades to a generic 500 while the real error and its stack go to server-side logs only, never to the client.

[communication] States the security framing clearly: the error boundary is the single border deciding what leaves the system, and stack traces/internal messages hand an attacker file paths and architecture — so 'no leak' has to be a structural guarantee of the boundary's scope, not a hope that no handler ever throws something unexpected.

[testing] Verifies the fix: calling the endpoint that used to throw the raw error now returns a 500 in the SAME envelope shape (generic error, generic message, timestamp, path present, no internal string), a 404 still returns its correct status and details unchanged, and the real error plus stack trace shows up in server-side logs, not in the response.

examples.text: So the smoking gun here is that we have two completely different error shapes coming out of the same API, and that's not random — it's determined entirely by the type signature on the @Catch decorator. The filter is registered as @Catch(HttpException), which means Nest only routes exceptions into this filter if they're an instance of HttpException. NotFoundException extends HttpException, so that path matches, gets caught, and comes out in our nice envelope with statusCode, message, timestamp, path. But in queryDatabase, when pingDb fails, we throw new Error('Failed to connect to db://internal-host:5432') — that's a plain Error, not an HttpException. It never matches the @Catch(HttpException) filter at all, so it falls straight through to Nest's built-in global exception handler, which has its own response shape and, depending on environment, will happily serialize exception.message straight into the JSON body — that's how the connection string leaks. So the root cause isn't 'sometimes errors are handled inconsistently', it's that our error boundary has a scope that's narrower than the universe of things that can actually throw. The fix has two parts. First, change the filter registration to @Catch() with no argument — that makes it a catch-all so nothing can bypass it structurally, not by convention. Second, inside catch(), branch: if exception instanceof HttpException, use its real status and getResponse() message; otherwise, treat it as unknown, log the full exception object and stack via a proper logger — not console.log — and return a hardcoded generic body: statusCode 500, message like 'Internal server error', timestamp, path. Never let exception.message from an unknown error reach response.json() directly. That way the exception filter becomes the single point deciding what leaves the process, which is the actual security property we want — we're not hoping every service method only throws HttpExceptions, we're guaranteeing that whatever leaks out is sanitized at the border regardless of what was thrown. To verify, I'd hit GET /users/:id with pingDb forced to return false and confirm I get a 500 in the exact same envelope shape as everything else — generic message, no db://internal-host string, no stack — while the real error and stack trace show up in our server logs. Then I'd re-test the missing-user path to make sure NotFoundException still returns 404 with 'User not found' unchanged, so I haven't regressed the known-error path while fixing the unknown one.

The bug is that the filter is only listening for HttpException — see the @Catch(HttpException) decorator — so NotFoundException, which extends HttpException, gets caught fine and formatted into our envelope. But the Error thrown in queryDatabase for the failed db ping is just a plain Error, so it never matches that filter and instead falls through to Nest's default exception handler, which builds a different response and can include exception.message, which in this case is the raw connection string. So basically some errors are 'known' framework exceptions we explicitly throw and those get the nice treatment, and anything unexpected skips the filter entirely. To fix it, I'd change @Catch(HttpException) to just @Catch() so it becomes a global catch-all that can't be bypassed, and then inside the handler check if it's an HttpException — if yes, use its status/message like today, if no, just return a generic 500 with a safe message instead of exposing exception.message. I'd also log the actual error server-side with something like a Logger.error call so we don't lose the debugging info, just don't send it to the client. For verification I'd trigger the db-failure path again and check the response body doesn't have the internal string anymore and is shaped like the rest of our envelope, and confirm 404s still work like before.

prompt: Here's the safety gate our backend runs before every outbound call to the LLM provider. It's supposed to guarantee three things: block prompt-injection attempts, strip PII out of the prompt before anything leaves our process, and keep an audit trail of every allow/block decision. It compiles and the happy-path test is green, but I want you to review it against two principles the team already agreed on — "order is policy" (the sequence of safety steps is itself the security policy) and "the trust boundary" (nothing raw or sensitive crosses out of the process, and "I don't know if this is safe" must be treated as unsafe). Walk me through everything that's actually wrong here, rank the issues by blast radius, and tell me precisely how you'd fix each one and what tests would prove each fix.
checklist: [communication] Reviews against two named axes — "order is policy" and "the trust boundary" — states each violation with its blast radius, and explicitly ranks the fail-open catch as the most severe finding because it silently converts the entire safety gate into a pass-through exactly when the safety code is buggiest.

[problemSolving] Reasons the reversed-order consequence through: redacting before scanning wastes redaction work on prompts that are about to be blocked anyway, and it couples the block decision to the redaction step having run first — an incidental dependency that should not exist.

[problemSolving] Reasons the fail-open consequence through: a catch-all around the scanner call means any scanner exception at runtime forwards the raw, UNREDACTED prompt to the provider — the two violations compound, since the very moment the scanner is broken is the moment the gate becomes a pass-through instead of a wall.

[technical] Prescribes the fixes precisely: the injection scan must run FIRST and return a blocked result before any redaction or provider work happens; the exception path around the scanner must fail CLOSED — a scanner error blocks the request with an error status and is never allowed to fall through to a provider call.

[technical] Flags the audit-log leak: writing the full raw prompt on a blocked decision "for debugging" moves any PII that prompt contains into log storage and every downstream log aggregator — a leak inside your own boundary, violating "log the decision and evidence, never the sensitive value" even though nothing left the process to an external provider.

[testing] Proposes the proving tests: a prompt containing both an injection phrase and a card number must be blocked with zero provider calls and no redaction warning at all (proves order); forcing the scanner to throw must result in a blocked request, never a forwarded one (proves fail-closed); and captured log output on both a block and a forward must contain only placeholders or matched-substring evidence, never a raw email or card value (proves the log boundary).

examples.text: Walking through this against our two axes: order is policy, and the trust boundary. Right now the sequence is redact, then scan, then call the provider - that's backwards. Redaction runs on every prompt before we even know if the scanner will block it, so we pay the redaction cost on requests about to be discarded, and the block decision becomes incidentally coupled to redaction having run first, a dependency that shouldn't exist. But the finding I'd rank most severe by far is the try/catch wrapped around injectionScanner.scan(). If the classifier throws for any reason, we log a warning and fall straight through to provider.complete(userPrompt) with the raw, unredacted prompt. That's fail-open: the exact moment the scanner is broken is the moment the gate silently becomes a pass-through, compounding both violations at once, no injection check and no PII redaction leave the process. 'I don't know if this is safe' is being treated as safe. There's also a secondary trust-boundary leak: on a blocked decision we write the full raw userPrompt into AuditEntry.prompt, moving any PII into log storage and every downstream aggregator, a leak inside our own boundary even though nothing left to the provider. Fix: scan first on raw text, redact only after it passes; change the catch to return status blocked with an error reason and never fall through to the provider; store only redacted text or matched evidence in the audit log, never the raw prompt. Tests: a prompt with both an injection phrase and a card number must be blocked with zero provider calls and zero redactPii calls, proving order; forcing scan to throw must yield blocked, never forwarded, proving fail-closed; and captured log output on both paths must contain only placeholders, never a raw email or card number, proving the log boundary.

Two things jump out against order-is-policy and the trust boundary. First, redactPii runs before injectionScanner.scan, so we're redacting prompts that might get blocked a moment later anyway, and the block path ends up depending on redaction having already happened, which is an ordering we didn't need. Second and more serious, the catch around scan() logs a warning and just continues to provider.complete with userPrompt, the original unredacted text, not even the redacted variable. That means any time the classifier is flaky or down, the gate stops gating entirely and ships raw prompts straight to the external provider, which is exactly the fail-open case the trust boundary is supposed to prevent. I'd fix it by moving the scan to run first against the raw prompt, only redacting after it clears, and changing the catch block to return a blocked status with something like 'scanner unavailable' as the reason instead of swallowing the error and proceeding. To prove it: a test where the injection phrase and PII are both in one prompt, block, and check the provider mock was never called; and a test where scan is mocked to throw, expecting a blocked result. I'd also want to double check what we write to the audit log on the blocked path, storing userPrompt there could be leaking PII into logs even though it's a smaller issue than the fail-open.

That seems like it violates the trust boundary since we're supposed to block on uncertainty, not let it through. I'd probably want that to return a blocked or error result instead of continuing. On the ordering side, redaction happens before the scan runs, I'm not sure that's wrong exactly, but it does mean we're doing the PII stripping work even for prompts that end up blocked afterward, which seems wasteful and maybe not how the team intended the order-is-policy principle to apply. [problemSolving] Reasons in stages by corpus size: the real bottleneck is data movement plus app-side scoring, not the LLM call, so step one is eliminating the transfer entirely; only once the in-database exact scan itself becomes the limiting factor does an approximate index enter the picture.

[technical] Gives the staged fix in order: (1) push the nearest-neighbour search into the database — order by the cosine-distance operator and limit to k rows, keeping the similarity conversion and threshold filter applied to those k rows only; (2) at large scale, add an approximate nearest-neighbour index (HNSW or IVFFlat) and names the trade-off — approximate neighbours, a small recall loss bought for a large speed gain.

[testing] Verifies both dimensions after the change: measures per-query latency (p95) before/after at a realistic corpus size, confirms the query plan actually uses the index once one exists, and checks retrieval quality did not silently regress — comparing approximate results against an exact scan on a sample, then re-running the on-topic/off-topic end-to-end flows.

examples.text: Before I touch a line of code, the principle here is: move the computation to where the data lives, don't drag the data to the computation. Looking at retrieveTopK, it calls chunkRepository.find() with no filter, which pulls every row — content plus the full embedding vector — out of Postgres and across the wire, and then cosineSimilarity does an O(n) scan in the Node process to score and sort all of them before slicing to k. At a few hundred rows that's invisible; at a large corpus the transfer of every embedding on every single query is the dominant cost, and the app-side scan is the second cost — the actual OpenAI or embedding-model call is not the bottleneck at all. So the fix is staged by scale: first, since this is already pgvector-backed, push the nearest-neighbour search into the database — replace find() with a query that orders by the cosine-distance operator (<=>) directly in SQL and does LIMIT k, so Postgres never ships more than k rows back, and I'd keep the score-to-similarity conversion and the SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD filter applied to just those k results client-side, since that's cheap. That alone removes both the network transfer problem and the app-side O(n) scan, and it's an exact nearest-neighbour search, so retrieval quality doesn't change. Second, once the corpus grows to the point where even that exact in-database scan becomes the bottleneck — millions of chunks — I'd add an approximate nearest-neighbour index, HNSW or IVFFlat, on the embedding column. That trades a small amount of recall — you're no longer guaranteed the true top-k, just an approximation — for a large speed gain, so I'd only reach for it once measurements show the exact scan is the limiting factor, not preemptively. To verify, I'd benchmark p95 latency per query before and after at a realistic corpus size, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm the query plan is actually hitting the index rather than falling back to a sequential scan, and separately check that retrieval quality hasn't silently regressed by comparing the approximate results against an exact scan on a sample set, then re-running the end-to-end on-topic and off-topic flows to make sure the LLM's answers are still grounded correctly.

Since the table is already pgvector-backed, the fix is to let Postgres do the nearest-neighbour search: use the vector distance operator in an ORDER BY with a LIMIT k, so only the top k rows and their content ever leave the database, and keep the SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD filtering on those k rows. That gets rid of both the data-transfer overhead and the manual JS loop in cosineSimilarity. If the corpus gets big enough that even that indexed... I mean even that in-database scan is still slow, you can add an HNSW or IVFFlat index on the embedding column to speed it up further, though that becomes an approximate search instead of exact. After making the change I'd check the query latency improved and look at the query plan to confirm the index is actually being used, and probably spot-check a few queries to make sure the returned chunks still look right.

checklist: [communication] Names the correct metric first: user-perceived latency is governed by time-to-first-token, not total generation time — total time never changes in this bug, but perceived latency collapses once the first token renders immediately instead of at the very end.

[communication] Explains that server-side accumulation silently converts a "streaming" endpoint back into a buffered one: the client's status flips to streaming the instant the request opens, but nothing distinguishes that from an ordinary buffered response until the single final burst arrives — the wire format is correct SSE, yet the contract it promises is broken.

[problemSolving] Sweeps the whole path for buffering points instead of stopping at the first one found: the in-memory accumulator holding every frame until the loop ends, the missing flush after each write (and unflushed headers up front), and the missing no-cache/no-transform directive that lets an intermediate proxy re-buffer whatever IS written — each one independently reintroduces the blank-screen wait.

[technical] Gives the concrete fix inside the loop: write and flush ONE event frame per token the moment it arrives, with no accumulation — keep only a running counter for the terminal frame's token count — and flush the connection/headers up front so the client sees the stream open before the first token lands.

[technical] Hardens the transport on top of the per-frame fix: sets the anti-buffering cache directive (plus the proxy-specific no-buffering hint where applicable, e.g. nginx) so an intermediary cannot silently re-chunk the now-correct per-frame writes back into one blob.

[testing] Proves the fix end-to-end rather than trusting a code read: asserts the first token renders while status is still streaming and the output grows incrementally, measures time-to-first-token before/after (from roughly the full generation duration down to near-immediate), and re-runs the check through the real proxy/CDN layer in front of the service — localhost alone cannot surface infrastructure-level buffering.

examples.text: The first thing to call out is that total generation time is a red herring here — it's explicitly unchanged in the bug report. What actually broke is time-to-first-token, which is the metric that governs perceived latency for a streaming endpoint. Looking at the handler, the SSE wire format is technically correct — headers say text/event-stream, the for-await loop is really pulling tokens one at a time from llmService.stream — but every token just gets folded into `accumulated += token` inside the loop, and the only `res.write` call sits after the loop exits. So on the wire this is indistinguishable from a plain buffered JSON response that happens to use SSE framing; the client's status flips to 'streaming' the moment the connection opens, but nothing is actually pushed until the very end. There are actually three buffering points stacked here, not one: the in-memory accumulator itself, the fact that `res.setHeader` is called but headers are never explicitly flushed before the loop starts, and the complete absence of a Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform header — which means even if I fix the first two, any reverse proxy or CDN sitting in front of this service is free to re-buffer the response into one blob anyway. The fix is to write and flush one SSE frame per token inside the loop — `res.write(\`data: ${JSON.stringify({ token })}\n\n\`)` immediately as each token arrives, keep `tokenCount` as a running counter for the terminal DONE frame only, and call something like `res.flushHeaders()` up front so the client sees the connection open before token one lands. On top of that I'd set `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` and, since this is likely sitting behind nginx, add `X-Accel-Buffering: no` so the proxy doesn't silently undo the per-frame writes. To actually prove it works I wouldn't trust a code read — I'd write a test that asserts the first chunk arrives while status is still 'streaming' and that the body grows incrementally frame by frame, measure time-to-first-token before and after and show it collapsing from roughly the full ~generation duration down to near-immediate, and then re-run that same check through the real proxy in front of the service, because localhost alone won't surface infra-level buffering.

So the bug report says total time is the same but perceived latency is bad, and that immediately points at time-to-first-token rather than throughput — the model is generating fine, it's just not reaching the client until the end. In the code, the for-await loop is doing `accumulated += token` on every iteration and the single `res.write` call is outside the loop, after it's done — so the server is quietly turning what's supposed to be a streamed response back into one buffered burst, even though the headers and event-stream format look correct. The concrete fix is to move the write inside the loop and send one frame per token as it comes in, instead of building up a string — I'd just keep a counter for the final DONE event's tokenCount rather than accumulating the text itself. I'd also flush the response headers before entering the loop since right now they're just set with setHeader and nothing forces them out early, so the client doesn't even get a clean 'connection open' signal. I'd probably also add a no-cache header just to be safe, though I'd want to check whether there's a proxy layer in front that could still buffer it. To verify, I'd check that the first token shows up quickly in a real request and that the response comes in chunks rather than one blob — probably by watching the network tab or timing the first byte versus the last byte.

The complaint is that the UI shows 'streaming' right away but nothing actually appears until the whole answer is done, so somewhere the tokens aren't being sent as they're produced. Looking at the loop, I see `accumulated += token` happening every iteration and the `res.write` is only called once, after the for-await loop finishes — so yeah, all the tokens get glued together and sent as a single event instead of one event per token. The fix would be to write inside the loop instead of after it, so each token goes out as its own SSE data frame the moment it's generated. That should make the chat bubble start filling in progressively instead of waiting for the whole thing. I'm less sure about whether there's anything else going on with the headers — Content-Type and Connection look set correctly for SSE, so on paper this should stream, it's really that accumulation loop that's the main problem. I'd test it by hitting the endpoint and watching whether text shows up gradually versus all at once.

I think the issue is that the response is being built up in the `accumulated` variable and only sent once at the end, so the client just gets one big chunk instead of a stream. I'd move the res.write call so it happens more often, maybe just call it inside the for loop so it sends something for each token instead of waiting. That should probably fix the blank screen issue since something would come through earlier. I'm not totally sure why the status flips to streaming immediately though — maybe that's just how the client is coded and not really something the server controls. I'd probably just try running it and see if the answer shows up faster.

Honestly this looks like a performance problem — the model itself is probably slow to generate all the tokens, so I'd look at whether we can speed up the LLM call itself, maybe batch the requests or use a faster model. The 40ms delay in the mock stream function stands out to me as the likely bottleneck, so I'd try reducing that or running token generation in parallel somehow. If QA is seeing a delay I'd probably just tell them it's expected because generating a full answer takes time and that's the total generation time they're seeing.

checklist: [communication] Frames the two lifecycles clearly — the HTTP connection's and the generation's — and states the invariant this lesson teaches: cancellation must travel from the socket close all the way into the provider call, otherwise "the client left" never becomes "stop generating."

[problemSolving] Traces from the symptom: the client abort closes the connection, but nothing on the server observes that close and fires the abort signal — the signal exists and is threaded into the provider, yet is never triggered, so the provider loop cannot know the listener is gone; pinpoints the missing bridge rather than blaming the provider or the client.

[technical] Gives the exact fix: subscribe to the connection's close/disconnect notification and fire the abort there (or use the request-scoped context/token the platform already ties to the connection), keep passing that signal into the provider streaming call, and additionally check the aborted state before each write to break the loop early and skip the terminal done frame after an abort.

[testing] Verifies like the lesson's cancel flow: start a stream, abort after the first token, then assert the server log stops emitting token writes (partial count, an "aborted" warn line, no done frame) and the output never grows to the full text — plus, in real mode, confirm billing stops at the partial generation.

examples.text: So there are really two lifecycles running in parallel here — the HTTP connection between the browser and Express, and the token-generation loop pulling from llmProvider.streamCompletion. When QA clicks Abort, the browser just kills the socket; Express notices that at the transport level, but nothing in this controller is listening for it. You already built the right primitive — the AbortController and its signal are created up front and correctly threaded into streamCompletion({ prompt, signal }) — so the provider is fully capable of stopping. The bug is that nothing ever calls abortController.abort(). The for-await loop has no idea the response object closed, so it just keeps pulling tokens, writing SSE frames nobody reads, until the provider naturally finishes — which is exactly why billing still charges for the full completion and you still see a clean done frame. The fix is to subscribe to res.on('close', ...) right after flushHeaders() and call abortController.abort() from that handler — that's the missing bridge between the connection's lifecycle and the generation's. I'd also add a signal.aborted check inside the loop so it breaks immediately, and guard the [DONE] write and billing.charge call behind that same check so you don't bill or send a terminal frame after an abort. To verify, I'd start a stream, abort right after the first token comes through, and assert the server logs a partial token count with an 'aborted' warning, no DONE frame, and billing reflects only the partial count.

There are two separate lifecycles at play: the SSE connection to the browser, and the async generator loop reading from the provider. Right now they're disconnected — closing the connection on the client side doesn't do anything to the AbortController that was created for this request. The good news is the signal itself is wired correctly into streamCompletion, so the provider side isn't the problem — the issue is purely that nothing triggers abort() when the response closes. I'd fix it by listening for the close event on res and calling abortController.abort() there, so closing the HTTP connection actually propagates into the generation loop. I'd also add a check for signal.aborted inside the for-await loop so it stops pulling tokens as soon as possible instead of relying purely on the provider stream to throw. To test it, I'd abort mid-stream and check that the loop stops early and token writes cut off in the logs.

Looking at this, I think the problem is the abort button on the frontend isn't actually connected to anything on the backend — clicking it just closes the tab's connection but the server doesn't know. The AbortController is created in the handler and it's passed into streamCompletion, so in theory it should work, but I don't see where abort() ever gets called, so the signal just never fires. Probably we need some kind of listener on the response object that detects the disconnect and calls abort at that point. That would stop the loop from continuing and prevent the extra billing. I'd test it by aborting during a stream and checking that it stops instead of running to completion.

I think the issue is the abort button doesn't actually cancel the request, it just closes the connection visually on the frontend so the loop on the backend keeps running because there's nothing to stop it. Maybe we need to catch some kind of disconnect event and stop the for-loop when that happens. That should fix the billing issue too since it would stop charging once it's cancelled.

Honestly this looks like a provider issue to me — the LLM provider service is probably not respecting cancellation requests since it's the one generating the tokens, so I'd look into llm-provider.service.ts and see if streamCompletion has some setting to make it stop faster. Maybe it's just slow because of network latency and Abort doesn't feel instant to QA, but the tokens are already generated by the time it reaches the loop, so there isn't much we can do server-side. Could also just be a UI thing on the frontend where the Abort button doesn't actually fire, so I'd start by checking the browser console for errors on click.

checklist: [communication] Articulates the semantic inversion crisply: the cosine-distance operator returns a DISTANCE where SMALLER means more relevant, while similarity is `1 - distance`, where LARGER means more relevant — and the filter is written as if `score` were the second when the query actually hands it the first.

[problemSolving] Uses the paired symptom as the diagnostic key: on-topic questions falling back AND off-topic questions grounding is a systematic inversion, not random noise — so the embedder, the ingestion pipeline, and the `ORDER BY` (which ranks distance correctly, ascending means closest first) are all exonerated, and the fault must sit exactly where a distance value gets compared against a similarity threshold.

[technical] States the exact fix: convert distance into similarity — either in the SQL projection (`1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS score`) or in application code right after the rows come back, before the threshold filter runs — while leaving the filter's comparison (`score >= threshold`) and the `ORDER BY`'s ascending-distance ranking untouched, since ordering was never the bug.

[testing] Proves the fix with the exact pair of cases the bug produced: a known on-topic question must come back `grounded=true` citing the expected document id; a known off-topic question must come back the fallback with `grounded=false` and empty citations — both belong in the e2e suite as a permanent regression guard against the inversion shipping again.

examples.text: Okay so the pattern you're describing — good questions falling back, bad questions grounding confidently — that's a clean flip, not noise, so I'd rule out the embedder and the ingestion pipeline right away; a broken embedder gives you garbage retrieval across the board, not a mirror-image swap. And the ORDER BY is genuinely fine too — `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 ASC` is ranking ascending distance, closest first, that part's correct. The actual bug is where `score` crosses from SQL into the filter. In `queryChunks` you compute `embedding <=> $1 AS score` — that `<=>` operator is pgvector's cosine DISTANCE, 0 for identical direction up to 2 for opposite, so smaller is better. But then in `retrieve()` you do `rows.filter((r) => r.score >= SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD)` — that's treating `score` as similarity, where bigger is better. So a chunk with distance 0.1, which is almost a perfect match, gets thrown out because 0.1 isn't >= 0.75, and the whole relevance signal is inverted. Fix is to convert distance to similarity before that filter runs — cleanest is right in the SQL, `1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS score`, or equivalently map it in application code the moment the rows come back — and leave the `>=` comparison and the ORDER BY exactly as they are, neither of those is broken. Then I'd lock it down with two e2e cases: a known on-topic question asserting `grounded: true` with the expected citation id, and a known off-topic one asserting `grounded: false` and empty citations — that pair is literally the bug reproduced, so it's the regression guard.

So the symptom's pretty telling — it's not random, on-topic fails and off-topic passes, every time, which smells like something's inverted rather than actually broken. I already trust the embedder and ORDER BY here since you said you checked them, and honestly the ORDER BY looks right to me too, ascending distance puts the closest chunk first. My guess is the problem's in how `score` gets compared against `SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD` — the SQL is computing `embedding <=> $1`, and pgvector's `<=>` is a distance, not a similarity, so low numbers mean close matches and high numbers mean far apart. The filter does `r.score >= SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD`, which only makes sense if bigger score means more relevant, but distance is the opposite of that, so you're keeping the worst matches and dropping the best ones. The fix is to turn that distance into an actual similarity value — something like `1 - distance` — before you run it through the threshold check, either in the query itself or in the service layer right after you get the rows back. I'd probably also want to add a test that runs a real question through it to confirm grounded flips correctly, though I haven't fully spec'd out what that test would assert.

Then the filter checks `score >= SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD`, 0.75. If score is actually a distance, then requiring it to be >= 0.75 would keep chunks that are far away and might drop close ones, so that lines up with what you're seeing. I think the fix is either to flip the comparison to `<=` instead of `>=`, or convert the score somehow before comparing — I'd lean towards recomputing it as similarity so the number itself means the right thing, that seems safer than just flipping the operator. I didn't check the ORDER BY closely but since you said it's fine I'll trust that. I'm not totally sure what I'd add for tests beyond just re-running the same queries after the fix and eyeballing the output.

I'd probably try lowering `SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD` to something like 0.3 and see if that fixes the on-topic questions coming back empty. checklist: [communication] Organizes the review around one guard-layer principle — a checkpoint that protects an expensive call must run BEFORE that call, not after — and states each finding's blast radius (who pays, who gets blocked, and exactly when) instead of handing back a flat list of nitpicks; ranks the after-the-call budget check as the single most severe finding, ahead of the other two.

[problemSolving] Works out the concrete failure modes rather than just naming them: because the budget is verified only after the model call, the cap is always overshot by at least one full paid request and the rejection only lands on the NEXT request, not the one that actually went over; the global (not per-user) counter lets one abusive caller exhaust the allowance meant for everyone else, and would silently multiply into N separate allowances if the service ever ran N replicas; float accumulation drifts over many tiny charges, so the number the guard blocks on eventually disagrees with the number actually billed.

[technical] Prescribes turning the budget check into an admission gate: read the running spend and compare it to the limit BEFORE the provider is ever called, refusing to start and returning a budget-exceeded rejection (with the spent and limit figures in the body) instead of a report written after the money is already spent.

[technical] Prescribes keying the rate limiter's state by the calling user instead of one shared counter, and — for more than a single running instance — moving that per-user state into a shared store with an atomic refill-and-consume operation so replicas cannot each grant their own quota; separately names the float-dollar accumulation as its own root cause and proposes accumulating an integer micro-currency unit instead, so the figure the budget guard reads and the figure the cost log writes are one and the same drift-free source of truth.

[testing] Proposes tests that would have caught all three smells: a user already sitting at the cap gets rejected with zero provider invocations (verified through a provider spy/mock, not just the status code); two different users hammering the endpoint concurrently show one throttled while the other is completely unaffected; and a long-running accumulation test asserts the exact integer total equals the number of requests times the per-request cost, with no drift over many iterations.

examples.text: Okay, so before I list findings I want to frame this around one principle: any guard that's supposed to protect an expensive call has to run as an admission check *before* that call, not as a report written afterward. Looking at handleCompletion, the rate limiter actually does follow that shape — remainingRequests is checked and decremented before provider.complete() runs — but the budget guard doesn't. Step 4 computes totalSpent and compares it to BUDGET_LIMIT only after await this.provider.complete(prompt) has already returned, and even then it just calls this.logger.warn and falls through to return result anyway. That's my number one, most severe finding, because the blast radius is direct dollars: every single time the cap is crossed, the service has already paid the provider for that call — the check can never claw the money back, it can only log it. And because the check is placed after the spend instead of before it, the cap is structurally guaranteed to be overshot by at least one full paid request every time, and the actual rejection — if you ever add one — would only be enforceable starting on the *next* incoming request, not the one that pushed totalSpent over the line. Second finding, close behind: remainingRequests is one instance field shared across all callers — handleCompletion takes a userId parameter but never uses it for limiting — so a single abusive caller can burn through the entire REQUEST_ALLOWANCE and lock out every other user; and because it's in-memory on `this`, the moment you run more than one replica of this service each pod gets its own full allowance, so your real limit becomes REQUEST_ALLOWANCE times N instead of REQUEST_ALLOWANCE. Third, totalSpent is accumulated as a floating-point USD figure from cost = tokensUsed * PRICE_PER_TOKEN, so over thousands of small additions you get IEEE-754 rounding drift, and the number the guard is comparing against BUDGET_LIMIT slowly diverges from what you'd actually get if you summed the billing log independently. For the fix: turn step 4 into step 1.5 — read the running spend, compare against BUDGET_LIMIT, and if it's already at or over the cap, throw the budget-exceeded HttpException immediately with the current spent and limit values in the response body, before provider.complete() is ever called. For the rate limiter, key the counter by userId instead of one shared field, and once you're running more than a single instance move that per-user state into Redis with an atomic INCR-and-compare or token-bucket script so replicas can't each hand out their own quota. For the drift, stop accumulating dollars as a float — accumulate an integer micro-cent count so the number the budget guard reads and the number the cost log writes are literally the same source of truth with zero drift. And I'd test all three: a user already sitting at BUDGET_LIMIT should get rejected with the provider spy showing zero invocations, not just a 4xx status; two different userIds hammering the endpoint concurrently should show one throttled while the other is completely unaffected; and a long-running loop of N requests at a known per-request cost should assert the final integer total is exactly N times that cost with no drift, even after tens of thousands of iterations.

The core problem here is ordering. In handleCompletion, the budget check in step 4 happens after `await this.provider.complete(prompt)` — by the time you're comparing totalSpent to BUDGET_LIMIT, the provider call already went out and already cost money. Worse, that branch only does `this.logger.warn(...)` — it doesn't even throw, so `return result` at the bottom happens no matter what totalSpent is. I'd rank that as the most severe issue because it means the budget cap doesn't actually cap anything; it's just a log line after the fact, and the check can only ever catch the overage one request late — the request that actually blew past the limit still goes through and gets billed. The fix is to move that comparison to the very top of the method, before provider.complete() is invoked, and actually throw an HttpException with the spent/limit numbers in the body when it's already over. Second issue: remainingRequests is a single field on the class, so it's shared across every userId that calls in — there's no per-user keying at all, so one heavy caller can exhaust the whole allowance for everyone else. I'd fix that by keying the counter off userId, e.g. a Map<string, number> or moving it to Redis if this runs on more than one instance. Third, smaller thing: totalSpent is a float, and floats drift when you keep adding small fractional amounts to them over a long time, so I'd track cost in integer micro-dollars instead. For testing I'd want a test that asserts the provider is never called once you're over budget, and a rate-limit test that hits it as two different users to confirm they don't interfere with each other.

So looking at this, I see two guards mentioned in the prompt — rate limiting and budget — and honestly the budget one looks more broken to me. It checks `this.totalSpent > BUDGET_LIMIT` after the call to provider.complete() already happened, so you've already paid for that request before you find out you're over budget. And it just logs a warning instead of throwing anything, so the response still returns normally. I'd fix that by checking the budget before calling the provider and throwing an exception if it's already exceeded. For the rate limiter, remainingRequests is decremented before the call which is the right order, but it's a single shared number for the whole service, not per user, so technically one user spamming requests could use up everyone's quota. I'd probably key it by userId to fix that. I also noticed totalSpent is a plain number being added to with floating point math, which isn't great for money — you'd normally want to use integers or a decimal library for currency to avoid rounding issues over time. Not fully sure how big a deal that last one is in practice, but it's worth flagging. For tests, I'd write one that checks that going over budget stops the request from happening, and one that checks that the rate limiter blocks after the allowance is used up.

checklist: [communication] Frames the review around the security invariant a persisted-query store must hold — the hash is a CONTENT identifier, so the mapping is only trustworthy if the server proves `hash = SHA-256(query)` at registration — before diving into individual lines of code.

[problemSolving] Constructs the concrete attack to demonstrate severity: an attacker registers their own query under a hash the legitimate app is known to use; every later hash-only request from real clients now executes the attacker's query — cache poisoning that flips a bandwidth optimisation into an injection vector.

[technical] Prescribes the layered fix: verify `sha256(query) === hash` before every store write (restoring standard persisted-query semantics); then evaluates the stronger posture — a build-time trusted-document allowlist where the server ships with the only accepted hashes and rejects unknown ones, eliminating the registration path as attack surface entirely; also flags the unbounded store (add TTL/eviction).

[testing] Verifies both directions: a registration attempt with a mismatched hash/query pair must be rejected and must NOT overwrite an existing entry; a legitimate register-then-hash-only round trip still works; and an abuse test confirms junk registrations cannot evict or replace known-good mappings.

examples.text: So the core invariant of Automatic Persisted Queries is that the hash has to be a content identifier, not just an opaque key -- the whole protocol only works because the server is supposed to guarantee hash equals SHA-256 of the query text. Looking at `register(hash, query)`, it's literally `this.store.set(hash, query)` with zero verification that the hash the client sent actually matches that query. So I wouldn't approve this. Here's the concrete attack: I intercept or just directly call the register mutation with a hash I know the legitimate app uses for some benign query -- say a `getUserProfile` hash -- but I pair it with my own malicious query text, maybe one that walks a different resolver or dumps fields it shouldn't. Once my `register` call lands, every subsequent hash-only request from real clients, including ones that never talked to me, goes through `execute`, hits `store.get(hash)`, and now silently runs my query instead of theirs. That's cache poisoning -- an optimization meant to save bandwidth becomes an injection vector. The fix is layered: first, `register` must recompute `sha256(query)` and reject the write if it doesn't equal `hash`, restoring the actual APQ contract. That's the minimum bar. But I'd push further and ask whether we even need an open registration path -- a build-time trusted-document allowlist, where the server ships baked-in with the exact hashes it will ever accept and `execute` just rejects anything not on that list, removes registration as an attack surface entirely. Separately, that `Map` with no TTL and no eviction is an unbounded-growth issue on top of the security one -- worth flagging even if it's secondary. For tests I'd want: a register call with a hash that doesn't match the query gets rejected AND doesn't clobber an existing good entry for that hash; the normal register-then-hash-only round trip still works end to end; and an explicit abuse test where I try to overwrite a known-good hash with garbage and assert the store is unchanged afterward.

My first read of `register` is that it trusts the client-supplied hash outright -- `this.store.set(hash, query)` never recomputes the hash from the query, it just stores whatever pair it's given. That breaks the assumption the whole persisted-query mechanism depends on, which is that the hash is derived from the content, not asserted by whoever's calling register. Concretely, someone could call register with a hash the real frontend already uses and swap in their own query text, and from then on every hash-only call in `execute` for that hash returns the attacker's query, not the original one -- so it's poisoning the shared cache, not just a local bug. To fix it I'd add a check in `register`: hash the incoming query with SHA-256 and compare against the passed-in hash, throw if they don't match, before ever touching the Map. I'd also lean toward a trusted-document setup instead where the accepted hashes are baked in ahead of time so `register` isn't even an open door in production. I'd write a test for a mismatched hash/query pair being rejected, and one for the legit round trip still working. I didn't dig as much into the unbounded store growth, but it's probably worth a TTL too.

Looking at this, `execute` runs whatever query is sitting in the Map for a given hash, and `register` is the only place that Map gets written, via `store.set(hash, query)`. I think the risk is that nothing stops a bad hash/query pair from getting in there -- there's no check that the hash actually corresponds to the query, so in theory you could register something that doesn't match what the hash implies. That seems like it could let someone override an entry another client relies on, so persisted-query lookups by hash aren't necessarily trustworthy. The fix would be to validate the hash against the query before storing it. I'd also just double check that `execute`'s error path is sane -- looks fine, it throws PersistedQueryNotFound on a miss. For testing I'd add a case where you send a hash that doesn't match the query and make sure it's rejected, plus a normal happy-path test that register-then-execute works. I didn't think through the allowlist alternative or exactly how bad the blast radius is once one bad hash lands, and I glossed over the Map having no size limit.

This looks basically fine to me -- `register` stores the query under the hash, `execute` looks it up and runs it through `graphql()`, and there's a clean not-found error for cache misses, which matches how Apollo's persisted-query extension is supposed to behave. The main thing I'd flag is that `store` is a plain in-memory `Map` with no eviction, so on a long-running server it'll just keep growing, which could be a memory concern eventually -- maybe add some kind of LRU or max entries cap. I'd also ask whether this needs to be backed by Redis instead of an in-process Map if we're running multiple pods, since otherwise a hash registered on one instance won't be known to another. I'd want a couple of tests around the not-found path and the register-then-execute flow to make sure it behaves like standard APQ. Didn't really see anything wrong with what gets written into the store itself.

Yeah, this looks pretty solid to me, I'd approve it. It implements the standard APQ flow -- client sends a hash, if it's a miss the server says PersistedQueryNotFound, client resends the full query, register stores it, and from then on it's hash-only, which cuts down request size for repeat queries which is the whole point. The code is clean, `execute` properly awaits `graphql()` and passes through variables, error handling for the not-found case uses GraphQLError with the right extensions code so Apollo client will know to retry with the full query. Only real nitpick is maybe naming -- `store` could be a more descriptive name like `queryHashMap`. I don't see any correctness issues, the register/execute split maps cleanly onto the two request shapes APQ needs to support, and I'd just want to see it covered by the existing integration tests for the GraphQL module before merging, nothing new needed specifically for this file.

checklist: [communication] Explains the batch-window mental model before touching code: a batching loader only collapses keys that get registered WITHIN the same dispatch window into one call; anything that fully waits on one load before requesting the next closes that window early, one key at a time.

[problemSolving] Reads the evidence correctly: N single-key batch lines in the data-source log (instead of one multi-key lookup) is the fingerprint of broken batching, and traces the cause to the sequential wait inside the loop — not to the loader's own configuration or scope.

[technical] Gives the concrete fix: register every load BEFORE waiting on any of them — either let the per-element resolution return the loader's pending result directly so the engine schedules all N siblings within the same window, or explicitly gather every pending result together before waiting on the group — collapsing N sequential round-trips into exactly one batch; notes the per-request cache still deduplicates repeated keys on top of that.

[testing] Quantifies before/after: counts batch-log lines for the same nested query (N single-key lines collapsing to 1 multi-key line) and plots request latency against parent-list size (linear growth flattening out), then guards the fix with a regression check asserting "one batch per relation per request" over seeded data.

examples.text: So the loader itself is fine — the batch function does a single WHERE id IN lookup, it's scoped per-request, and the cache is wired up correctly. The problem is a mental-model issue: DataLoader only collapses keys into one batch if they're all registered within the same dispatch window — basically the same tick. The moment you do `await context.userLoader.load(post.authorId)` inside the for-loop and only move to the next post after that resolves, you're fully settling each load before the next `.load()` call even happens, so every key opens and closes its own window — you're effectively back to N+1 despite having a batching loader wrapped around it. That's exactly what the log line is telling us: seeing `[batch] users -> [id]` once per post instead of one line with all three ids is the fingerprint of batching being broken, and it lines up with the linear latency growth against post-list size — that's not a DB or config problem, it's the sequential await inside the loop. The fix is to fire every `.load()` call before awaiting any of them, so they all land in the same tick and DataLoader's scheduler groups them: `const authors = await Promise.all(posts.map(post => context.userLoader.load(post.authorId)))`, then zip the results back onto the posts. That collapses N round-trips into exactly one batch call regardless of list size. To verify, I'd count batch-log lines for this query and confirm it goes from N single-key lines to one multi-key line, then plot request latency against post-list size and expect it to flatten instead of growing linearly, and I'd lock it in with a regression test asserting 'one batch call per relation per request' over seeded data. Worth noting the per-request cache still dedupes if two posts share an author, but that's a separate concern from batching — it won't fix this bug on its own.

Looking at the loader config, that all looks right — single query, per-request scope, cache enabled, so it's not a configuration problem. The issue is in the resolver's for loop: `await context.userLoader.load(post.authorId)` blocks before moving on to the next post, so by the time the next `.load()` call happens, DataLoader has already dispatched and resolved the previous one. Each load basically gets its own turn instead of piling up together, so you end up with three separate single-key batches instead of one batch of three, which is exactly what the log is showing — one line per post. To fix it, I'd map over all the posts and call `.load()` on each without awaiting immediately, collect the promises, then `Promise.all` them together so every key is registered before any of them resolves. That should collapse it back down to a single batch call no matter how many posts there are, and the latency shouldn't keep climbing with list size anymore. I'd run it with a handful of posts afterward and check that the log line count drops to one instead of N.

So we've got a DataLoader on posts-to-author, and it's supposed to batch these lookups together. Looking at the resolver, it loops over posts and calls `userLoader.load()` for each one — my first thought is maybe DataLoader has some kind of batch window timeout, like it waits a few milliseconds to collect keys, and the loop with `await` in it is just slightly too slow so calls fall outside that window and each one dispatches on its own. It could also be something with the per-request cache expiring or not sharing state properly between calls, though the code does look like it's the same loader instance each time. Actually, thinking about it more — since there's an `await` right there inside the loop, that probably does mean each `.load()` call fully finishes before the next one even fires, so yeah, that would explain why they're not grouping. I'd change it so the loop doesn't await inside itself — maybe collect all the `.load()` calls first and then `Promise.all` them — so they get requested closer together. That should cut down on the number of separate batch calls, though I'm not 100% sure that's the whole story.

Yeah so the log is showing the users being fetched one at a time, so the loader isn't grouping them like it's supposed to. Maybe the batch size limit on the DataLoader needs to be increased, or there's something with the WHERE IN query not handling multiple ids correctly in this case. Another option — I could add a small delay before the batch fires so it has more time to collect requests, or honestly I might just skip DataLoader here and have the post service do a join in SQL directly so everything comes back in one query. I'm not totally sure why the loader isn't batching these together as-is, maybe it's something to do with how Apollo invokes the resolver separately for each post in the list.

Honestly the code looks fine to me — the loader's using WHERE id IN for the batch query, it's created fresh per request so there's no cache leaking across users, and the rowById map is built correctly before returning results. The resolver uses await which is just standard async/await for fetching data in Node, so I don't see anything wrong with the control flow there. If latency is climbing as the post list grows, that's probably just the database doing more work as there's more data to look up, or maybe the connection pool is undersized and requests are queuing. I'd look at adding an index on users.id — though that's already the primary key so it should already be indexed — or check if the Postgres query planner is doing something unexpected with the IN clause at larger sizes. It might also just be a scaling issue on the GraphQL side that isn't really about this loader specifically.

checklist: [communication] Frames the optimisation in terms of what APQ is supposed to buy — after a one-time register, every call carries a 64-character hash instead of the full query string — and shows the current setup structurally cannot deliver that beyond a single process.

[problemSolving] Connects the metrics to the topology: a ~75% PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND rate on 4 round-robin replicas is the arithmetic signature of per-process registries (a hit only when routing happens to land back on the registering replica), compounded by every restart wiping that replica's map.

[technical] Prescribes the fix: back the hash-to-query registry with a store shared across all replicas (Redis or equivalent) plus TTL/eviction so the registry stays bounded and survives restarts; then evaluates the stronger option — build-time trusted-document allowlists for first-party clients — which removes the miss storm AND the open registration surface entirely.

[testing] Validates with before/after metrics: the PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND rate drops to near-zero at steady state, the average request payload shrinks to hash-size, and a rolling-restart test confirms registrations survive replica churn; also load-tests the shared store so the extra lookup doesn't become the new bottleneck.

examples.text: So the whole point of Automatic Persisted Queries is a one-time cost: the client registers the full query string once, gets back a 64-character SHA-256 hash, and every call after that just sends the hash — you're trading a potentially multi-kilobyte query document for basically a hundred bytes. Looking at this code, that promise structurally can't hold here. The `persistedQueryCache = new InMemoryLRUCache()` is constructed inside `bootstrap()`, which means it's a plain in-process Map living in the memory of whichever single Node process happens to be running — and with 4 replicas behind a `ClusterIP` service with `sessionAffinity: None`, you've got four completely independent, unsynchronized copies of that registry. That maps exactly onto the numbers you gave me: with round-robin across 4 replicas, a hash-only request only succeeds if it happens to land back on the one replica that learned it during registration — that's a 1-in-4 hit rate, or a 75% `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` rate, which is precisely what you're seeing. And the near-100% spike after every deploy is the same mechanism compounding — a rolling restart wipes that in-memory map on whichever pods just cycled, so you briefly lose all four registries and every client has to re-register from scratch. The fix is to move the store out of process: swap `InMemoryLRUCache` for something backed by Redis — Apollo's cache interface is pluggable, so a `RedisCache` or similar KeyValueCache implementation shared across all 4 replicas fixes the topology problem directly, and you'd want a TTL plus eviction policy so it doesn't grow unbounded and actually survives individual pod restarts. If I wanted to go further, for first-party clients — your own web and mobile apps — I'd move to build-time trusted document allowlists: generate the hash-to-query manifest at build time, ship it as part of the deploy, and have the server validate against that pre-registered set instead of accepting arbitrary runtime registrations. That kills the miss storm entirely since there's no 'first call always misses' step, and it closes the security surface of letting anyone register arbitrary queries against your persisted-query cache. To validate, I'd want to see the `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` rate drop to near-zero at steady state, confirm average request payload size actually shrinks down toward hash-size in your metrics, and run a rolling-restart test — bounce all 4 pods one at a time — to prove registrations survive replica churn instead of evaporating. I'd also load-test the Redis path itself, since if that lookup becomes the new bottleneck under traffic you've just moved the problem rather than solved it.

APQ's whole value proposition is that after the client registers a query once and gets a hash back, every future call for that query just sends the hash instead of the full query text, so your payloads shrink a lot over time. The bug here is that `persistedQueryCache` is a fresh `InMemoryLRUCache()` created inside each server process at boot, and since we're running 4 replicas with `sessionAffinity: None`, each one keeps its own private copy — nothing is shared. So when a client registers on replica A, only replica A knows about it; the other three still miss. That lines up with the 75% miss rate — round robin across four replicas basically gives you a 1-in-4 chance of hitting the right one — and restarts make it worse because whichever pod cycles just forgets everything it had cached, so you get a burst of misses right after a deploy. To fix it I'd back the persisted query cache with Redis instead of the in-memory LRU cache so all four replicas read and write the same registry, and I'd set a TTL on entries so it doesn't just grow forever. That alone should fix cross-replica lookups and let entries survive individual pod restarts since Redis is external to any one process. I'd verify it by watching the `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` rate in monitoring after the change and confirming it drops a lot compared to the current 75%, and probably do a restart to double check the hashes are still there afterward.

APQ is supposed to let clients send a hash instead of the whole query after the first call, so it saves bandwidth. Looking at the code, the cache is `InMemoryLRUCache`, which is just in-memory, so it's local to whatever process it's running in. Since there are 4 replicas and the load balancer is round robin, they're probably not sharing that cache with each other, which would explain why the hash isn't found a lot of the time — the request might go to a different server than the one that has it cached. And restarts would probably wipe it out too since it's in memory. I think the fix is to use something like Redis instead of the in-memory cache so it's a shared store all the replicas can use, that should make it more consistent. I'd probably also add expiration on the entries so it doesn't get too big. To check it worked I'd look at the error rate for `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` and see if it's lower after switching to Redis, and maybe test it again after a deploy to make sure it still works.

So this is an APQ setup — I know APQ is about caching queries by hash so you don't have to send the full query every time, it's supposed to make things faster. The code sets up an `InMemoryLRUCache` for the persisted queries. I guess since it's in-memory, restarting the server would clear it out, and that could explain the failures after a deploy. With multiple replicas maybe there's some kind of sync issue too. To fix it, I would probably just increase the cache size or add some kind of shared cache like Redis so it's more reliable across the servers. For testing I'd just keep an eye on the error logs and see if the `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` errors go away after making the change, and maybe run it in staging for a bit to be safe.

Okay, so this is setting up an Apollo GraphQL server with Express — typeDefs, resolvers, the usual stuff. Persisted queries here are basically a caching layer so repeated identical queries don't have to be re-parsed by the schema every time, which speeds up resolution on the server side. Honestly a 75% `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` rate sounds like it's mostly a client-side issue — maybe the frontend isn't sending the hash correctly, or there's a version mismatch between what the client generated and what the server expects, so I'd probably start by checking the Apollo Client config on the frontend rather than this server file.
