checklist: [technical] Identifies that the dynamic playlist wrongly carries `s-maxage=31536000, immutable` — the static-asset directive — so a live/changing playlist is frozen at the edge for a year and viewers are stuck on a stale version with no natural recovery.

[problemSolving] Explains the correct dynamic strategy — a short `s-maxage` plus `stale-while-revalidate` so the cache stays near live state — and reserves long-TTL plus `immutable` for versioned static assets whose URL changes when the content changes.

[technical] Spots that throwing a hard 404 for an unknown key lets the edge cache that error response — a bare error status with no cache directive of its own is fair game for a shared cache's own caching policy — turning a transient miss into a sticky one; the origin should answer unknown keys with a non-cached or short-TTL fallback instead.

[communication] Frames the user-visible impact — viewers pinned to a stale playlist for up to a year, a briefly-missing key that looks permanently gone — rather than only diffing header values line by line.
[testing] Recommends an integration test asserting the exact `Cache-Control` per asset type and a second test asserting that unknown keys are not long-cached at the edge.

examples.text: So the core bug is right there in that if/else block — both branches set `res.setHeader("Cache-Control", staticCacheControl)`, which is `public, s-maxage=31536000, immutable`. That directive is fine for the `.ts` segments because their key is content-addressed — the URL changes when the bytes change, so caching them for a year and telling shared caches never to revalidate is safe. But the playlist branch got wired to the exact same header, and the `.m3u8` is the opposite of immutable — the packager rewrites it every few seconds. Once the edge caches that with `s-maxage=31536000, immutable`, it will serve that exact byte content for up to a year and never revalidate, which is exactly the 'stuck on a playlist that never updates' symptom QA is seeing. The fix is to split the branches back apart: playlist gets something like `public, s-maxage=2, stale-while-revalidate=10` — a short TTL so the edge stays close to live, plus stale-while-revalidate so you don't thunder the origin on every refresh — and keep the long `immutable` TTL reserved for the versioned segment URLs only. Second issue: the `if (!object) { res.sendStatus(404); return; }` branch sends a bare 404 with no Cache-Control header of its own, and a shared edge cache is free to apply its own default caching policy to an uncached error response — so a segment that's momentarily missing at publish time, maybe because the packager hasn't flushed it yet, gets cached as 'not found' at the edge and stays that way well past when the object actually exists. That should either set an explicit short-lived or no-store Cache-Control on the 404 path, like `Cache-Control: no-store` or `s-maxage=1`, so a retry a second later actually hits the origin again instead of a cached miss. For testing I'd write an integration test that hits the handler for a playlist key and a segment key and asserts the exact Cache-Control string per asset type — not just presence of a header, the literal s-maxage/immutable/stale-while-revalidate values — plus a second test that requests a key before it exists, then creates it, then requests again through the same cache layer and asserts the second request is not served the cached 404.

Looking at this, the caching header logic clearly got collapsed into one path during that refactor — the if/else for playlist versus segment both just call `res.setHeader("Cache-Control", staticCacheControl)` with the same immutable, year-long value. That's the root of the stale-playlist bug: `staticCacheControl` was designed for the versioned `.ts` segments where the URL itself encodes the content, so caching forever is safe, but the `.m3u8` playlist mutates in place every few seconds under the same key, so pinning it to `s-maxage=31536000, immutable` means the edge will never go back to origin for a fresh copy. The right fix is to give the playlist branch its own short-TTL policy, something with a small s-maxage and stale-while-revalidate so viewers stay near live without hammering the origin on every poll, and leave the long immutable caching only for the segment branch. On the 404 side, I also noticed the handler just does `res.sendStatus(404)` with no cache header when `store.get(key)` returns nothing — that's a bit risky at a shared edge since a plain error response can get picked up by the cache's default rules and stick around, which would explain segments that look permanently missing right after publish. I'd want to explicitly mark that response as short-lived or no-store to be safe. For verification, I'd add a test asserting the Cache-Control value per branch, and probably some kind of check that a not-found response doesn't get treated as long-lived by the cache.

The main thing I see is that both branches of the if/else end up calling the same `staticCacheControl` header, so the playlist and the segment get identical caching treatment even though the code comment says that immutable directive is meant for versioned assets. Since the playlist is supposed to update frequently, giving it a year-long cache is probably why viewers are stuck on an old version — I'd change that branch to use a much shorter cache time instead of the full year value. For the 404 case, the handler returns `res.sendStatus(404)` when the object isn't found, and I think that response might be getting cached somewhere, which could explain the 'not found' lingering after the file exists, though I'm not fully sure why a 404 would be cached if there's no Cache-Control on it. My fix would mostly be to just not use `immutable` for the playlist and maybe add some kind of retry or shorter expiry on the missing-key path. To test it I'd check what Cache-Control header comes back for a playlist request versus a segment request and make sure they're different, and maybe test hitting a missing key and then checking it again after it's created.

I think the issue is with the `classifyAsset` function — it decides whether something is a playlist or a segment based on the `.m3u8` extension, so if that logic is ever wrong the headers could get mixed up. Also the `Content-Type` header looks fine, `application/vnd.apple.mpegurl` for playlists and `video/MP2T` for segments, so that part isn't the problem. The cache header is set with `staticCacheControl` which has `immutable` in it, and immutable usually just means the browser won't re-request it, so maybe that's just a browser-side thing and not really an edge cache issue — I'd guess the real bug is more about the CDN configuration outside this file rather than the handler itself. For the 404 case, I'd probably just add some logging so we can see when a key comes back not found, and maybe retry the store.get call a couple times before giving up. I don't have a strong sense of how to test the caching part specifically, maybe just manually check the response headers in the browser dev tools after deploying.

Honestly this code looks pretty clean to me — it splits playlist and segment types, sets appropriate content types for each, and returns a 404 when the store doesn't have the key, which all seems like standard practice. I don't see an obvious bug in the caching logic itself; `s-maxage=31536000, immutable` is a pretty common long-cache pattern I've seen used for static CDN assets in general, so it's probably fine here too. If viewers are stuck on an old playlist, I'd guess that's more likely a client-side issue, like the video player not polling for the new playlist often enough, rather than something wrong in this origin handler. For the missing-segment problem, that sounds like it could just be a race condition in the packager writing files out of order, so I'd look at the publishing pipeline instead of this file. I'm not sure what specific tests I'd add here since I don't see a defect to target — maybe just general smoke tests that the endpoint returns 200 for existing assets.

checklist: [problemSolving] Diagnoses the waste: with no in-flight lock, N concurrent first-requests for a cold video each run the full three-rung ladder and race to overwrite each other's output — N times the CPU for one video.
[technical] Proposes coalescing: a per-videoId in-flight lock (or handing the encode off to a job queue) so only the first request actually transcodes and every other request awaits that single run.

[problemSolving] Reasons lazy vs eager: lazy saves CPU on clips nobody ever watches but makes the first viewer wait; eager makes the first play instant but wastes work on a long tail that's never watched — so eager-encode hot/likely content and keep lazy as the fallback for the tail.
[communication] States the metric that confirms the win: the count of duplicate encode runs (or CPU spent) per cold video dropping from N down to exactly one.
[testing] Suggests firing many concurrent encode requests for one fresh video id and asserting that exactly one encode run actually happens.

examples.text: So the actual bug isn't in the ffmpeg call itself, it's the gap between step 1 and step 2 — `objectStorage.exists(masterKey)` is just a read, there's no lock or claim on that videoId, so when dozens of requests for the same cold video land in the same second, every single one of them sees `alreadyEncoded === false` and falls into the for-loop over RUNGS. That means you're not paying for one 1080p/720p/480p ladder, you're paying for N of them concurrently — literally N times the CPU a single video's encode should cost — and on top of that they're all writing to the exact same `renditions/${videoId}/${rung}.ts` and master playlist keys at roughly the same time, so you've got a write race where whichever request finishes last wins and the others' work is just thrown away. The fix is to coalesce those requests: put a per-videoId in-flight lock — could be a Redis SETNX-style lock or an in-memory promise map — around the cold path, so the first request through actually kicks off the transcode and every other concurrent request for that same videoId just awaits that in-flight promise instead of starting its own ffmpeg run, or alternatively hand the whole thing off to a job queue where the request enqueues a job keyed by videoId and dedupes if one's already running. Beyond just fixing the storm, I'd also question the lazy-only design given this is a viral-content pipeline — lazy transcoding is great for the long tail of videos nobody ever watches because you never spend CPU on them, but it means your first viewer eats the full ladder latency, and for content that's trending or predicted to be hot you actually want to eager-encode at upload time so the first play is instant, keeping lazy as the fallback for everything else. To prove this actually fixed it I'd track the count of duplicate encode runs per cold video — that number should go from N down to exactly 1 — and I'd write a test that fires a bunch of concurrent `getOrCreateRenditions` calls for a brand-new videoId and asserts `ffmpegTranscode` only actually got invoked once per rung.

The problem is that the exists-check at the top is racy — there's nothing stopping two or ten requests from all checking `objectStorage.exists(masterKey)` at the same moment, getting `false`, and then all independently running the full three-rung transcode loop. So instead of one video costing one ladder's worth of CPU, it's costing however many concurrent first-requests showed up, and that lines up exactly with the CPU spike you're describing. To fix that I'd add some kind of lock keyed on videoId, so only one of those requests actually does the ffmpeg work and the rest just wait on it and reuse the result — could be a distributed lock in Redis, or if this is a queue-based system, push the encode job onto a queue and dedupe by videoId so the queue only processes it once. I'd also double check the write step at the end isn't stepping on itself since multiple writers to the same key is asking for corruption. To validate it, I'd want to see that after the fix, spamming the same cold video with concurrent requests only triggers one actual transcode run instead of one per request.

Yeah so looking at this, the issue is probably that the exists check and the actual encoding aren't atomic — like, request A checks, it's not there, request B checks at basically the same time, also not there, and now both of them are going through and doing the ffmpeg transcode for all three rungs. If that happens dozens of times for the same video that would definitely explain a CPU spike that's way more than what one video should cost. I think the fix would be some kind of locking so that only one request does the work — maybe like a mutex per video, or check again right before you start encoding. I'd probably also look at whether you can cache more aggressively or maybe pre-warm popular videos ahead of time so you're not hitting this cold path as often for stuff that's likely to blow up. Not totally sure what the best mechanism is here — Redis lock probably, or some kind of a queue.

I think the code is doing the transcoding synchronously inside the request handler, which seems kind of slow for something that spiked CPU that much. Maybe the ffmpeg step itself is just expensive for 1080p and doing it three times per video for the three rungs adds up, and if a bunch of requests come in around the same time for the viral video that's just naturally going to be a lot of ffmpeg calls stacking up. Maybe the CPU spike is just because the video is popular and popular videos naturally use more server resources, like more playback requests means more load on the CDN and server in general. I'd probably look at scaling up the transcoding fleet horizontally, adding more instances so it can handle bursts like this, or maybe put a CDN in front so requests don't hit the origin as much. Could also just be a hardware issue on the transcoding boxes, might be worth checking if they need better GPUs for the ffmpeg encode step.

checklist: [problemSolving] Diagnoses pollution: including utm_*/marketing query params in the URI key makes every share link its own entry, so identical content never HITs and the zone fills with duplicates.
[technical] Prescribes stripping non-content-affecting params from the cache key (and normalizing param order) so equivalent requests collapse to one entry.

[technical] Identifies Vary: Cookie as an unbounded explosion (one entry per session) that must be removed for a shared cache, and Vary: Accept-Encoding as needing normalization to a canonical encoding set.
[communication] Explains the mechanism linking key/Vary design to the HIT-ratio drop and origin-load rise, not just 'fix the config'.
[testing] Verifies by watching the HIT ratio / X-Cache-Status distribution recover after the key and Vary changes, and alerting on future drops.

examples.text: Two things shipped in the same deploy and they compound each other. First, the cache key: proxy_cache_key uses dollar-scheme dollar-request-method dollar-host dollar-request-uri, and request_uri includes the full query string. So playlist.m3u8 with utm_source=fb&utm_campaign=launch, the same path with utm_source=tw&utm_medium=social, and the bare playlist.m3u8 all hash to three different keys even though they're byte-identical responses from origin. Since these are share and campaign links, every click mints a slightly different utm combination, so you're generating a new cache entry per click instead of per asset — that's the bulk of the MISS storm on X-Cache-Status. Second, the new session middleware is mounted globally before any route, and it sets Vary: Cookie on every response, including the public manifest, segment, and thumbnail routes that never touch the session. Vary: Cookie tells the edge to cache one entry per distinct cookie value, and saveUninitialized true means almost every client gets a fresh session cookie, so that's an unbounded one-entry-per-visitor explosion stacked on top of the query param problem. There's also Vary: Accept-Encoding being appended on the raw client header string instead of a normalized set, so gzip, gzip-deflate, and gzip-br-with-quality-values all fragment further even though they should collapse to the same cached body. Fix: strip utm_* and any non-content-affecting params from the cache key — build a normalized key from the path plus a whitelist of params that actually change content, and sort remaining params so order doesn't matter. For Vary, these are public, non-personalized assets, so Cookie should never appear in Vary for them — scope the session middleware off those routes or explicitly strip Vary: Cookie before it reaches the cacheable response, and normalize Accept-Encoding to a canonical set like gzip or br before it hits the Vary/cache logic. To verify, I'd watch the HIT ratio and the X-Cache-Status distribution recover — MISS should drop back down and HIT should climb close to where it was before the deploy — and I'd set up an alert on HIT ratio dropping below a threshold so the next regression like this gets caught automatically instead of discovered from origin load spiking.

So looking at this, the cache key is built off request_uri which pulls in the whole query string, and the utm_* params from the campaign links mean the same manifest ends up under a bunch of different keys — one per link variant basically, so it never re-hits. That's the main driver of the MISS spike. Then on the origin side, the session middleware is global, app.use with no path scoping, and it stamps Vary: Cookie on every response including the public video assets — since every visitor gets their own session cookie, that turns into one cache entry per session instead of one shared entry for everyone. Between those two you get exactly the pattern ops is seeing, mostly MISS on requests that should be identical. The fix on the nginx side is to normalize the cache key so it ignores utm_source, utm_campaign, utm_medium and whatever other tracking params aren't affecting the actual bytes returned — just hash on path and maybe a small whitelist of real params. On the origin side, take Cookie out of Vary for these routes since they're not personalized, that middleware just shouldn't be adding Vary: Cookie for public content. I'd double check the Accept-Encoding Vary too since it's on the raw header, but that's a smaller piece. After applying that I'd expect the HIT ratio to come back up and origin load to drop.

checklist: [problemSolving] Uses the curl-works-but-browser-fails asymmetry to localize the fault to a browser-only constraint (CORS), not the encoding, the bytes, or the status code.
[technical] Identifies that the segment (.ts) response is missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin while the manifest has it, so the browser blocks the cross-origin segment fetch despite a 200 OK.
[technical] Gives the fix: set Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the segment response (and variant-playlist responses) — i.e. every HLS-serving endpoint, not just the manifest.
[communication] Articulates why a browser enforces CORS on fetch() while curl does not, so the identical server response behaves differently per client.
[testing] Verifies by loading in a real browser player (or asserting the ACAO header is present / no console CORS error) after the fix, not by re-running curl which never reproduced it.

examples.text: OK so the fact that curl gets a clean 200 with the right bytes on the exact same segment URL is actually the whole diagnostic clue — it tells me the server-side logic, the file read, the status code, the content-type, none of that is broken. curl doesn't enforce same-origin policy at all, it just makes a raw HTTP request and shows you whatever comes back. A browser is different — when hls.js does a fetch() or XHR for a cross-origin resource, the browser engine itself checks the response headers before handing the data to JavaScript, and if there's no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header matching the requesting origin, it blocks the response from ever reaching the player code, even though the network request itself succeeded and you'd see the 200 in the Network tab. So this is a browser-only enforcement layer, not a server bug in the traditional sense. Looking at the actual routes: the master.m3u8 handler explicitly does res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*'), which is exactly why the manifest loads and hls.js gets far enough to parse quality levels. But the variant .m3u8 route and the .ts segment route both skip that header — the comments even call it out, 'No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header set here.' So the manifest is a red herring that makes it look like CORS is 'handled,' when really it's only handled on one of three endpoints. The fix is to set Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and ideally Access-Control-Allow-Methods if you ever do range requests with preflight) on every HLS-serving endpoint — master manifest, variant playlists, and segments — not just the top-level manifest. I'd probably factor it into a shared middleware for the whole /hls router so nobody forgets it on the next endpoint they add. And to verify, I would not re-run curl — curl already proved this passes at the HTTP layer and will keep passing after the fix, so it tells me nothing new. I'd load the actual player in a real browser, check the Network tab for the ACAO header on the segment responses, and confirm playback advances past the first segment with no CORS error in the console.

The curl-vs-browser split is the key signal — curl doesn't care about origins, it just hits the URL and shows me the response, so a 200 with correct bytes means the file, the path, the status code are all fine. Browsers enforce CORS on top of that for fetch/XHR requests, hls.js is doing those under the hood for every segment, so even a fine response can get blocked before the JS ever sees it. Looking at the routes, the manifest handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * so it loads fine, but the variant playlist route and the segment route don't set that header at all — that's the gap. Fix is to add the ACAO header to the segment (and variant) responses too. I'd test it by opening the page in a browser and watching the video actually play instead of stalling, and checking DevTools doesn't show the CORS error anymore.

So curl works but the browser doesn't — that usually points to something the browser is doing that curl isn't, and CORS is a common one since it's a browser-side security thing. So probably the browser is blocking the segment request because of that missing header. I'd add Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the segment endpoint to fix it. Then I'd just refresh the page and see if it plays now.

checklist: [problemSolving] Separates "the HTTP call did not throw" from "the entry was actually evicted" — `{ purged: true }` only means no exception was raised while sending the PURGE request, not that a stored cache variant actually matched and got removed.

[technical] Explains the cache key is URI-only (`proxy_cache_key "$request_uri"`), but the PURGE request carried `Accept-Encoding`, so it targeted an encoding-specific variant that doesn't match the stored entry (a Vary mismatch, surfaced as a 412) and evicted nothing.

[technical] Gives the fix: send the PURGE request without `Accept-Encoding`, and make the edge ignore `Vary` (`proxy_ignore_headers Vary`) so exactly one cache entry is stored per URI and PURGE always matches it unconditionally.

[communication] Clearly distinguishes the origin (which only delegates the eviction via the PURGE verb) from the edge (which owns the actual cache-eviction decision) — doesn't conflate "the origin said purge" with "the edge did purge".

[testing] Verifies by asserting `X-Cache-Status` is `MISS` on the very next request through the edge after the corrected purge — not by trusting the handler's own optimistic `{ purged: true }` response body.

examples.text: So the response body `{ purged: true }` is basically a lie you can't blame on the handler — it only means the axios call didn't throw, not that a variant actually got evicted from the edge's cache store. Those are two completely different facts and the code conflates them. Looking at the NGINX config, `proxy_cache_key` is `$request_uri` only, so the key itself has no notion of encoding. But there's no `proxy_ignore_headers Vary` on that location, and the origin responses come back gzipped with `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, so NGINX stores a separate cache variant per encoding under the hood even though the logical key is URI-only. Now look at `purge()` in EdgeCacheService — it reuses the same `httpService` instance that `fetchManifest` uses for normal GETs, and that shared axios client has a default `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate` header baked in. That header rides along on the PURGE request too. So the PURGE is asking NGINX to evict the gzip-encoded variant, but depending on what got cached first, that may or may not be the variant editors are actually being served — this is a classic Vary mismatch, and NGINX's purge module typically comes back with a 412 Precondition Failed when it can't resolve a matching cache entry, not a clean success. The fix is two-pronged: on the NestJS side, send the PURGE with a stripped-down request — no `Accept-Encoding`, ideally a dedicated axios instance or explicit header override, not the shared content-fetching client. On the NGINX side, add `proxy_ignore_headers Vary;` to the location block so it stops honoring `Vary: Accept-Encoding` and only ever stores one entry per URI, matching what `proxy_cache_key` already claims. Structurally, NGINX is the one that owns cache eviction; the NestJS origin only sends the verb and trusts the edge's response — so the moment the edge can't match a key, 'purged' should never have been true in the first place. To actually verify this fix, I wouldn't trust the `{purged:true}` body at all — I'd hit the manifest URL right after the purge and check `X-Cache-Status` on that very next response; it needs to read MISS, then HIT on the one after. That's the only proof the stale entry is actually gone.

The bug is that `purge()` treats 'no exception thrown' as equivalent to 'the cache entry got evicted,' and those aren't the same thing — the try/catch only guards against network failures, it never inspects the actual status code coming back from NGINX. If you look at the cache config, the key is `proxy_cache_key "$request_uri"`, so on paper it's URI-only. But since there's no `proxy_ignore_headers Vary`, and the origin is sending gzipped responses with a Vary header, NGINX ends up caching per-encoding variants anyway. The PURGE request in the NestJS service goes out through the shared `httpService`, which has default headers including `Accept-Encoding`, so it's implicitly targeting one specific encoded variant. If that doesn't match what's actually stored, NGINX won't find anything to purge and will likely return an error status like 412 — but the code never looks at that, it just returns `{ purged: true }` as long as no exception happened. To fix it, I'd make the purge call not send `Accept-Encoding` at all, and add `proxy_ignore_headers Vary;` on the edge so there's only ever one cache entry per URI. I'd also want to check `res.status` in the purge handler rather than just relying on the promise resolving. For verification, checking the response headers on the next request through the edge — `X-Cache-Status` should flip to MISS — would confirm it actually worked instead of just trusting the handler's own return value.

I think the issue is a mismatch between what the origin thinks it purged and what NGINX actually has cached. The purge function catches errors and returns false only on exception, so as long as the HTTP call goes through it says `purged: true`, but that doesn't necessarily mean the entry was removed — NGINX could reject the purge with some kind of error status and the code wouldn't notice. Looking at the config, the cache key is just the request URI, but I don't see `proxy_ignore_headers Vary` anywhere, and the comments mention the origin sends gzip and a Vary header, so NGINX is probably caching multiple copies per URI based on encoding. If the PURGE request is going out with different headers than what was originally cached, it might not target the right variant. My guess is the shared HTTP client the purge method uses might be adding an Accept-Encoding header that wasn't part of the original cached response's fingerprint, causing this disconnect. To fix it, I'd probably strip unnecessary headers from the purge call and think about whether the Vary handling on the edge needs to be adjusted so purges reliably hit the cached entry. I'd test it by requesting the manifest again after a purge and seeing if I get fresh content instead of stale data.

Well, `{ purged: true }` is returned in the try block so I guess it's saying the purge worked, but the catch block would set it to false if there was an error, so functionally it looks correct to me on the surface. Maybe the problem is that the NGINX purge location only allows certain IPs — `allow 127.0.0.1` and `allow 10.0.0.0/8` — so maybe the NestJS service isn't running from an IP in that range and it's getting denied? That could explain the stale manifests. Or possibly the `inactive=60m` setting on the cache path means entries are kept around for an hour before NGINX even considers evicting them regardless of purge calls. I'd probably add more logging around the purge call to see what's happening, and maybe increase the cache zone size in case it's an eviction-under-memory-pressure issue. I'd suggest just calling the purge twice or adding a retry to be safe.

Honestly this looks like a caching bug but I'm not totally sure where. The NestJS code looks fine to me — it makes an HTTP request, catches errors, and returns whether it succeeded, that's a pretty standard pattern. Maybe the issue is that `proxy_cache_valid 200 302 10m` means cached items live for 10 minutes no matter what you do, so purging doesn't really do anything until that timer runs out naturally? Or it could just be a network latency thing where the purge request arrives before the origin finishes writing the new metadata, so there's a race condition somewhere in the deployment pipeline, not really in this code. I'd suggest just restarting the NGINX edge service whenever you republish a video, that should clear out whatever's stuck in the cache. Also maybe increasing `max_size=10g` would help since the cache might be too full and not accepting new writes correctly.

checklist: [problemSolving] Spots that cleanup now sits at the end of the try block, right after the upload succeeds — so any error thrown by the encoder or the upload routes control straight to the catch, and the two temp files (the downloaded source, the encoder output) are never deleted. Over repeated failures that leaks disk space toward exhaustion (ENOSPC), which eventually fails every transcode on the box.

[technical] Prescribes moving the cleanup calls back into a block that is guaranteed to run on every exit path — a `finally` clause, or a deferred cleanup registered immediately after the temp paths are computed and before any operation that can fail — so both temp files are removed on success AND failure alike, restoring the exact guarantee the pattern exists for.

[technical] Spots the second smell: the output key is still derived purely from the input path (its extension swapped for a fixed suffix), with no per-job namespace — so retrying a FAILED job with the same input path silently overwrites the previous attempt's artifact. Proposes namespacing the key with the job's own id so every attempt writes to an isolated location.

[communication] Orders the two findings by blast radius instead of listing them as equal-weight nits — names the silent temp-file leak as the higher-severity operational risk (it degrades the whole host over time and eventually takes down every job, not just the retried one), with the key collision as a narrower correctness bug that only bites on retry.

[testing] Suggests a failure-injection test — force the encoder step or the upload step to throw — and asserts that no temp files remain afterward and that each job's artifact key is unique, so the cleanup guarantee and the key-isolation guarantee are both verified rather than assumed.

examples.text: Two things jump out here, and I'd rank them by blast radius rather than treat them as equal nits. The bigger one first: the cleanup calls -- fs.unlink(sourcePath) and fs.unlink(outputPath) -- sit at the very end of the try block, right after storage.upload succeeds. That means they're only reachable on the happy path. If encoder.run throws on a corrupt input or a codec it doesn't support, or if storage.upload throws on a network blip or a bucket permission error, control jumps straight to the catch and both temp files under TMP_DIR are orphaned on disk. Because failed jobs get re-enqueued with the same inputPath, this isn't a one-off leak -- every retry of a flaky job downloads another copy of the source and produces another encoder output, and none of them ever get deleted. That's unbounded disk growth that eventually hits ENOSPC and takes down every job running on that worker, not just the one that keeps failing. The fix is to move the unlink calls into a finally block right after sourcePath and outputPath are computed, so they run on every exit path -- success, encoder throw, or upload throw -- restoring the guarantee that cleanup is supposed to give you. I'd probably use a small helper that swallows unlink errors individually (ENOENT if the file was never created) so a cleanup failure doesn't mask the original error. Second, narrower issue: outputKey is derived purely from job.inputPath -- swap the extension for '-720p.mp4' -- with job.id nowhere in that computation. Since retries reuse the same inputPath, a retried job writes to the exact same key as the previous attempt. If the first attempt partially uploaded a corrupt or truncated file before failing, or if two jobs race, the retry silently clobbers it -- there's no isolation between attempts. I'd namespace the key with job.id, something like a prefix or subfolder keyed by job.id before the -720p.mp4 suffix, so every attempt writes to its own location and nothing overwrites a previous run. For testing I'd write a failure-injection test that mocks encoder.run to throw and asserts the temp dir is empty afterward, another that mocks storage.upload to throw and asserts the same, and a third that runs the same job twice and asserts the two resulting output keys are different -- that verifies both the cleanup guarantee and the key isolation are actually enforced, not just assumed to work because the happy path looks fine.

The main problem is the fs.unlink calls for sourcePath and outputPath are inside the try block after the upload call, so they only run if everything succeeds. If encoder.run or storage.upload throws, we go to the catch, log it, rethrow, and the two temp files just stay on disk in TMP_DIR. Given that failed jobs get retried with the same job, this will keep happening on every retry of a bad job and slowly eat disk space until the box runs out and starts failing unrelated transcodes too. I'd fix it by wrapping cleanup in a finally block instead of leaving it at the end of try, so it runs whether we succeeded or threw. There's also a smaller issue with outputKey -- it's built from job.inputPath by swapping the extension, and it doesn't include job.id at all. So if a job fails and gets retried with the same inputPath, the retry writes to the same output key as before, which could overwrite a partial or bad upload from the failed attempt. I'd add job.id into the key somehow so retries don't collide. For testing, I'd add a test where I make the encoder throw on purpose and check that the temp files got cleaned up afterward, and maybe a test that runs the job twice and checks the output keys differ.

Looking at the try/catch, the cleanup with fs.unlink happens at the end of the try, so it only runs on success -- if something throws before that point the files aren't deleted. That's a leak I guess, temp files pile up over time. I'd move that into a finally so it always runs regardless of what happened in the try. I also noticed outputKey uses job.inputPath and not job.id, so retries would probably use the same key each time, which seems like it could be a problem if two attempts of the same job overlap or overwrite each other. Not totally sure how bad that is in practice but it's worth flagging. To test it I'd probably just run the function with a bad input and see if the temp folder still has files in it afterward.

I think the try/catch looks mostly fine, it does log the error and rethrow it, which is good for observability. One thing I'd maybe mention is that the cleanup happens near the end so if something fails super early, like right at download, the files might not even exist yet so there's nothing to clean up anyway. The output key thing with job.inputPath is a little unusual but path.extname and the regex replace look correct for swapping the extension, so I think the naming logic itself works fine. Testing-wise I'd just add a basic unit test that calls transcodeJob with a mock job and checks it doesn't throw.

Honestly this code looks pretty solid to me -- it downloads the file, runs the encoder, uploads the result, and cleans up after itself, all inside a try/catch with proper error logging before rethrowing, which is exactly what you want for a worker like this. The TMP_DIR constant and randomUUID for the file names are a nice touch too since it avoids naming collisions between concurrent jobs on the same machine. If I had to nitpick something I'd say maybe add more logging around the download and upload steps individually so you know which stage failed, and maybe use a config value instead of hardcoding '/tmp/transcode'. Testing-wise I'd just add the usual unit tests for the happy path, mock out storage and encoder and confirm the function resolves without throwing.

checklist: [problemSolving] Identifies the double-admit race: two concurrent admits both ZRANGE the same front N before either ZREM runs, so both SADD the same tokens — the same person is admitted to two checkouts.

[technical] Replaces read-then-remove with an atomic ZPOPMIN key N (one command that reads-and-removes the N lowest scores), so on a single-threaded engine each token is taken exactly once; if logic grows, wrap it in a Lua script.
[technical] Flags the missing EXPIRE on the admitted SET — abandoned grants never expire, permanently shrinking effective capacity; add a TTL sized by p99 checkout time so slots self-recycle.
[communication] Ranks the double-admit (correctness / downstream oversell risk) above the TTL leak (gradual capacity erosion) and explains the atomicity principle clearly.
[testing] Verifies: fire two concurrent admits and assert the admitted sets are disjoint (no token appears twice); check the admitted key has a TTL and abandoned grants disappear after it.

examples.text: So the core bug is in admit(n) itself, not anywhere else in the file. Step 1 does a ZRANGE to peek the front n tokens, and step 2 does a separate ZREM to delete them — those are two independent round-trips to Redis, not one atomic operation. The comment even says it, 'anything can happen to WAITING_KEY between step 1 and here.' Since the worker can fire from multiple app instances on the same 500ms interval, two admit(n) calls can both run their ZRANGE before either one's ZREM lands, so they read the exact same front-N tokens, and both end up SADD-ing the same shopper tokens into ADMITTED_KEY — that's your two-checkout-tabs bug, and it's a correctness bug, not a performance one, so I'd rank it as the P0 fix. The right fix is to replace the read-then-remove pair with ZPOPMIN WAITING_KEY n — that's a single command that atomically pops and returns the n lowest-score members in one round trip, so on Redis's single-threaded command execution each token can only be popped by one caller, full stop. If admission ever needs extra logic beyond a plain pop — like a capacity check against ADMITTED_KEY size — I'd wrap that in a Lua script via EVAL so the whole read-check-remove-insert sequence stays atomic server-side. Second issue, lower severity but still real: there's no redis.expire() anywhere for ADMITTED_KEY, and no per-member TTL either, so every abandoned checkout — someone who gets admitted and just closes the tab — permanently occupies a slot in that SET forever, which is exactly the 'shrinking capacity over time' symptom. I'd add an EXPIRE sized around your p99 checkout completion time, or even better, track each admission as its own short-lived key so slots self-recycle instead of the whole set expiring as one unit. For testing, I'd write a concurrency test that fires two admit(n) calls at literally the same time and assert the two returned token arrays are disjoint — no shopper should appear in both — and a second test that checks the admitted key actually carries a TTL and that entries fall off after it expires.

The main thing jumping out is that admit() reads with ZRANGE and then removes with ZREM as two separate calls, and since this thing gets triggered from multiple instances concurrently, two calls can both read the same front-n tokens before either one removes them — that's your double-admit, same person landing in two checkouts. The fix is to swap those two steps for ZPOPMIN, which pops and returns in one atomic command so nobody can double-read the queue. I'd call that the higher priority issue since it's a real correctness bug affecting checkout, versus the second thing I noticed, which is that ADMITTED_KEY never gets an expire set on it, so slots that were granted but never used just sit there forever and your usable capacity keeps shrinking. I'd add an EXPIRE on that key based on how long checkout normally takes. To verify the fix I'd run two admits at once and check nobody shows up in both result arrays.

Looking at admit(), I think the issue is that it's not thread-safe when called concurrently — the ZRANGE and ZREM are two different Redis calls so if the worker runs on multiple instances at the same time you could get overlap and grab the same shoppers twice. Maybe adding some kind of lock around the whole function, like a distributed lock with Redlock or something, would fix that so only one instance runs admit() at a time. As for the capacity shrinking, I'm guessing it's related to the admitted set just growing and never being cleaned up — probably need some kind of cleanup job or expire on it, though I'm not 100% sure how to size that. I'd probably rank the double-admit as worse since users are actually seeing it. I don't have a concrete test plan beyond just running admit multiple times and checking manually.

I think the code looks mostly fine, it's using Redis commands correctly for a sorted set and a set. Maybe the bug is that zrange and zrem should be wrapped in a try/catch in case one of them fails, so tokens don't get lost. For the capacity issue, maybe there's a memory leak somewhere, could be worth checking the Redis instance's memory config. I'd probably add some logging to see what's happening. Not totally sure why it'd double-admit someone though, the code does remove tokens after reading them so it seems like it should work in most cases.

Honestly this code looks fine to me, I don't see anything broken here. It's using ioredis correctly, connects to Redis, has a join function and an admit function, standard stuff. Maybe the double-admit thing is a frontend bug, like the UI just showing the checkout page twice by accident, not really a backend problem. For the capacity shrinking maybe you just need to buy more Redis memory or scale up the instance. I'd probably just add some console.log statements to see what's going on and go from there, this doesn't really look like a hard problem.

checklist: [problemSolving] Explains that the hot single-row lock serializes all writers, so any extra work done inside the `FOR UPDATE` section multiplies every waiter's queue time and drives lock waits into statement/transaction timeouts.

[technical] Shrinks the critical section to the minimum — lock, check, subtract, append ledger, commit — moving the pricing call, remote logging, and non-essential SELECTs OUTSIDE the transaction (before acquiring the lock or after commit).

[technical] Offloads the spike to the atomic in-memory counter (the Lua decrement) for the hot path and reconciles to the durable locked row asynchronously, so the database is not the throughput bottleneck during the peak.

[testing] Measures before/after: p99 latency and lock-wait/timeout rate under a concurrent burst on one SKU, confirming throughput rises and timeouts drop while final stock stays correct and non-negative.

[communication] Presents the two fixes as two distinct levers, not one blur: trimming the critical section lowers the cost paid per transaction while every writer still queues behind the row lock, whereas offloading to the atomic counter removes the database from the hot path entirely — states clearly which lever buys what.

examples.text: So the core issue is that SELECT stock FROM skus WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE takes a row lock on that one SKU, and everything you do before COMMIT — the pricingService.getPrice call, the products and customers SELECTs, the auditLog.emit — all runs while that lock is held, so every other buyer hitting the same SKU queues up behind you, and it's that queueing that turns into p99 lock-wait and statement timeouts, not the arithmetic itself. First fix: shrink the critical section down to lock, check currentStock < qty, UPDATE skus SET stock = stock - $1, insert into stock_ledger, commit — and move the pricing call, the product/buyer lookups, and the audit emit either before BEGIN or after COMMIT, since none of them need the row lock to be correct. That lowers the cost each transaction pays, but every writer still serializes through Postgres one at a time on that row. To actually survive a spike on one hot SKU I'd pull the fast path out of the database entirely — an atomic in-memory counter, like a Redis Lua script doing a check-and-decrement — as the hot path, and reconcile that against the durable locked row asynchronously, so the database isn't gating throughput during the peak. I'd validate with a load test hammering one SKU concurrently, comparing p99 latency and lock-wait/timeout rate before and after, and confirming final stock stays correct and never negative — and I'd present these as two separate levers: trimming the critical section lowers what each transaction pays while everyone still queues on the lock, whereas the atomic counter removes the database from the hot path altogether.

Looking at decrementStock, the FOR UPDATE lock on the sku row is what's serializing everyone, and since the pricing call, the product/customer selects, and the audit log emit all happen between the lock acquisition and the update, every concurrent buyer is stuck waiting behind all of that extra latency, not just the actual decrement. I'd move pricingService.getPrice, the productResult and buyerResult queries, and auditLog.emit outside the transaction — pricing and audit clearly don't need to be inside the lock — so the critical section becomes just lock, check stock, update, write to stock_ledger, commit. That should shrink how long each transaction holds the row lock and reduce the timeout rate significantly. For the actual flash-sale spike I'd also want something like an in-memory atomic counter sitting in front of Postgres so the hot path isn't hitting the row lock at all, though I'd need to think more about how to reconcile it back to the database reliably. I'd check the fix worked by watching p99 latency and timeout counts during a concurrent burst test on one SKU.

The problem is the lock is held too long — while you're holding FOR UPDATE on the stock row, you're also calling out to the pricing service and doing a couple of extra SELECTs and an audit log write, and all of those take time over the network, so the lock stays held longer than it needs to. I'd try to move some of those calls out of the transaction, like the pricing lookup, since it doesn't really need the lock to run. That should help with the timeouts because each transaction finishes faster and clears the lock sooner. I'd probably also add some caching or retry logic around the pricing call so it doesn't add as much delay. If I tested it with a bunch of concurrent requests on the same SKU I think it would hold up noticeably better than now.

checklist: [problemSolving] Quantifies the real cost: pulling the whole sorted set and scanning for the token is an O(N) operation that also ships every member across the wire on every single call — multiplied by a million-deep queue and every waiting visitor polling every few seconds, this is what saturates both Redis CPU and network, not the business logic of "find my position".

[technical] Replaces the full-scan lookup with the sorted set's own rank operation — an O(log N) skip-list walk that returns the index directly, with no scanning and no transferring of the member list (exposed as a 1-based position).

[technical] Reduces poll pressure further on top of the O(log N) fix: check the admitted set first with an O(1) membership lookup so already-admitted visitors short-circuit before ever touching the queue, and widen the client poll interval (or return an estimated wait) so a million clients are not hammering the endpoint every few seconds.

[testing] Benchmarks position-lookup latency and Redis CPU/network utilization at roughly a million members under concurrent polling, before and after the change, to confirm the per-poll cost actually drops from O(N) to O(log N) rather than trusting that the fix "looks right".

[communication] States the diagnosis as two distinct costs paid on every single poll, not one vague "it's slow": the CPU cost of walking and serializing the whole skip list, and the network cost of shipping that entire member list over the wire — and is explicit that the rank-based fix removes both, not just one.

examples.text: So the core problem is that ZRANGE(0, -1) pulls back every single member of the sorted set on every poll — that's O(N), and it's also serializing and shipping the entire member list over the wire just to find one token, not the O(log N) lookup this should be. With up to a million visitors sitting in that ZSET and every one of them polling getQueuePosition every three seconds, you're multiplying that full-set fetch-and-scan by hundreds of thousands of requests a minute — that's exactly what's saturating both Redis CPU and the network, it's not the indexOf() itself that's expensive, it's dragging the whole set back before you even get to scan it. The fix is to swap the ZRANGE-plus-indexOf for ZRANK on waitingRoomKey — sorted sets maintain an internal skip list, so ZRANK does an O(log N) walk and hands you the index directly, no scanning, no member-list transfer, just add one for the 1-based position. On top of that, handleGetQueuePosition currently skips the admittedKey check entirely, so even an already-admitted visitor pays the full scan — I'd add an O(1) SISMEMBER check against admittedKey first so those requests short-circuit before touching the queue at all, and I'd widen POLL_INTERVAL_MS or have the endpoint return an estimated wait so a million clients aren't hammering it every three seconds. Before calling it done I'd benchmark position-lookup latency and Redis CPU/network at roughly a million members under concurrent polling, before and after, so I can actually show the per-poll cost dropped from O(N) to O(log N) instead of just assuming the rewrite helped.

The problem is that zrange(waitingRoomKey, 0, -1) pulls the entire sorted set back into the app on every call — that's O(N), and with up to a million people in the queue that's a huge amount of data crossing the wire on every single lookup, on top of the indexOf scan after it. Since every waiting client is polling every few seconds, you're repeating that full-set transfer constantly, and that's what's saturating both Redis CPU and the network, not the actual position logic. The fix is ZRANK — Redis computes the rank straight off the skip list structure in O(log N), so instead of fetching and scanning the whole member list yourself you just ask Redis for the index directly and add one to it for the 1-based position. That alone should cut both the CPU work and the network payload dramatically. I'd want to load-test this — seed something close to a million entries and compare latency and Redis resource usage between the old zrange approach and the new ZRANK version — to confirm it actually holds up at that scale before shipping it.

Yeah, pulling back the whole set with zrange every time is expensive, especially once you've got close to a million visitors in there — that's a lot of data moving every time someone polls. I think the main issue is it doesn't scale, it's basically linear against the queue size. One thing I'd look at is caching the position for a few seconds so we're not hitting Redis on every single poll, or maybe just spacing out how often clients are allowed to check. I also noticed there's an admitted set that this function doesn't really use — that seems like it should probably be checked somewhere too. If we ran a load test with something close to real traffic I'd expect we'd see it's a lot faster once we're not fetching the full list every time, though I'm not 100% sure what the Redis command would be to avoid that.

We could probably scale Redis horizontally, put it behind a cluster, or add a cache layer like a CDN in front of the API so not every request even reaches Redis. Maybe we add some rate limiting on the client side, or bump up the Redis instance size so it has more CPU to handle the load. I'd add some basic monitoring or logging around this endpoint so we can see how many requests are coming in.

Honestly I don't really see a bug in the logic here — getQueuePosition correctly finds the token and returns the right index, and it still throws if the token isn't found, so the function itself looks correct to me. checklist: [problemSolving] Traces the lost update: two concurrent transactions both findOne the same stock, both subtract, both save — the second overwrites the first, so total decremented exceeds real stock and oversells.

[technical] Explains a plain transaction under Read Committed does NOT serialize a read-modify-write on the same row; you need SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (lock: pessimistic_write) so the second reader blocks until the first commits.

[technical] Gives the exact fix: add lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } to the findOne so it emits SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, keeping the critical section short (lock, check, subtract, append ledger, commit).

[communication] Articulates the difference between an atomic transaction (all-or-nothing commit) and serialized access to a row (mutual exclusion) — the transaction gave the former, the lock is needed for the latter.
[testing] Verifies with a parallel burst (e.g. 200 concurrent decrement-by-1 on stock 100) and asserts exactly 100 succeed and final stock floors at 0, never negative.

examples.text: So walking through this line by line — the transaction wraps the findOne, the subtract, and the two saves, so it looks atomic, but atomic isn't the same as serialized. Under the default Read Committed isolation, that `manager.findOne(Stock, { where: { productId } })` is a plain SELECT with no lock. So picture two buyers hitting it at nearly the same time: transaction A reads quantity 100, transaction B also reads quantity 100 before A has committed. Both pass the `stock.quantity < qty` check, both compute 100 - 1 = 99 in memory, and both call `manager.save(stock)`. Whichever commits last just overwrites the other's row with its own stale 99, so you've effectively lost one of the decrements — that's a classic lost-update. Multiply that by 200 concurrent requests against a stock of 100 and you get exactly the oversell you're describing, because the ledger rows in StockLedger still get appended correctly, but the Stock.quantity itself doesn't reflect all of them. The fix is to turn that findOne into a locking read: `manager.findOne(Stock, { where: { productId }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } })`, which TypeORM compiles into `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. That makes the second transaction's read block until the first one commits or rolls back, so it sees the already-decremented value and correctly throws OutOfStockException once stock hits zero. I'd keep everything between the lock and the commit as short as possible — just the check, the subtract, and the ledger write — so we're not holding row locks any longer than necessary under flash-sale load. And to actually prove it's fixed, not just theoretically fixed, I'd write a test that fires 200 concurrent decrementStock(productId, 1) calls against a seeded stock of 100, then assert exactly 100 resolve successfully, the other 100 throw OutOfStockException, and the final quantity lands at exactly 0 — never negative.

The bug is a lost update. The transaction guarantees the read, the subtract, and the two saves either all commit or all roll back together, but it doesn't stop a second transaction from reading the row before the first one finishes. So with two requests running concurrently, both do `findOne` on the same Stock row, both see the same quantity, both subtract their qty in application memory, and both save — the second save just clobbers whatever the first one wrote. That's how you end up with more decrements going through than the stock actually allows. The engineer's mental model is wrong: 'wrapped in a transaction' only buys you atomicity of that transaction's own writes, it says nothing about isolation from other transactions reading the same row concurrently under the default isolation level. To fix it you need to make the read block concurrent readers — a pessimistic write lock on that findOne, so it turns into a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and the second transaction has to wait for the first to commit before it can even see the row. Once that's in place the second reader will see the already-decremented quantity and correctly fail if it's not enough. I'd also want to load-test it with a burst of concurrent requests against a small stock number to confirm the final count never goes negative before calling it done.

I think the issue is some kind of race condition on the stock row — two requests are probably reading the same quantity at the same time and both think there's enough left, so they both subtract and both go through, which is why you end up below zero. The transaction is supposed to prevent that, but it seems like it's only protecting the commit itself, not really stopping two transactions from touching the row at the same time. So I'd guess the fix is to add some kind of locking around the read — maybe a row lock, or serialize access somehow — so that only one request can be modifying that stock row at a time. TypeORM has locking options you can pass into findOne for this, I believe there's a pessimistic lock mode you can set. I'd also want to double check the isolation level the transaction is running at, since I know Postgres defaults to Read Committed, which might not be strict enough here. To confirm it's fixed I'd probably just try running a bunch of requests against it and see if the stock ever goes negative.

Yeah, under heavy concurrent load, database transactions can sometimes have race conditions, so probably that's what's happening here with the 200 requests coming in at once. I'd guess adding some retry logic or maybe a queue in front of the endpoint would help smooth it out so requests aren't all hitting the database at exactly the same time. It could also just be that the connection pool is too small and requests are getting weird interleaved behavior because of that, so bumping up the pool size might reduce how often it happens. I'm not totally sure why the transaction alone doesn't stop it, but I'd probably try wrapping the whole thing in some kind of lock or mutex on the application side as a safety net. Honestly I'd want to look at the actual database logs under load to see what's really going on before committing to a fix.

Honestly the code looks fine to me — it's inside a `this.dataSource.transaction()` block, and the whole point of a transaction is that it's all-or-nothing, so if something fails it rolls back and nothing bad should happen. My guess is this is actually a frontend issue, like the checkout button isn't getting disabled after the first click, so users are double-submitting orders, or maybe it's a caching problem where the frontend is showing stale stock numbers to more people than there actually is stock for. I don't see anything wrong with decrementStock itself — the OutOfStockException is right there guarding against negative stock, so if it's still going negative I'd suspect it's something outside this file entirely, maybe a different service also writing to the Stock table, or a webhook that's firing twice. I'd probably start by adding more logging around the checkout flow and maybe increasing the database connection pool in case it's just timing out under the 200 concurrent requests.

checklist: [problemSolving] Names exactly why splitting the guard into a read then a conditional write reopens the race the idempotency key was meant to close: two concurrent callers can both read "no key yet", both pass the check, and both proceed to create an order.

[technical] Replaces the two-step guard with a single atomic claim — one `SET key PENDING NX EX 30` — so that among any number of concurrent callers exactly one succeeds (first-wins, returns OK) and every other caller is told the key already exists.

[technical] Explains how the losing caller then tells in-flight apart from finished: a follow-up read of the key shows either the winner is still processing (respond with a conflict) or has already cached a result (replay it) — never a blind retry of the write.

[communication] Clearly separates "checking and claiming as one uninterruptible command" from "reading then writing as two round trips", and states plainly why only the former closes the window a concurrent second caller could step into.

[testing] Verifies with two concurrent same-key requests (widening the processing window if needed): exactly one call creates the order, the other is rejected or replayed, and the database ends up holding exactly one row — with a database-level uniqueness constraint standing behind Redis to catch anything that still slips past it.

examples.text: So the bug is right there in the split between step 1 and step 2. `redis.get(idempotencyKey)` and `redis.set(idempotencyKey, "PENDING", "EX", 30)` are two separate round trips to Redis, and nothing holds the lock in between. So picture two requests with the same idempotency key landing within a millisecond of each other during the flash sale: both call GET, both get back null because neither has claimed the key yet, both pass the `if (existing)` check, and both fall through to the plain SET and then both call `ordersRepository.create`. That's exactly the race the idempotency key was supposed to prevent — the check and the claim aren't a single operation, so there's a window between 'nobody has this key' and 'I've claimed this key' where a second caller can walk right through. The fix is to collapse steps 1 and 2 into one atomic command: `redis.set(idempotencyKey, "PENDING", "EX", 30, "NX")`. NX means set-if-not-exists, and Redis guarantees that among any number of concurrent callers, exactly one of those SET NX calls returns 'OK' — that's the winner — and every other caller gets back null immediately, atomically, no separate read needed. Now for the caller that loses: they shouldn't just retry the write, because that would just get NX-rejected again or, worse, overwrite a real result. Instead they do a GET on the key — if it's still "PENDING", the winner hasn't finished yet, so return the conflict/retry-later response; if it's a JSON blob, the winner already finished and cached the result, so parse it and replay that exact order back to the client instead of hitting the repository again. And I'd want to actually prove this fixes it, not just trust the code read — spin up two concurrent calls to `createOrder` with the same key, maybe artificially widen the window between the SET NX and the repository call to make the race reliably reproducible in a test, and assert that `ordersRepository.create` only ran once and the orders table ends up with exactly one row. I'd also put a unique constraint on the idempotency key column in the orders table itself as a belt-and-suspenders check, because if Redis ever loses that key — eviction, restart, whatever — the database is the last line of defense against a duplicate row.

The problem is that the guard used to be one atomic thing and now it's two: a GET to check, then a separate SET to claim. Between those two calls there's a gap, and under real concurrency two requests can both do the GET, both see nothing there, and both think they're the first to claim the key — so they both proceed into `ordersRepository.create` and you end up with two orders for one idempotency key. The way you close that is to make the claim itself the check, using `SET idempotencyKey "PENDING" EX 30 NX` — with NX, only the very first caller gets 'OK' back, everyone else gets nothing, so there's no window where two callers can both think they own the key. For whoever loses that race, you don't want to just fail them silently — you read the key again, and if it says PENDING you tell them there's a conflict/to retry shortly, and if it's already got the cached JSON result you just return that instead of re-doing the work. I'd want to verify this with a couple of requests hitting the same key at the same time to make sure only one order gets created.

I think the issue is the GET and the SET are two different Redis calls now instead of being combined, so there could be a timing issue where two requests both check at almost the same time before either one has actually written anything, and that's how you'd get two orders. Before it was probably one command that did the check-and-set together so it couldn't be interrupted, and now that it's split, another request can sneak in during that gap. To fix it I'd go back to using an atomic Redis operation for the claim step, something like SET with NX so it only succeeds if the key isn't already there — that way if two requests race, only one of the SETs actually goes through. For the one that doesn't get the lock, I guess you'd need to handle that case, maybe return an error or check again a bit later to see if the result is ready and give that back instead of trying to create the order again.

Looking at the code, there's a GET and then a SET, so I guess if those happen too close together something could go wrong, maybe a race condition between them. I'd probably just add a lock around the whole function or use a mutex so only one request can run createOrder at a time, that should stop duplicates. For the request that doesn't get the lock, maybe just have it wait and try again after a short delay until the first one finishes.

Honestly the code looks fine to me — it checks Redis first, and if there's nothing there it goes ahead and creates the order, which seems like the right idempotency pattern. If duplicates are getting created under load, I'd guess it's more of a database performance issue, like maybe the connection pool is too small and `ordersRepository.create` is timing out and getting retried by the client, or the 30-second expiry on the PENDING key is just too short for a flash sale so it's expiring before the order finishes and letting a new request in. I'd probably start by increasing the Redis TTL and maybe adding more database connections, and see if that resolves it before changing the order-creation logic itself.

checklist: [technical] Flags the missing body fingerprint: store a hash of the request body with the cached result; on a duplicate key with a DIFFERENT fingerprint return 422 (incorrect key reuse), never silently replay the old answer nor process the new body.

[problemSolving] Flags fail-open on Redis errors as wrong — it lets every request through, collapsing to no guard; prefer fail-closed (degrade UX) so the DB UNIQUE constraint still enforces correctness.
[technical] Points out the raw unique-violation should be caught and converted to a replay — re-read the existing order and return it — not surfaced as a 500.
[communication] Prioritizes the findings by blast radius (duplicate charges / wrong replay first) and frames them under defense-in-depth rather than nitpicking style.
[testing] Suggests tests: same key + changed amount returns 422; Redis-down still yields exactly one order via the DB constraint; crash-after-insert retry replays instead of 500.

examples.text: Okay, walking through this by blast radius. The scariest one is at the top: `redis.get(cacheKey)` returns the cached response and replays it unconditionally — there's no fingerprint of the original request body stored alongside it, so if the same Idempotency-Key ever gets reused with a different body, say a different amount or item list, we just silently hand back the old order's response instead of rejecting it. I'd store a hash of the body next to the cached result, and on a hit, compare fingerprints — if they match, replay; if they don't, return a 422, because that's a client bug or a key collision, not something we should paper over. Second, the catch block around the Redis call: on a Redis error we log and fall through as if there was no cached entry, which means during any Redis outage the fast-path guard just disappears and every request proceeds straight to the DB — that's fail-open, and it defeats the purpose of having the guard at all. I'd flip that to fail-closed, degrade gracefully — maybe a 503 or a controlled retry — and lean on the DB UNIQUE constraint as the real backstop rather than pretending Redis being down means no guard is needed. Third, `db.insertOrder` on a duplicate key is going to throw the unique-violation, and nothing here catches it, so it bubbles up as a raw 500 — instead that catch should detect the unique-violation code, re-read the existing order by idempotency key, and return that as a 200/201 replay, same as the cache-hit path. For tests I'd want: same key with a mutated amount returns 422, Redis down still produces exactly one order end-to-end because the DB constraint holds, and a crash right after insert but before caching, on retry, replays the existing row instead of 500ing.

So a few things jump out, roughly in order of how bad they'd be in production. The biggest one: the cache path just does `JSON.parse(cached)` and returns it with no check that the body matches what was cached originally — there's no fingerprint stored, so a reused key with a different payload gets the old response back, which is silently wrong. That needs a body hash stored with the cached value, compared on lookup, and a 422 if they don't match. Then the Redis-down branch worries me too — it logs a warning and just continues, so every request sails through to the DB during an outage, which basically means the idempotency guard doesn't exist for as long as Redis is unhealthy; I'd rather fail closed there. And the unique-constraint violation on `insertOrder` isn't handled at all, so a legit retry racing the first request just gets a 500 instead of the order it's actually waiting for — that should be caught and turned into a replay by re-fetching the row. I'd probably also want a test for the Redis-down scenario making sure only one order lands in the DB, though I didn't get as far as writing out the exact test list.

Looking at this, the main issue I see is the error handling — when Redis throws, it just logs and moves on, so requests keep going to the database anyway. That's probably fine actually, since the DB has the unique constraint as a backstop, so worst case is just an extra DB hit, not a correctness problem I think. The bigger thing is that duplicate insert case — if two requests come in with the same key at the same time, the second one is going to hit the UNIQUE constraint and just crash with a 500, which is bad because the client did nothing wrong, they're just retrying like they're supposed to. That should probably be caught and turned into just returning the order that already exists instead of erroring. I'd also flag that the code caches the response but doesn't really validate anything about what's being cached — feels like there's a gap there but I'm not 100% sure what the exact fix would look like without more context on how the fingerprinting would work.

I think the code is mostly reasonable for what it's trying to do — Redis for the fast path, DB constraint as the fallback, that's a pretty standard idempotency pattern. One thing that stood out is the try/catch around the Redis call — feels a little heavy for just a cache lookup, might be simpler to just let it throw honestly. I'd probably also rename `cacheKey` to something more descriptive and maybe pull the response-building object into its own helper function since it's constructed twice. The `insertOrder` call could maybe use a try/catch too just to be safe, in case something goes wrong there, though I'm not totally sure what error would come up in practice.

Overall this looks pretty solid to me — it's using Redis for speed and has a UNIQUE constraint in the database as a backup, which covers the idempotency requirement pretty well. Types look clean, the `CreateOrderBody` interface is defined properly, and I like that they're using `idempotency-key` from headers which is the standard convention. Maybe I'd add some more comments explaining what idempotency means for someone newer to the codebase, and possibly switch `console.log` style logging to something more structured, though it looks like they're already using a logger which is good. I don't see any blocking issues here, this seems ready to ship as is.

checklist: [technical] Names the decay defect precisely: incrementing the demand counter with no TTL/expiry on the key accumulates from the start of the day, so a cell that was busy at lunch pins at the surge cap and never cools even after real demand has dropped — the multiplier reflects a daily running total, not current pressure.

[problemSolving] Proposes a time-windowed demand signal instead of an unbounded counter — a TTL on the key (e.g. expire after ~60s) or a real sliding window — so old demand ages out and the multiplier tracks recent pressure rather than a cumulative total.

[problemSolving] Flags the static supply baseline as a separate defect: a hard-coded constant cannot represent how many drivers are actually free in a cell right now; proposes deriving supply from a live signal (a per-cell available-driver count) instead.

[communication] Prioritizes correctly: names the demand-decay bug as the more urgent, user-trust-critical issue (riders get overcharged for demand pressure that has already passed) and keeps it clearly separate from the supply-modelling improvement.

[testing] Proposes a concrete test: drive a cell's quotes up to the cap, stop generating demand, advance the clock past the TTL/window, and assert the next quote's multiplier has fallen back toward 1.0.

examples.text: The core bug is in getSurgeMultiplier and recordDemand together: `demand:${cellId}` is an INCR with no TTL, no expiry, nothing that ages it out. That key just accumulates forever from whenever it was first created — realistically since midnight or since the process started. So if a cell got slammed during lunch rush, that counter sits at whatever it climbed to and never comes back down, even an hour later when nobody's requesting rides there. Once demand crosses AVERAGE_DRIVERS_PER_CELL times SURGE_CAP, you're pinned at 3.0x forever because Math.min just keeps clamping to the cap — the multiplier is reporting a daily running total, not what's happening right now. That's the more urgent bug because it directly overcharges riders for demand pressure that's already gone — that's a trust and possibly a legal/regulatory issue, way worse than a supply-modeling inaccuracy. Fix: don't use a bare INCR, use something time-windowed — either `redis.multi().incr(key).expire(key, 60)` so the key naturally decays about 60 seconds after the last request, or better, a proper sliding window with a sorted set storing timestamps and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to evict anything older than the window before counting. Separately, AVERAGE_DRIVERS_PER_CELL as a hardcoded constant of 20 is also wrong on its own — it can't reflect that a cell has 2 drivers online right now versus 40 — I'd replace that with a live per-cell available-driver count, something drivers heartbeat into Redis with their own short TTL. For the test, I'd want something like: hammer recordDemand on a cell until getSurgeMultiplier hits 3.0, then stop generating demand, advance the clock (fake timers or Redis TTL manipulation) past the window, and assert the next call returns close to 1.0 again — that's the regression test that would have caught this before merge.

Looking at this, the demand counter is a straight `INCR` with no expiration set anywhere, so `demand:${cellId}` just grows unboundedly — there's nothing that removes old demand from it, so a cell that was busy earlier in the day stays maxed out at SURGE_CAP even after things calm down. That's the bug I'd flag as the one to fix before merge since it means riders keep paying surge pricing for demand that isn't there anymore. I'd add a TTL to the key — something like expiring it after a minute of no new INCR — so it resets itself once requests taper off. I'd also add a test that pushes the multiplier to the cap, waits past that expiry, and checks it comes back down. On the supply side, AVERAGE_DRIVERS_PER_CELL being a constant 20 for every cell also seems off since cells obviously don't have the same number of drivers, so that's worth calling out too, though I'd treat the decay issue as the blocking one.

So the demand tracking uses `redis.incr` on a per-cell key, and I don't see it ever getting reset or cleared, which means it just keeps going up over time. That seems like a problem because the multiplier would stay high even if the actual demand right now is lower than it was before. I'd probably add some kind of expiration on the key so it doesn't hold onto old data forever. The supply side is also just a fixed number, `AVERAGE_DRIVERS_PER_CELL = 20`, which is the same for every cell — that doesn't seem right either since different areas probably have different numbers of drivers available. Between the two I'd say the demand counter issue is more important since it affects what customers get charged directly. For testing, I'd want a test that checks the multiplier changes over time somehow, verifying it doesn't just stay maxed forever.

I think the surge calculation itself looks fine — dividing demand by supply and capping at 3.0 makes sense as an approach. Maybe the constant for average drivers could be tuned per city instead of being global.
