checklist.text: [problemSolving] Identifies the waste: re-shipping the full script body per request costs bandwidth and forces Redis to re-cache/parse it each time, which scales badly with RPS.
[technical] Gives the optimization: load the script body once at startup to get a SHA1, then call the script by that digest per request, sending only the 40-character hash — atomicity is unchanged.
[communication] Emphasizes this is purely a transport optimization, not an algorithm change — the correctness and the atomic guarantee are identical before and after.
[testing] Handles the case where Redis no longer has the script cached (restart or cache flush): catch it, reload the script, then confirm throughput/latency improves and results stay unchanged.

examples.text: So the actual bug here isn't in the token-bucket logic itself, the Lua script is correct and stays atomic. The problem is purely in how it's transported: this.redis.eval(RATE_LIMIT_SCRIPT, 1, key, ...) ships the entire multi-line script body over the wire on every single call to isAllowed. At high RPS that's real bandwidth waste, and worse, Redis has to re-hash and re-cache an identical script thousands of times a second instead of just executing something it already knows. The fix is to switch to the SCRIPT LOAD / EVALSHA pattern: call SCRIPT LOAD once, for example lazily on first use or in a constructor init, to get back the SHA1 digest, cache that digest in the class, and on the hot path call redis.evalsha(sha, 1, key, limit, windowMs, now) instead of eval. That keeps every request down to a tiny 40-character hash plus the KEYS/ARGV instead of the full script text, same atomicity, same single round trip, same algorithm, just a cheaper wire format. The one thing you must handle is a NOSCRIPT error from Redis, which happens if the script cache gets evicted, restart, failover to a replica that never had it loaded, or someone runs SCRIPT FLUSH, so I'd wrap the evalsha call in a try/catch that falls back to a one-time eval or re-SCRIPT LOAD and re-caches the SHA. Honestly the cleanest way to get all of this for free is ioredis's redis.defineCommand('rateLimit', { numberOfKeys: 1, lua: RATE_LIMIT_SCRIPT }), it internally does EVALSHA-with-NOSCRIPT-fallback-to-EVAL for you, so isAllowed just calls this.redis.rateLimit(key, limit, windowMs, now) and gets the optimization transparently without me hand-rolling the SHA caching and retry logic.

The issue is that RATE_LIMIT_SCRIPT is a full Lua source string, and every call to isAllowed passes it straight into redis.eval(...), so Redis is re-parsing and effectively re-hashing the same script on every request instead of reusing a cached copy. The standard fix is EVALSHA, you load the script once with SCRIPT LOAD, get back its SHA1, store that on the class, and then call redis.evalsha(sha, 1, key, limit, windowMs, now) on the hot path instead of eval. That cuts the payload down to just the hash plus the arguments, so you stop paying for the script body on every round trip, and the atomicity is untouched since it's still one Lua execution on the server. I'd also add a fallback for NOSCRIPT, if Redis restarts or the script cache gets cleared, evalsha will fail and you need to reload the script and retry. I didn't fully work out whether to do the SHA caching myself or lean on ioredis's defineCommand, but either approach solves the core problem of shipping the script every time without changing the check-and-increment logic at all.

Looking at isAllowed, it calls this.redis.eval(RATE_LIMIT_SCRIPT, 1, key, ...) every time, and since RATE_LIMIT_SCRIPT is a constant, it's the same string being sent over and over, that's wasteful at high RPS. I think the fix is to cache the script somehow on the Redis side so we don't have to send it each time. Redis has some way to preload a script and reference it by an id or hash afterward, so instead of eval you'd call that shorter reference. I'd store whatever identifier Redis gives back after the first load and reuse it for subsequent calls, and if that reference ever becomes invalid I guess you'd need to redo the load. The core check-and-increment logic in the Lua script itself doesn't need to change, just the way we're calling it, so atomicity should be preserved either way.

The script does look like it's being sent on every request which seems inefficient for a hot path. Maybe we could reduce that by making the Lua script shorter or moving some of the logic like the remaining calculation out into the TypeScript side so there's less text to send. Another idea could be to only call the script for the increment part and do the GET check separately in application code, which would cut the size of what needs to run on Redis each time. We could also try connection pooling or reusing the same Redis client instance across requests, since that might avoid extra overhead per call. I'm not fully sure how Redis caches scripts internally, but reducing the amount of Lua that runs each time feels like the right direction.

Honestly the code looks fine to me, the Lua script does an atomic GET/INCR/PEXPIRE which is correct, and eval is just the normal way to run a Redis script, so I don't see a real problem with calling it on every request. If we wanted to make it faster we could maybe switch the whole rate limiter to use a simple in-memory counter in Node instead of Redis, or replace the sliding-window logic with a basic fixed counter that resets every few seconds since that would be less code to run. We could also just increase the Redis instance size or add more replicas to handle the higher RPS instead of touching the client code. I don't think there's anything wrong with how the script is being sent, eval is the standard Redis API for running Lua so that part shouldn't need to change.

checklist: [problemSolving] Quantifies the blow-up: one sorted-set entry per in-window request means O(N) RAM per client, and every check pays O(log N + M) for the eviction plus the count — a cost that lands hardest on exactly the hottest keys.

[technical] Names the optimization: swap the hot key onto a weighted two-bucket counter — keep only a `curr` and a `prev` integer, estimate the sliding count as `prev * (1 - elapsedRatio) + curr` — for O(1) memory and O(1) work per operation at roughly 0.003% error.
[communication] Frames the change as an explicit accuracy-versus-memory trade, not a free win, and states plainly where the exact log must stay anyway — billing, strict/contractual quotas, audit.

[testing] Verifies the swap before rolling it out: runs the counter and the log side by side at the target request rate and confirms they agree within the accepted error bound, not just that the counter "looks close.".

examples.text: So the core problem is that `SlidingWindowLogLimiter` keeps one ZSET member per request — `zadd(key, now, requestId)` with a fresh `randomUUID()` every single call — so memory per client is O(N) where N is the request count inside the window, not O(1). And the two ops on the hot path, `zremrangebyscore` then `zcard`, are O(log N + M) and O(log N) respectively, so the cost of every admission check scales with exactly the clients sending the most traffic — the eviction and count get more expensive on the busiest keys, which is backwards. My fix for the pure-limiting case, where we don't need exact per-request accounting, is to drop the ZSET entirely and replace it with a weighted two-bucket counter: just two integers per client, `curr` and `prev`, each covering one window-sized bucket. On a check I compute `elapsedRatio` into the current bucket, estimate the count as `prev * (1 - elapsedRatio) + curr`, and increment `curr` with a single `INCR`+`PEXPIRE`. That's O(1) memory and O(1) work per operation, full stop — no more ZSET, no eviction pass, no per-request UUID. The known error on this estimator is tiny, on the order of 0.003% at reasonable traffic, because it's a weighted approximation of a rolling window, not a real sliding window. I'd frame this explicitly to the team as an accuracy-for-memory trade, not a free win — we're accepting slight over/under-admission at the boundary between buckets in exchange for killing the O(N) blowup. And there are places where that trade is not acceptable: anywhere we bill on request count, any strict contractual quota, or anything that needs an audit trail — those need to keep the exact ZSET log, or write the accepted events to a separate durable log even if the counter drives the limiting decision. Before I ship the swap I wouldn't just eyeball that the numbers look close — I'd run the old ZSET-based limiter and the new counter side by side against the same replayed traffic at the target request rate, log both counts, and assert the counter stays within the accepted error bound the whole run, not just at a snapshot. Only after that comparison holds would I cut the hot clients over.

Looking at `isAllowed`, the `zadd(key, now, requestId)` line is the smoking gun — every request adds a new ZSET member, so a client sending a lot of traffic in one window ends up with a proportionally large sorted set, meaning RAM per client is basically linear in request volume. And `zremrangebyscore` plus `zcard` on the hot path both cost more as that set grows, which is exactly the wrong shape since it's the highest-volume clients paying the highest per-check cost. For a limiter that just needs to say yes/no and doesn't need to reconstruct exact request history, I'd swap this for a sliding-window counter: two integer buckets, current and previous window, and estimate the in-window count as a weighted blend of the two based on how far we are into the current bucket. That gets you to constant memory and constant-time Redis ops — an `INCR` and expiry instead of a growing ZSET. The obvious downside is it's an approximation, not exact — I'd call that out as a trade-off we're choosing on purpose for the hot clients, and I'd keep the exact log path for anything where correctness actually matters, like billing or a hard contractual cap. Before rolling it to production I'd want to run it against production-shaped traffic and compare against the existing limiter's decisions to make sure it's not diverging in a way that matters, though I'd want to think more about what tolerance is actually acceptable rather than just picking a number.

The issue is that this limiter stores every request as its own entry in Redis, so for clients making a ton of requests the sorted set just keeps growing, and that's eating memory and slowing things down since `zremrangebyscore` and `zcard` have to walk more data. So the fix is to not store every request individually — instead of the exact ZSET log, use something like a fixed window counter, just increment a single key and check it against the limit, then reset it when the window expires. That's way cheaper, O(1) instead of growing with traffic. The trade-off is you lose exactness at the window boundaries — a fixed window can let through roughly double the limit right at the edge where two windows meet, so it's not as precise as the log approach, but for most rate limiting use cases that's an acceptable trade since we just need to protect the backend, not bill exactly. I'd probably want to test it a bit before deploying, run some load against it and see the counts come out roughly right compared to what we had before, and keep the old version around for services where the exact count actually matters.

I think the main problem here is that we're creating a new random UUID for every request and storing it in Redis, which adds overhead — `randomUUID()` plus a network round trip to `zadd` on every single call is expensive, and doing it for the busiest clients makes it worse. I'd look at batching the writes, or maybe caching the UUID generation somehow so we're not calling crypto on the hot path. Also the `pexpire` is being called every time an entry is added which seems redundant — we could probably set that less often. For the eviction, maybe we could run `zremrangebyscore` on a background job/cron instead of on every request so the hot path check is just `zcard`, that would take load off. I'd test it by hitting the endpoint a bunch of times locally and checking it doesn't error and the limit still triggers around the right count.

Honestly this code looks fine to me — it's using Redis which is already fast, and sorted sets are a good data structure for this kind of thing since they're ordered by score. If memory is the issue I'd just say we should scale up the Redis instance to a bigger tier, or add more memory to the box, since that's usually the quickest fix for something like this. We could also shard the rate limiter keys across multiple Redis instances so no single node has too much data. I don't think we need to change the actual algorithm since it's working correctly and giving exact answers, which is important — we don't want to make the rate limiter less accurate just to save a bit of RAM, that seems like a bad trade to make. Maybe just add monitoring/alerts on Redis memory usage so we know before it becomes a real problem, and scale horizontally if it keeps growing.

checklist: [problemSolving] Traces the bug: two requests in the same millisecond share the member, so the second ZADD overwrites rather than adds; ZCARD counts one fewer, so the limiter admits an extra request.
[technical] Names the root cause — a ZSET member must be unique; the timestamp alone collides — and gives the fix: make the member unique (e.g. `${now}-${uuid}`) while keeping the score = now.
[communication] Explains ZSET semantics clearly (member identity vs score ordering) rather than vaguely "add some randomness."
[testing] Verifies by firing many requests within a single millisecond and asserting ZCARD equals the number granted and the (limit+1)th is correctly denied.

examples.text: So the bug is in this line: `pipeline.zadd(key, now, now)` — they're using `now` as both the score and the member. In a ZSET, ZADD only appends a new entry if the member doesn't already exist; if the same member is added again, it just updates that member's score in place, it doesn't create a second entry. Since `now` is a millisecond-resolution timestamp, any two requests from the same user that land in the same millisecond produce the exact same member value. So the second request's ZADD collapses onto the first one's entry instead of adding a new one, and ZCARD right after reports one fewer entry than the number of requests actually recorded. That means the limiter's count is under-counting, so it keeps returning `true` and admits more requests than the configured limit — the burst gets through specifically because of how many requests collide on the same millisecond. The fix is to give every request a unique member while keeping `now` as the score, something like `pipeline.zadd(key, now, `${now}-${crypto.randomUUID()}`)` — that way ZREMRANGEBYSCORE still evicts correctly by timestamp, but ZCARD counts every request. To verify, I'd write a test that fires, say, 150 requests for one user all within the same millisecond — either by mocking `Date.now()` or just hammering it in a tight loop — and assert that ZCARD after the burst equals the number of requests actually made, and that request 101 onward is denied while the first 100 are granted.

Looking at the ZADD call, they pass `now` as both score and member: `pipeline.zadd(key, now, now)`. ZSET members have to be unique — if you ZADD the same member twice, Redis just overwrites the score for that member rather than inserting a new element. Because `now` comes from `Date.now()`, which only has millisecond granularity, two requests arriving in the same millisecond will have the same member value, so the second one overwrites the first instead of adding a new entry. That means ZCARD undercounts the real number of requests, and the limiter compares that undercounted value against `limit`, so it can admit more than `limit` requests when there's a same-millisecond collision. The fix is to make the member unique per request — append something like a random suffix or an incrementing counter to the timestamp so the member is unique but the score is still `now` for correct window eviction. For testing, I'd simulate a burst — fire more than `limit` requests in rapid succession, ideally forcing several into the same millisecond — and check that ZCARD matches the actual number of ZADD calls and that requests past the limit get rejected.

I think the issue is around the ZADD — score and member are both `now`. If I remember right, ZSET entries need a unique member, so if two calls happen to use the same value there could be some kind of overwrite instead of adding a new one. That would make the count lower than it should be, which explains why more requests get let through than the limit allows, since ZCARD is being compared to `limit`. It only shows up with same-millisecond requests because that's when the member value would repeat. The fix would probably be to make the member more unique somehow, maybe adding an id or something on top of the timestamp, while still using `now` for the score so eviction still works based on time. To test it, I'd try sending a bunch of requests really fast to the same user and see if the count ends up matching what's expected instead of being too low, and check whether it still blocks once you're over the limit.

Redis pipelines batch commands but I'm not 100% sure they're transactional against concurrent clients, so maybe that's causing the extra requests to slip through. To test it I'd probably just run the rate limiter a bunch of times and see if the count looks about right, and log the ZCARD value to check it's not too far off.

Honestly, scanning through this, I don't see anything wrong with the logic itself — it evicts old entries, adds the new one, counts, and sets expiry, which seems like a pretty standard sliding window pattern. If it's letting extra requests through under bursty traffic, my guess is it's more of an infrastructure thing, like maybe the Redis instance is under memory pressure or there's network latency causing the pipeline to time out and retry, which could double-count or skip commands. Or maybe it's a client-side issue where `allowRequest` is getting called twice for the same request due to some retry logic elsewhere in the app that isn't shown here. I'd probably just add more logging around the call site and bump up the `limit` value a bit as a stopgap, then keep an eye on it in production to see if the extra requests are actually a real problem or just noise in the metrics.

checklist: [problemSolving] Identifies that Redis Cluster routes each key by `CRC16(key) mod 16384`, so the three differently-named keys (`quota:u:<userId>`, `quota:t:<tenantId>`, `quota:g`) land on different slots, and a multi-key script spanning slots is rejected outright.

[technical] Gives the fix: wrap a shared hash-tag `{q:<tenantId>}` into all three keys so only the braced substring is hashed, pinning them to one slot and one node where the multi-key Lua runs atomically.
[communication] Explains clearly why standalone Redis worked and the cluster did not — standalone has no slot partitioning, so there is nothing to route — without hand-waving it as "a cluster quirk".

[testing] Verifies the fix via a cluster-info query that the three keys report the same slot (`sameSlot: true`), and flags the trade-off it introduces: a whale tenant's keys all concentrate on one hot slot/node.

examples.text: The root cause is Redis Cluster's key routing. Every key gets hashed with CRC16 and mapped into one of 16384 hash slots, and those slots are sharded across nodes — so when the script calls redis.eval with KEYS[1]=quota:u:<userId>, KEYS[2]=quota:t:<tenantId>, and KEYS[3]=quota:g, those three strings almost certainly hash to three different slots, possibly on three different nodes. Cluster mode refuses to run a multi-key command unless all the keys resolve to the same slot, which is exactly the CROSSSLOT error you're seeing — it's not a networking blip, it's the cluster correctly rejecting a script it can't guarantee atomicity for across nodes. On standalone Redis there's only one node and no slot concept, so buildKeys() worked purely by accident — nothing was ever routing those keys anywhere. The fix is to force all three keys into the same slot using a hash tag: wrap a shared substring in curly braces, like `quota:u:{q:${tenantId}}:${userId}`, `quota:t:{q:${tenantId}}`, and `quota:g:{q:${tenantId}}` — Redis only hashes the part inside the braces, so as long as that braced tag is identical across the three keys, CRC16 produces the same slot for all of them and the Lua script runs atomically on one node again. I'd verify it by running CLUSTER KEYSLOT on the three constructed keys — or better, a small integration test that asserts they resolve to the same slot ID before deploying. The trade-off is that I've now pinned this tenant's global-plus-user-plus-tenant traffic onto a single slot and therefore a single node, so a very high-volume tenant becomes a hot key/hot node — it sacrifices some of the horizontal scale-out we moved to cluster mode for in exchange for atomicity, so I'd want to watch node-level CPU/ops-per-sec for whale tenants.

This is a hash-slot issue, not a flaky-network issue. Redis Cluster splits the keyspace into 16384 slots and assigns them by CRC16 of the key, and it deliberately refuses any command — including an EVAL with multiple KEYS — that touches keys living in different slots. buildKeys() generates quota:u:<userId>, quota:t:<tenantId>, and quota:g, and there's nothing tying those three strings together, so on a multi-node cluster they land on different slots and the script throws CROSSSLOT every time. It worked in staging simply because standalone Redis is a single node with no slot partitioning at all, so slot placement was never actually a factor there. The fix is to use a hash tag — put a common tag like {tenant-id} in braces inside all three key names so Redis only hashes that substring, forcing all three onto the same slot so the atomic Lua script can run again. One trade-off worth calling out: pinning everything to one slot means a very active tenant's traffic concentrates onto one node instead of spreading out, so we lose some of the load distribution cluster mode was supposed to give us.

I think the problem is that Redis Cluster doesn't allow scripts that use keys spread across different nodes — that's basically what the CROSSSLOT error is telling us. The three keys here, the user one, the tenant one, and the global one, are named differently so the cluster probably puts them on different shards, and the Lua script can't run across shards at once. It ran fine in staging because staging is just one Redis node, so there was nowhere else for the keys to go. To fix it I'd try to force the keys onto the same node — I believe you can do that with something called a hash tag, wrapping part of the key in curly braces so Redis groups them together, though I'd want to double check the exact syntax. I'm less sure how I'd confirm it's actually fixed beyond just re-running the load test and seeing the CROSSSLOT errors go away.

My guess is this is some kind of cluster-mode limitation with running scripts across keys — Redis Cluster is stricter about multi-key operations than a single instance. Since it broke right when we switched to cluster, I'd probably start by checking if ioredis needs different configuration for eval calls in cluster mode, or maybe we need to pass a specific node instead of letting it route automatically. As a fix I might just split it into three separate INCR calls instead of one Lua script, and if we need atomicity we could use a MULTI/EXEC transaction, or just retry the whole consume() call on failure since the increments are idempotent enough for rate limiting. I'm not fully sure why the key names matter here specifically.

Honestly this looks like a transient issue with the Redis Cluster deployment itself — CROSSSLOT sounds like a networking or replication error where the cluster nodes lost sync with each other after the migration. I'd probably start by checking the cluster's health, maybe running CLUSTER INFO to see if a node is down or if there's a failover happening, since promoting to cluster right when this started feels like a timing coincidence with some infra hiccup. As a quick mitigation I'd wrap the consume() call in a try/catch and just fail open, allowing the request through if Redis throws, so we don't block production traffic while we investigate. I don't see anything actually wrong with the RateLimiter code itself — the Lua script and key naming both look fine to me.

checklist: [problemSolving] Spots that `ZADD` runs even when the request is rejected, so an over-limit flood keeps adding entries to the ZSET and memory grows unbounded regardless of the actual limit.
[technical] Gives the fix: only `ZADD` when `count < limit` (record-on-grant) and return early on reject without recording anything; add `PEXPIRE` for one window so idle keys self-free.
[communication] Frames the principle clearly — rejected traffic must never grow RAM — and states that this bounds memory to roughly the limit per active client, not per attempt.

[testing] Verifies by flooding a key far above its limit and asserting the ZSET's cardinality stays near the limit instead of climbing with the attempt count, then confirms the key expires after a window of silence.

examples.text: So the bug is right here at the end: `count` gets read first, then we unconditionally do `zadd(key, now, member)` before we even check `count < limit`. That means every single request, whether it's accepted or rejected, adds a new member to the ZSET. If a client is flooding way past their limit, `zremrangebyscore` is only trimming entries older than the window, but within the window itself the ZSET just keeps accumulating one entry per attempt forever — the cardinality is bounded by attempts-in-window, not by `limit`. So a client sending 10,000 requests/sec against a limit of 100 ends up with a ZSET that has thousands of members, not 100. The fix is to flip the order: compute `count`, and only call `zadd` when `count < limit` — record-on-grant, not record-on-attempt. Reject requests should return early without touching the ZSET at all. I'd also add a `pexpire key windowMs` right after the `zadd` so that if a client goes silent, the key expires on its own instead of sitting there forever — that's actually a separate leak because `zremrangebyscore` only runs on the next request, so a client that stops entirely leaves stale data with no TTL. To verify, I'd write a test that floods a single key at, say, 50x the limit and assert `zcard` stays near `limit` instead of growing linearly with the number of attempts, then let the key sit idle past the window and confirm it disappears via TTL. The core principle: rejected traffic is by definition not supposed to be counted, so it must never grow Redis memory — that keeps memory roughly O(limit) per active client instead of O(attempts).

Looking at this, the problem is that `zadd` runs before the return statement, so it happens for every request regardless of whether it's under or over the limit. Even requests that get rejected still get written into the ZSET. Under a sustained flood way above `limit`, that means the ZSET just keeps growing with every attempt — memory scales with total requests, not with the configured limit. To fix it, I'd move the `zadd` so it only happens when `count < limit`, and just `return false` immediately otherwise without writing anything. That should keep the ZSET capped around `limit` entries per client. I'd probably also throw a `pexpire` on the key so it cleans itself up eventually if the client stops sending traffic — I think that's part of why memory doesn't come back down even when a client goes quiet. For testing, I'd hammer one client key far past its limit and check that the sorted set size stops growing once it hits `limit`, instead of climbing with the flood.

Okay so `zadd` is called on every request here, after we compute `count` but before we return the verdict. I think that means rejected requests still write to the set. If there's a flood of requests over the limit, the ZSET keeps getting new members added even though those requests are denied, so it grows without bound. The fix would be to only add to the ZSET when the request is allowed — basically check the limit first and skip the write if it's rejected. That should keep memory more under control since you're not storing rejected attempts. I'm less sure about the 'never comes back down' part of the bug — maybe that's related to the expiry cleanup not running if nobody hits the key again, so `zremrangebyscore` never gets a chance to trim it. I'd probably add some kind of expiration on the key too. To check it works I'd send a bunch of requests over the limit and see if the ZSET size looks reasonable instead of just growing forever.

Hmm, I see `zadd` and `zcard` and `zremrangebyscore` all being called, so it looks like it's tracking a sliding window correctly. Maybe the issue is that `zremrangebyscore` isn't removing enough old entries, so stuff piles up over time? Or maybe `windowMs` is being passed in wrong somewhere and the window is bigger than expected, so more requests fall inside it than intended. I'd probably add some logging around the count value to see what's happening, or double check that `windowStart` is being calculated correctly. I don't really see why rejecting a request would still store it though, so I'm not totally sure that's actually a problem — the ZADD seems necessary to keep the log complete for the sliding window to work. Maybe I'd just try lowering the limit or adding a max size to the ZSET as a safety net.

This looks like a pretty standard rate limiter to me, using Redis sorted sets to track timestamps, which is a common pattern. I think the ZREMRANGEBYSCORE call handles expiring old entries so the window slides correctly, and ZCARD gets the count, and ZADD records it — that's basically how sliding window logs are supposed to work in every tutorial I've seen, so I'm not sure there's really a bug in the logic itself. Maybe the memory growth is more about Redis's overall configuration, like maxmemory policy not being set to an eviction policy like allkeys-lru, or maybe there's a separate memory leak somewhere else in the service unrelated to this specific function. It could also be that there are just way more unique clientIds than expected, so it's actually the number of keys, not the size of any single key, that's the real problem — like maybe clientId isn't being normalized and IPs are used raw creating tons of one-off keys. I'd probably start by checking Redis INFO memory stats and looking at overall key count trends rather than this code specifically.

checklist: [technical] Flags the most dangerous issue first: caching a per-user/authenticated response (one carrying `Set-Cookie` or an auth header) under a URI-only cache key means user A's private body gets served straight to user B — only safe, public `GET`s should be cached, and authenticated or `Set-Cookie` responses must bypass the cache entirely.

[problemSolving] Flags negative-caching of errors: `proxy_cache_valid any 1h` pins 4xx/5xx responses for a full hour, so a transient origin error keeps being served long after the origin has recovered — cap error caching at a tiny negative TTL at most, or don't cache errors at all.

[communication] Explains the cache-key/Vary correctness gap: keying only on `$request_uri` while the response itself varies by auth state/cookie breaks correctness, not just efficiency, and recommends turning `proxy_cache_lock` on to avoid a stampede on a hot key.

[testing] Verifies the fix with concrete evidence: call the personalized endpoint as user A then as user B (B must never see A's data), and force the origin into an error then repair it (the edge must stop serving the stale error once it's no longer valid).

examples.text: The scariest bug here is right at the top: `proxy_cache_key $request_uri;` with no auth dimension folded in, combined with forwarding `Cookie` and `Authorization` straight through to the same shared `edge_cache` zone. That means a personalized response for `/dashboard` — one that carries `Set-Cookie` or reflects a specific session — gets stored under a key that any other client hitting the exact same URI will also match, so user B literally gets user A's authenticated body back from cache. This location block is fronting both static assets and authenticated pages with the same policy, which is the real design flaw — public, cacheable `GET`s and personalized responses should never share a cache path. The fix is to either split routing (a `location` for `/assets/` etc. that stays cached, and a separate block for authenticated routes that sets `proxy_cache off` or uses `proxy_no_cache`/`proxy_cache_bypass` keyed on `$http_cookie`/`$http_authorization` and `Set-Cookie` presence), and to bypass/skip cache write whenever the upstream response has `Set-Cookie`. Second issue: `proxy_cache_valid any 1h` caches every status class including 4xx/5xx for a full hour, so the origin 500 during the outage kept getting served stale for far longer than the outage itself — that should be something like `proxy_cache_valid 200 302 10m; proxy_cache_valid 500 502 503 504 1s;` or just not cached at all. I'd also flip on `proxy_cache_lock on;` since concurrent misses on a hot key right now stampede both origin_app servers simultaneously with no coalescing. To verify: hit the personalized endpoint as user A, then immediately as user B from a fresh session, and confirm B never sees A's payload or `Set-Cookie`; separately, force the origin to return 500, confirm the edge serves errors only briefly, repair the origin, and confirm 200s return promptly instead of being pinned for the old 1h TTL.

The big one is that `proxy_cache_key` is just `$request_uri` — it doesn't include anything about who's logged in — while the response for something like `/dashboard` clearly varies per user and can carry `Set-Cookie`/`Authorization`-gated content. Since public assets and authenticated pages share the exact same `location` and cache zone, that's how user A's dashboard data ends up served to user B: it's a cross-user data leak, not just a stale-content bug. Fix: separate the routing so authenticated paths either skip the cache (`proxy_cache off`) or explicitly bypass storing/reading whenever the response has `Set-Cookie`, and reserve the shared cache for actually public, unauthenticated GETs. The other incident — the hour of 500s after the origin recovered — comes from `proxy_cache_valid any 1h`, which caches error responses with the same long TTL as successful ones; that should be a much shorter TTL for error statuses, or errors shouldn't be cached at all. I'd verify the auth fix by curling the personalized route as two different sessions and confirming they get different bodies, and verify the error-caching fix by killing the origin, hitting the URL to get a 500, restoring the origin, and checking the edge starts returning 200 quickly instead of holding onto the 500 for the full hour.

Looking at this config, the cache key is only built from `$request_uri`, so it's not accounting for the fact that some of these pages are personalized per user. That's probably how the wrong-account-data bug happened — the cache doesn't know the difference between different logged-in users hitting the same path, so it can serve one person's cached page to someone else. I'd want to exclude authenticated routes from this cache or add something to the key that distinguishes sessions. For the second incident, `proxy_cache_valid any 1h` sets a full hour of caching for any response, which would include error pages — so if the origin returned a 500 during the outage, that error would stick around in cache for an hour even after things came back up, which lines up with what happened. I'd shorten how long error responses get cached, maybe to a few seconds. To check both fixes actually work, I'd try logging in as two separate users and see if their dashboard responses differ, and I'd also simulate an origin failure and see how quickly the edge stops serving the error after the origin is healthy again.

I think the problem is the caching is too aggressive overall — `proxy_cache_valid any 1h` is caching everything for an hour, which seems too long for a fast-moving app, so I'd probably lower that TTL across the board to something like 5 or 10 minutes so stale content doesn't stick around as long. That would help with the error-page issue somewhat since things would refresh sooner. For the personalized data appearing on the wrong account, my guess is it's a session or cookie handling problem on the app side rather than really an nginx thing, though I notice the config does forward the Authorization header through, so maybe there's some header mismatch happening at the proxy level too. I'd also add more logging via `add_header X-Cache-Status` — actually that's already there — so I'd just watch that header in production to see if requests are hitting or missing cache more than expected. To test, I'd just refresh the dashboard page a few times and see if the error goes away and if the personalized data still looks wrong.

Honestly this config looks pretty standard for an nginx caching setup — it's got SSL configured properly with the cert and key paths, the upstream has two servers so there's load balancing across origin_app-1 and origin_app-2, and the cache zone is sized reasonably at 100m with a 10g max size. My guess for the wrong-user-data bug is that it's probably a load balancer round-robin issue where requests are somehow crossing between the two upstream servers, so maybe I'd look at adding session affinity with `ip_hash` on the upstream block. For the hour of errors after the outage, that seems like it's just how long it took the ops team to actually notice and restart things, so it might not even be an nginx config issue at all — I'd check the deployment logs and see if there was a delay in the fix reaching production before touching this file.

checklist: [problemSolving] Diagnoses the bottleneck: a synchronous Postgres SELECT+UPDATE per chunk dominates PATCH latency, and the offset is validated on every chunk but only needs durable persistence occasionally.

[technical] Proposes the two-tier split: keep the live offset in a Redis key `upload:<sessionId>` for O(1) GET/SET on each PATCH validation, and keep Postgres as the durable source of truth; Redis is rebuildable from the committed chunk total if it evicts the key.
[communication] Defends the trade-off clearly (speed in the hot tier, durability in the cold tier) and calls out the reconstruct-on-miss path so a Redis restart doesn't corrupt or lose the offset.
[testing] Verifies: measure PATCH latency before vs after; then kill Redis mid-upload and confirm the offset is rebuilt from Postgres and the upload still resumes at the correct byte.

examples.text: So looking at handleChunk, the problem is that every single chunk does two synchronous Postgres round-trips in the request path — a SELECT to read committed_offset just so we can validate the Upload-Offset header, and then an UPDATE to persist the new offset before we return. Both of those go through TypeORM's query() straight to the connection pool, so under load you're serializing on Postgres latency and pool contention twice per chunk, and that's on top of the actual object storage write. The thing is, we don't actually need durable persistence on every chunk — we only need a fast, correct answer to 'what's the next expected offset', and that only needs to be durable if the process crashes or the client disconnects and comes back later. So I'd split it into two tiers: a hot Redis key, something like `upload:<sessionId>`, that holds the live offset as an integer — GET it to validate, INCRBY or SET it after the chunk write, both O(1) round-trips to Redis instead of Postgres. Postgres stays as the source of truth, but I'd only flush to it periodically — say every N chunks or every few seconds — rather than inline on every PATCH. The key thing to defend here is that Redis is explicitly a cache that's rebuildable, not a second source of truth: if the key evicts or Redis restarts, on the next PATCH we fall back to computing the offset from the last committed value in Postgres, or even better, from the actual bytes written in object storage, so we never trust an ambiguous state. To verify this I'd first benchmark PATCH p50/p99 latency before and after under concurrent chunk load, and then specifically test the crash scenario — kill Redis mid-upload, hit the endpoint again, and confirm it reconstructs the correct offset from Postgres/storage and the client resumes at the right byte instead of getting corrupted or silently losing progress.

The hot path issue is that handleChunk hits Postgres twice synchronously per chunk — once to SELECT committed_offset for the ordering check, and once to UPDATE it after the write completes — and since this runs on every chunk of every in-flight upload, that's two DB round-trips multiplied by however many chunks a file has, which is clearly what's dominating PATCH latency versus the actual chunk write. My redesign would move the offset tracking into Redis — keep a per-session key with the current offset, do the read-check and the increment against Redis instead of Postgres, since Redis GET/SET is basically O(1) and way cheaper than a Postgres round-trip under concurrency. Postgres would still own the durable record, just updated less frequently — maybe batched or on a timer instead of inline with every single PATCH request. For the crash-safety side, if Redis loses the key we'd need to fall back and rebuild it from Postgres so we don't just start trusting offset zero or something stale. To validate the change I'd measure latency before and after under load, and I'd also want to simulate Redis going down mid-upload to make sure the session doesn't get corrupted, though I'd probably need to spend more time working out exactly how the rebuild reads the true byte count so it's not off by one chunk.

I think the slowness comes from talking to Postgres inside handleChunk — there's a SELECT at the start and an UPDATE at the end, and since this function runs per chunk, that's a lot of database calls piling up when there's a lot of concurrent uploads. Given we already have Redis in the stack, I'd move some of this into Redis so we're not hitting Postgres so often — cache the offset there and read/write it instead of going to the database every time. Postgres would still be used, just maybe not on every request, more like periodically to keep it in sync. I think the ordering validation, the part that throws ConflictException, could probably stay mostly the same, it's really about where the offset value comes from. For durability, if the cache goes away, I'd want to fall back to whatever Postgres has, though I'm not 100% sure how to make that not just be stale or wrong right after a crash. Testing-wise I'd load test the endpoint and check the response times went down, and try turning Redis off to see what happens to the session.

The code does a database read and then a database write inside handleChunk, so I'd guess that's part of why it's slow, since it's running for every chunk that comes in. Since Redis is already available, we could probably use it to speed things up — like caching some of the session data there instead of always querying Postgres. I'd keep the object storage write the same since that seems necessary. For making sure nothing breaks, I think we'd just need to make sure Redis and Postgres have the same data, though I'm not totally sure what happens if Redis restarts — maybe we'd just re-read from Postgres again next time someone hits the endpoint. To test it I'd probably just try uploading a file and see if it still works and check that it's a bit faster than before.

Honestly the code looks like it's already doing the right thing — it validates the offset, writes the chunk to storage, and updates the row, so I'm not sure there's a bottleneck here beyond maybe the object storage write itself being slow over the network, that's usually the biggest cost in an upload endpoint. If we wanted it faster we could probably just add an index on session_id in the upload_sessions table, or maybe increase the connection pool size so Postgres queries don't queue up as much. For Redis, since it's already in the stack, we could use it to cache the whole file being uploaded so we don't need object storage at all for smaller files. I don't think there's really a data-loss risk here since Postgres already commits everything, so I wouldn't change much about how the offset itself is tracked, and I'd probably just add a try/catch around the ObjectStorageClient call as the main improvement.

checklist: [problemSolving] Names the failure as a cache stampede / thundering herd: with a plain TTL and no coalescing, the instant a hot entry expires every concurrent reader MISSes at the same moment, and all of them stampede the shielded origin together — origin load spikes periodically, in lockstep with the TTL, not steadily over time.

[technical] Gives the primary fix: enable request coalescing at the edge so only ONE of the concurrent MISSes is allowed to actually rebuild the cache entry, while every other concurrent request for that same key waits for that single in-flight rebuild instead of independently calling the origin.

[technical] Adds the serve-stale complement: while the one coalesced request is revalidating, the edge keeps answering the other waiting requests with the still-cached (slightly stale) copy instead of blocking them behind the lock until the rebuild finishes.

[communication] Explains why this stays correct: the staleness window is short and bounded to roughly one origin round trip (the time the single rebuild takes), which is a deliberate, acceptable trade for turning thousands of simultaneous origin hits into one.

[technical] Connects the fix to revalidation: pairing coalescing with an ETag / If-None-Match check means the one rebuild request that is allowed through can often come back as a cheap 304 Not Modified rather than re-transferring the full body, making the single refill even cheaper.

[testing] Verifies the fix with a concrete load test: drive concurrent traffic across a TTL expiry boundary for the same hot key and assert the origin receives roughly ONE request per key per refill cycle (not thousands), while every client still receives a 200 response throughout.

examples.text: So the reason the origin gets hammered periodically instead of steadily is that this is a classic cache stampede, or thundering herd. Because the TTL is fixed and there's no jitter, every reader that has been hitting the cache for the same hot key shares the exact same expiresAt timestamp. The moment Date.now() crosses that expiresAt, entry.expiresAt > Date.now() flips to false for every single one of those thousands of concurrent callers at basically the same instant. They all fall through the if-block into the MISS branch together, and since getFromEdge has zero coordination between concurrent invocations, each one independently calls await origin.fetch(key) — so you get thousands of simultaneous origin calls, then it goes quiet until the next TTL boundary, hence the sawtooth pattern lined up with the TTL. The primary fix is request coalescing: I'd keep a Map<string, Promise<string>> of in-flight rebuilds, and on a MISS, before calling origin.fetch, check if there's already a promise in flight for that key. If there is, every other caller just awaits that same promise instead of calling origin again — only the first one actually fetches, and once it resolves and calls cache.set, I remove it from the in-flight map. Second, I'd pair that with serve-stale-while-revalidate: instead of blocking the other concurrent readers behind that single in-flight fetch, I'd let the entry live a bit past expiresAt as 'stale but usable' — so while the one coalesced request is out revalidating, everyone else just gets the old cached body immediately, no waiting. That's safe because the staleness window is bounded to roughly the time of one origin round trip, which is the deliberate trade-off — you're accepting a few hundred milliseconds of slightly-stale data across the whole fleet in exchange for turning thousands of origin hits into exactly one. I'd also add an ETag on the cached entry, and have the single coalesced rebuild send If-None-Match — if the origin content hasn't actually changed since last time, you get back a cheap 304 instead of re-transferring the full body, so even that one allowed-through request is often nearly free. To verify, I'd write a load test that fires a large burst of concurrent requests for the same hot key straddling a TTL expiry boundary, and assert on the origin mock that it receives roughly one call per key per refill cycle — not proportional to client count — while every single client still gets back a 200 with a valid body throughout, none of them erroring or blocking indefinitely.

This is a cache stampede — the fixed TTL means every concurrent caller for the same hot key has an identical expiresAt, so when Date.now() passes it, they all miss at the same moment and each one independently does await origin.fetch(key), which is why the origin sees a spike lined up exactly with the TTL instead of steady traffic. The main fix is coalescing the MISS path: track in-flight fetches per key, so if a rebuild for this key is already running, other callers just wait on that same promise rather than firing their own origin.fetch. On top of that I'd let the edge keep serving the stale cached body to everyone else while the one coalesced request is revalidating in the background, so readers aren't blocked, they just get a slightly old response for a short window. I'd verify it with a test that hits the same key with a lot of concurrency right as it expires and check the origin only got called once instead of thousands of times. I didn't think as much about the ETag angle — you could probably also send a conditional request so the rebuild can come back as a 304 if content is unchanged, which would make the single refill even cheaper, but the coalescing plus serve-stale combo is the core of the fix here.

Looking at the code, the problem is that getFromEdge has no locking around the origin.fetch call, so when the TTL for a hot key expires, all the concurrent requests for that key see the entry as stale at the same time and each one goes and hits origin.fetch on its own — that's basically a stampede, everyone piling on the origin right when the TTL boundary hits, which explains the periodic spikes matching the TTL. To fix it I'd add some kind of per-key mutex or in-flight tracking so that only one request actually calls the origin at a time and the rest wait for that result and reuse it instead of all calling origin.fetch independently. That should smooth out the spike since you'd go from thousands of origin calls down to basically one per key expiry. I'd test it by sending a bunch of concurrent requests around when the cache expires and checking the origin doesn't get called an excessive number of times.

I think the issue is just that too many requests are hitting the cache at once when it expires, so the origin gets overloaded. Maybe you could add a lock so requests wait their turn instead of all going through, or just retry with backoff if origin.fetch fails under load. You could also make the cache bigger or add more edge nodes to spread the load out so no single node takes the whole spike. I'd probably just watch the origin's request count in production and see if it goes down after making these changes.

Looking at this code, I think the origin is getting hit hard because the TTL of 30 seconds is just too short for how popular this key is, so it's expiring and refetching way more often than it needs to — if we bump the TTL up to something like 10 minutes the cache would stay warm longer and origin.fetch would get called a lot less. I'd also double check the Map isn't leaking memory since it never evicts old keys, that seems like the real risk here for a long-running process. Maybe also add a try/catch around origin.fetch so if it throws, the whole getFromEdge function doesn't crash the caller. I don't see anything about concurrent requests being a specific problem — as long as the cache holds the entry, subsequent calls just read from cache.get, so it should already be handling repeat traffic fine within the TTL window.

checklist: [problemSolving] Traces the root cause: the handler takes the client-supplied hash as the chunk's claimed identity and uses it directly for the dedup lookup and the object key, instead of deriving identity from the bytes it actually received.

[problemSolving] Explains the failure mode concretely: a wrong (or malicious) claimed hash makes one content's bytes get looked up — and potentially stored — under another content's key, so a later HIT can return bytes that do not match what was asked for, and the dedup index ends up poisoned with an entry whose stored content does not equal its own key.

[technical] Gives the correct fix: recompute the hash server-side from the exact bytes received (after decoding), use that recomputed digest — never the client's claim — as both the lookup key and the object key, and reject the request with HTTP 400 when the client-supplied hash disagrees with it.

[communication] Names the underlying principle precisely: a client-supplied identity claim is unverified input, not proof; the server sits at the trust boundary and must be the sole authority on what a chunk's identity is, exactly the same discipline as validating any other untrusted input.

[testing] Verifies the fix on both sides: send a chunk whose declared hash does not match its actual bytes and confirm the request is now rejected; then send a chunk whose bytes are a genuine duplicate of one already stored and confirm it is still correctly deduplicated (reused object, zero new bytes written).

examples.text: So walking through HandleUploadChunk, the bug is right here: it decodes rawBytes from the base64 payload, but then it never uses rawBytes to compute an identity — it just takes req.ClaimedHash, the client-declared field, and uses that directly as the key into s.dedupIndex, and if it's a miss, it also uses claimedHash as the objectKey it stores rawBytes under. So the store's identity for a chunk is whatever the caller says it is, not what the bytes actually hash to. The failure mode is exactly what the bug report describes: if a client sends bytes that don't match its claimedHash — buggy client, corrupted upload, or just malicious — those bytes get filed under someone else's hash. If that claimedHash happens to collide with an existing entry, a later legitimate dedup HIT for the real content returns objectKey pointing at the wrong bytes. And even in the miss branch, you now have a dedupIndex entry whose stored object doesn't actually hash to its own key, which is the index poisoning they mentioned. The fix is to compute the real SHA256 server-side from rawBytes right after the base64 decode, use that computed digest as both the dedup lookup key and the objectKey — never claimedHash for either — and if claimedHash is provided and doesn't match, return 400 immediately instead of trusting it. The underlying principle is trust-boundary discipline: a client-supplied identity claim is just untrusted input, same as any other field in the request body, and the server has to be the sole authority on what a chunk's content-address actually is — you never let the caller assert its own hash and act on it. To verify, I'd write two tests: one that sends a chunk with a claimedHash that doesn't match its actual bytes and assert we now get a 400 instead of a stored/poisoned entry, and one that sends bytes that are a genuine duplicate of something already stored and confirm it still returns dedup:true with the existing objectKey and zero new bytes written to s.objects.

Looking at the handler, the problem is in how it decides the chunk's key. It decodes rawBytes from base64, which is good, but then it ignores those bytes for identity purposes and just uses req.ClaimedHash for the dedupIndex lookup and as the objectKey when storing. So the store trusts whatever hash the client sends instead of deriving it from what was actually uploaded. That means someone could send a claimedHash that doesn't correspond to the actual data — accidentally or on purpose — and the chunk gets stored or looked up under the wrong key, so a later request for that hash could get back content that doesn't match. The fix is to compute the SHA256 of rawBytes on the server after decoding and use that as the real key everywhere, not the client's claim, and reject the request if it doesn't match what the client said. This is basically a case of not validating input — you can't let the client dictate something as important as the storage key without checking it against the actual data. To test it I'd send a chunk with a mismatched hash and make sure it gets rejected, and also send a real duplicate to make sure dedup still works correctly.

I think the issue is that this uses claimedHash from the request instead of actually hashing the data. So it just trusts what the client says the hash is, and stores things under that. That could cause chunks to get mixed up if the hash doesn't actually match the bytes — like you could end up serving the wrong content back to someone. The fix would be to compute the hash from rawBytes on the server side and use that instead of trusting the client value. That seems like a case of not trusting client input. I'd test it by sending some bad data and seeing what happens.

Yeah, it uses ClaimedHash for the dedup index which seems risky because it comes from the client. I guess if it's wrong then the wrong thing could get stored. Maybe you should double check it somehow before using it. I'd probably add some validation on that field. Not totally sure how I'd test it exactly, maybe just try uploading a chunk and see if it comes back right.

If there's a bug I'd guess it's something about concurrency, like maybe two requests hitting the lock at the same time causing a race, or maybe the JSON encoding of the response is silently failing somewhere since the error from json.NewEncoder isn't checked. checklist: [technical] Identifies the exact defect: hashing is computed over a full fixed-size window that the chunk's bytes were copied into, rather than over only the real slice of the source payload — for the final, shorter-than-full chunk this means the digest is taken over "real tail bytes + leftover padding," not over the real tail alone.

[problemSolving] Reasons about why this breaks content-addressing specifically: the same real tail bytes stored or uploaded anywhere else hash to the digest of THOSE bytes alone, while this chunk's digest is the hash of those bytes plus padding — the two digests never match, so a dedup lookup never finds the tail, and re-hashing the true stored bytes during an integrity check never reproduces the recorded digest either.

[communication] States the invariant plainly and correctly: unless the file's total size is an exact multiple of the fixed chunk size, the final chunk is legitimately smaller than a full chunk, and the sum of every chunk's recorded size must equal the file's total size — never padded up to it.

[technical] Gives the concrete fix without changing the chunking scheme: only the actual byte range should ever be hashed and recorded — hash the real slice of the source payload, clamped to its true end, and record each chunk's size as that slice's true length; never allocate a fixed-size window and hash the whole thing regardless of how many real bytes it holds.

[testing] Proposes a verifying test: chunk a file whose size is not an exact multiple of the fixed chunk size (e.g. one-and-a-half chunks), assert the last chunk's recorded size equals the true remaining byte count and that all chunk sizes sum to the total size, then store the identical tail bytes as their own separate object and confirm the hashes match — a dedup hit — instead of diverging.

examples.text: So the bug is right here: `n, err := r.Read(buf)` tells you exactly how many valid bytes came back, but then `sha256.Sum256(buf)` hashes the whole 4 MiB buffer instead of `buf[:n]`, and `store.Put(hash, buf)` stores the whole buffer too — same mistake in two places. On every full chunk that's invisible because n equals chunkSize, so buf really is all real data. But buf is a single buffer allocated once outside the loop and reused every iteration, never cleared, so on the final shorter chunk the bytes past index n are just stale leftovers from the previous Read call, not part of this file at all. That means the digest recorded for the last chunk is SHA-256 of 'real tail bytes plus leftover padding', not of the real tail alone — and Size is hardcoded to chunkSize instead of n, so the store thinks every chunk is full-size. That's exactly why dedup never hits: if those same tail bytes are stored anywhere else as their own object, they hash to the digest of just those bytes, which can never equal this chunk's padded digest. It also explains the integrity sweeps — reading back the actual stored bytes and re-hashing them reproduces the clean hash of the real tail, which never matches the padded hash that got recorded at write time. Fix: always slice to `buf[:n]` for both the hash and the Put call, and record `Size: n`, never hash a fixed window wholesale regardless of how many bytes were actually read. To verify I'd chunk a file that's 1.5 chunks long, assert the last chunk's Size equals the true remaining bytes and that all Sizes sum to the file's total size, then store that same tail slice as its own object and confirm the hashes now match — a real dedup hit.

I think the problem is in the Split loop — it does `sha256.Sum256(buf)` and `store.Put(hash, buf)` using the whole buf slice, but `r.Read(buf)` only guarantees the first n bytes are valid this time around. For a full 4 MiB chunk that's fine since n equals chunkSize, but the last chunk of a file is almost never a full window, so you're hashing n real bytes plus whatever was left in that buffer from before, since it's the same buf reused across the whole loop and never reset. So the digest for the last chunk isn't a digest of the actual tail data, it's a digest of tail-plus-junk. That breaks content addressing — the same real bytes stored somewhere else as their own chunk would produce a different, 'clean' hash, so the store never recognizes them as the same content and dedup silently misses. The fix is to hash and store `buf[:n]` instead of `buf`, and set Size to n rather than the constant chunkSize. I'd test this with a file whose size isn't an exact multiple of chunkSize and check the last chunk's recorded size matches what's actually left over.

Looking at the loop, buf is declared once outside and reused on every Read call, so I'm a little suspicious that on the last, smaller read it might still have old data sitting in the part that wasn't overwritten. The code hashes buf directly and stores buf directly rather than trimming it to what Read actually returned, so I think the last chunk could end up hashing more bytes than it should. That would make the hash not really represent the true content of that last piece of the file. I'm not 100% sure how that connects to the dedup-miss symptom exactly, but it seems like it would make the hash different from what you'd get hashing just the real bytes on their own, so a matching chunk elsewhere wouldn't be recognized. For the fix I'd say you need to only use the actual bytes read, not the whole buffer, and probably also fix how Size gets set since it's just always chunkSize right now which seems wrong for a partial chunk. I don't have a concrete test in mind, just something that uses a file that doesn't divide evenly into chunks.

My first thought is that buf is a shared buffer being reused across iterations, so there might be some issue with the data not being reset between reads — like maybe it's not fully overwritten every time. That seems like it could cause weird hash mismatches somewhere in there. The Size field is also just set to the constant chunkSize on every chunk, which looks off to me since I'd expect it to vary, though I'm not totally sure why that would cause the dedup problem specifically. Maybe you'd want to zero out the buffer at the start of each loop iteration to be safe. I'm not confident on the exact mechanism connecting this to the corruption alerts on read-back though.

Honestly the loop structure looks pretty standard to me — read into a buffer, hash it, store it, repeat until EOF. My guess is the dedup issue is more likely something on the store side, like maybe the map isn't safe for concurrent access if multiple goroutines call Put at the same time, or maybe SHA-256 just isn't a great fit here and they should switch to something faster like a non-cryptographic hash for speed. The corruption sweeps flagging perfectly fine data sounds more like a bug in whatever reads the data back afterward, or maybe a filesystem-level issue, rather than anything in this Split function. I don't really see anything in this chunking code itself that would produce wrong hashes since Read and Sum256 are both standard library calls doing what they're documented to do.

prompt: We're building the chunk-storage layer for our distributed file service — resumable, chunked uploads with content-addressed dedup, where every chunk is hashed with sha256 and identical chunks across different files should be stored only once. A senior engineer just submitted the `File` persistence model and the "mark a chunk as uploaded" service method for review, shown below. Walk me through the schema and this code as if you were reviewing the pull request: where does this design break down as the number of files and chunks grows, and what would you recommend instead? Be specific about how you'd verify your recommendation actually fixes the problem.
checklist: [technical] Points out you cannot index an individual chunk's sha256, so the global dedup lookup ("does this sha256 exist anywhere?") degrades to scanning and parsing every file's array; likewise "which chunkIndex is missing?" for resumable can't use an index either.

[problemSolving] Flags write amplification and races: every per-chunk update must read-parse-rewrite the entire array, and two concurrent chunk writes can lost-update each other; the separate chunkCount column can also drift from the real array length, so there is no single source of truth.

[communication] Recommends the normalized file (1) → chunk (N) model with a unique (fileId, chunkIndex) index, and fairly states the trade-off — a JSON blob is simpler to read as a whole, but it blocks exactly the per-chunk queries the system is built around.

[testing] Suggests validating the recommendation: an EXPLAIN on a sha256 filter should hit an index in the normalized model, and a concurrent two-chunk write must not lose either update — the failing case for the JSON design.

examples.text: So the root problem here is that `chunks` is one JSONB blob on the `File` row instead of its own table, and `sha256` and `chunkIndex` only exist as keys inside that array — they're not real, indexable columns. That means `findChunkBySha256` has to run `jsonb_array_elements` and unnest every row's entire array just to check whether a hash exists anywhere in the system, and dedup lookup is supposed to be the hot path here, so that's going to degrade badly as both file count and chunk count grow. `getMissingChunkIndexes` has the exact same structural issue for resume — there's no index that can answer 'which chunkIndex values are missing,' it has to pull the whole file and filter in JS. Then in `markChunkUploaded` we're doing a full read-parse-mutate-rewrite of the entire array to flip one `uploaded` boolean, which is heavy write amplification for a file with thousands of chunks, and worse — two concurrent calls for two different chunkIndex values both read the array before either writes back, so one save silently clobbers the other's update. On top of that, `chunkCount` is a standalone column with nothing enforcing it equals `chunks.length`, so there's no single source of truth for chunk count either. I'd recommend normalizing to a `Chunk` table — `fileId, chunkIndex, sha256, sizeBytes, uploaded` — with a unique index on `sha256` for dedup and a unique composite index on `(fileId, chunkIndex)`, which turns both queries into indexed lookups and turns the per-chunk update into an atomic single-row write that can't race with a different chunkIndex. I'd be honest that the JSONB version is simpler to read in one shot, but that's the wrong trade for a system whose whole job is per-chunk operations. To actually prove the fix, I'd run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the sha256 filter and confirm it hits an index scan, and I'd write a concurrency test firing two simultaneous chunk updates on the same file and assert both persist — that's the exact case that loses data today.

The big red flag for me is that `sha256` and `chunkIndex` live inside a JSONB array, not as actual columns, so `findChunkBySha256` can't use an index — it has to unnest `chunks` on every row of the `files` table just to check if one hash exists anywhere, which is exactly the query dedup depends on and it's going to get slower as the table grows. `getMissingChunkIndexes` has the same problem — no index to ask 'what's still missing,' it just loads the file and filters client-side. On the write side, `markChunkUploaded` reads the whole array, mutates one entry, and saves the whole array back — that's a lot of write amplification for one chunk, and if two uploads for different chunks land at the same time, they can both read before either writes, so one update overwrites the other. My recommendation would be to split this into a proper `Chunk` table keyed by `fileId` and `chunkIndex`, with `sha256` indexed for the dedup lookup — that gets both queries onto indexes and makes each chunk update a single-row write instead of touching the whole manifest. The JSONB approach is simpler to read as one blob, but this system needs per-chunk queries constantly, so that's the wrong optimization. I'd want to actually run this through an EXPLAIN plan on the dedup query before and after to confirm the index is really being used, not just assume the schema change fixes it.

Looking at the schema, the chunks are stored as a JSONB array on the file row, and I think that's going to cause performance problems as things scale, especially the `findChunkBySha256` method — it has to scan through the JSON for every file to find a match, which isn't going to be fast once there are a lot of files. I'd probably want to pull chunks out into their own table so sha256 can be indexed properly. For `markChunkUploaded`, it loads the file, updates one chunk in the array, and saves the whole file back, which seems like it's doing more work than it needs to for just marking one chunk uploaded. I think a normalized `Chunk` table with `fileId` and `chunkIndex` would be cleaner and let each of these methods query directly instead of loading everything and filtering in code. I'd want to test the dedup lookup with a decent amount of data to see how much slower it gets compared to a version with an actual index on sha256.

I think storing chunks as JSONB is a bit unusual — most of the time I'd expect a separate table for something like this. The `findChunkBySha256` method looks a little inefficient since it has to look inside the JSON column, so that might be slow for big files. Maybe adding an index on the file or using a different data type would help. The `markChunkUploaded` function seems fine to me, it finds the chunk and updates it and saves — I don't see anything obviously broken there, though I guess if a file has a lot of chunks, saving the whole thing each time isn't ideal. Overall I'd probably just suggest keeping an eye on performance once we have real data volume, and maybe revisit the JSONB decision later if it becomes a bottleneck.

Honestly this looks pretty solid to me — the `File` entity has all the fields you'd want, filename, owner, size, and the chunk manifest is right there on the row so you get the whole picture in one query, which seems convenient for the frontend. The `markChunkUploaded` method does what it says, finds the chunk by index and flips it to uploaded, that's straightforward. Naming is clean too, `ChunkManifestEntry` is a good descriptive name. If I had a nitpick it'd be more about style — maybe `chunkCount` could be a computed getter instead of a stored column, just so it's a little less code to maintain, but that's minor. I don't see any major issues with the dedup or resume logic, they both return the data you'd need. I'd probably approve this with maybe a small comment about renaming a variable or two.

checklist: [problemSolving] Identifies that appending outlinks instead of replacing them leaves stale edges behind: a page's outlinks are the CURRENT state of that page, not a running log, so an insert-only write on every re-parse makes the graph grow monotonically instead of reflecting what the page links to right now.

[technical] Gives the correct fix: delete the page's existing edges (the rows where the source column equals this page) before inserting the newly extracted set — outlinks are a set replaced per parse, never accumulated — and notes that an upsert keyed on (from, to) alone is not enough, since it still leaves any stale edge that isn't in the new set untouched.

[communication] Explains the downstream effect in terms a teammate would immediately understand: stale inbound edges inflate a URL's in-degree, which inflates its PageRank — a silent bug that produces no error and is brutal to trace on a real corpus because the ranking just quietly drifts.

[testing] Proposes a concrete verification: re-parse the same page with FEWER outlinks than the previous parse and assert the stored link count for that page equals the new count exactly, not the running sum of every parse ever performed on it.

examples.text: So this loop is doing an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (from_url, to_url) DO NOTHING for every extracted link, and that's the core problem — it's an insert-only write path with no delete step, so it treats link_graph as an append-only log instead of the current snapshot of what fromUrl links to right now. The docstring literally says outlinks can shrink, grow, or change entirely between parses, but saveOutlinks never accounts for shrinking or removal — old edges from a previous parse just sit there forever. What I'd tell the author is: before inserting the new batch, delete every existing row where from_url equals this page — ideally wrap the delete and the inserts in a single transaction so PageRank never reads a half-updated state — and then insert the fresh set. And I'd push back on 'just make it an upsert keyed on from_url/to_url' as the fix, because that still doesn't remove an edge that existed in the old parse but isn't in the new one; upsert handles changed or duplicate edges, not disappeared ones. The blast radius here is nasty because it's silent — PageRank reads in-degree straight off this table, so a page that used to link to X but no longer does will keep inflating X's in-degree and therefore its rank, and there's no error or exception anywhere to point you at it. Before I approve, I'd want a test that re-parses the same fromUrl with strictly fewer outlinks than the prior parse and asserts the stored link count equals the new count exactly — not the cumulative count across every historical parse — because that's the exact scenario this code currently fails.

Looking at saveOutlinks, the loop just does an INSERT with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for each link — there's no delete anywhere, so every re-parse only ever adds rows to link_graph, it never removes the ones that shouldn't be there anymore. Since a page's outlinks are supposed to represent what's on the page right now, not a history of everything it's ever linked to, this will make the table grow forever even if the real page content shrinks. My fix would be to delete the existing rows for that from_url first, then insert the new set — basically treat it as replace-the-set-per-parse, not accumulate. I'd flag it as not safe to merge as-is because PageRank reads in-degree off this table, so stale inbound edges are going to inflate ranks for pages that shouldn't have them anymore. I'd probably also ask for a test that re-crawls a page with a smaller link set and checks the row count matches, just to make sure the fix actually works before we ship it.

Hmm, so on every call it inserts the outlinks with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, which prevents duplicate inserts of the exact same edge, so I think it handles the case where a page keeps linking to the same things fine. The comment says outlinks can change between parses though, so if a link gets removed from the page, I don't think this code removes it from the table — it would just stay there from the last time. That seems like it could be a bug because the table would have extra links that aren't real anymore. I guess you'd want to clear out the old links for that page before writing the new ones, so the table matches the actual current page. I'm not 100% sure how that affects PageRank directly, but it seems like it would make the graph bigger than it should be, so I'd flag it for the author to look at before merging.

I think the ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is mainly there to avoid duplicate key errors if the same link gets parsed twice, so that part looks reasonable to me. The main thing I'd double check is whether from_url and to_url are indexed properly since this runs in a loop and could be slow for pages with a lot of outlinks — maybe a batch insert would be faster. I guess if links get removed from a page it might not clean up in the table, but that seems like a smaller edge case, not something that would block the merge. Overall I'd say it looks mostly fine, maybe just ask about performance on pages with a ton of links and move on.

This looks fine to me honestly — it's inserting the outlinks into link_graph with a conflict guard so we don't get duplicate rows, and the pool.query calls are parameterized so there's no SQL injection risk either. The function name and the types all line up with what saveOutlinks is supposed to do, and the JSDoc explains the schema clearly enough. I don't see anything that would block a merge here, it does what the docstring says — saves the outlinks for the page into the table. Maybe I'd add error handling around the pool.query call in case the DB connection drops mid-loop, but otherwise I'd approve this as is.

prompt: You're optimizing the storage layer of a high-performance web crawler. Crawled pages are persisted to a single Postgres table via a TypeORM entity: each row keeps lightweight metadata (url, host, statusCode, crawledAt) plus the entire raw HTML of the page inline in a `htmlBody` text column.
