checklist.text: [problemSolving] Diagnoses the actual cost: the endpoint runs a full-table SUM per direction over an immutable, ever-growing ledger table — that is O(rows), and the history below the newest rows never changes, so recomputing the whole sum from scratch on every single call is pure waste, not a scaling coincidence.

[technical] Proposes replacing the on-demand full scan with incrementally maintained running totals — a summary table (or a materialized view) kept up to date by a trigger or a CDC stream as new ledger rows are appended, refreshed on a short interval — so the per-request invariant check becomes an O(1) read of two numbers instead of an O(rows) aggregation.

[communication] Points out that the account balance is already an O(1) write-through cache updated inline with every transfer, so only the GLOBAL invariant SUM scales with the size of the ledger; frames the fix as separating a fast per-request read path from a periodic full-history verification, rather than just proposing "add a cache" without saying what maintains or invalidates it.

[testing] Verifies the cheap summary can never silently lie: cross-checks the incrementally maintained total against a periodic authoritative full-table SUM (e.g. a nightly reconciliation job) and alerts loudly the moment the two diverge, so a bug in the incremental path is caught instead of quietly masking a real imbalance.

examples.text: The core insight is that `ledger` is append-only and immutable — once a row is written it never changes, so `verifyInvariant()` doesn't need to re-sum the entire table every time; it only needs to account for rows that appeared since the last time we checked. I'd add a small `ledger_checkpoint` table (or a single row) that stores a watermark, either `lastVerifiedId` or `createdAt`, plus the running `totalCredit` and `totalDebit` accumulated up to that point. Then `checkInvariant()` becomes: read the checkpoint, sum only the rows past that watermark (I'd add a composite index like `(direction, id)` since right now only `accountId` is indexed), add that delta to the cached totals, compare, and if balanced advance the checkpoint to the new max id. Better still, I'd update those running totals directly inside `TransferService.transfer()`, in the same transaction that writes the debit/credit rows, the same way `account.balance` is already maintained as a write-through cache — that turns `checkInvariant()` into an O(1) read of two counters instead of any aggregation at all. Because the ledger is append-only, there's no risk of missing an update in the delta window; rows never get retroactively edited. To keep the guarantee just as strong as before, since we're now trusting an incrementally maintained cache instead of re-deriving from source on every call, I'd still run a full `SUM()` reconciliation as a scheduled background job that compares against the cached counters and alerts loudly on drift, so a bug in the incremental path still gets caught, just off the hot request path.

Since `ledger` rows are only ever inserted, `verifyInvariant()` doesn't have to rescan everything on each call — I'd keep a running total of credits and debits that gets updated incrementally whenever `TransferService.transfer()` writes a new debit/credit pair, similar to how `account.balance` is already kept as a write-through cache. I'd store those two running totals in a small dedicated table, and `checkInvariant()` would just read them and compare, which is O(1) instead of the two full-table `SUM()` queries it runs today. I'd update the running totals inside the same DB transaction as the ledger insert in `transfer()` so they can never drift out of sync with the rows that were actually written. One thing I'd still want is some periodic full-table reconciliation job, otherwise a bug in the increment logic could silently poison the cached totals forever without anything ever re-checking them against the real ledger.

I'd cache the totals somewhere instead of running `SUM()` over the whole `ledger` table on every `GET /ledger/invariant` call, since that's what's making it slow as the table grows. Maybe store `totalCredit` and `totalDebit` in Redis or a small table and update them whenever `transfer()` runs, so `checkInvariant()` reads from the cache instead of hitting the ledger table with two aggregation queries. I'd also consider just caching the whole response for a short TTL — since the ledger is append-only the answer barely changes between calls, so most requests in a short window could return the cached result without touching Postgres at all. That should bring the cost way down without changing the actual `SUM(CREDIT) === SUM(DEBIT)` check.

The two `SUM()` queries in `verifyInvariant()` are probably what's slow, so I'd add an index on `ledger.direction` so Postgres can find the CREDIT and DEBIT rows faster instead of scanning them all. I could also combine the two separate queries into one with a `GROUP BY direction`, which would cut it down to a single table scan instead of two round trips. That should make `checkInvariant()` a bit faster as the table grows into the millions.

Honestly the code looks fine to me — `checkInvariant()` uses `createQueryBuilder` and TypeORM already optimizes queries under the hood, so Postgres should be able to handle millions of rows without much trouble. If it's slow, maybe it's more of a NestJS wiring issue, like `LedgerService` not being registered as a singleton, or the `@Get('invariant')` route just needing some caching middleware at the HTTP layer. I'd probably just add `@nestjs/throttler` to rate-limit the endpoint so it isn't called too often — that should take care of the performance complaint without touching the query logic.

checklist: [problemSolving] Identifies the waste precisely: a full scan re-checks every account regardless of whether it has had any activity since the last run, and a single concurrency=1 worker walking billions of accounts every cycle cannot possibly finish inside the reconciliation window — the bottleneck is architectural, not a matter of making the SUM query faster.

[technical] Proposes partitioning the account base (by id hash, by country, or by product line) so each partition runs its own independent reconcile job with its own queue, letting partitions execute in parallel; and layers an activity-driven filter on top — a CDC stream (e.g. Debezium) off the ledger table, or Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY — so a run only re-checks accounts with new activity since the cut-off, instead of recomputing the SUM for every account that hasn't moved.

[communication] Explains the design as a trade-off, not just "shard it": argues why parallelism alone (partitioning) doesn't fix the waste (untouched accounts are still rescanned inside each partition) and why activity-driven filtering alone doesn't fix the throughput ceiling (a single worker per partition still exists) — the two changes are complementary, not substitutes for each other.

[testing] Insists on keeping the correctness invariants while scaling: each partition still runs with exactly one worker (concurrency=1) so no account is ever double-fixed by two workers racing on the same partition, and every run — partitioned or not — still reconciles against a cut-off timestamp so in-flight transactions aren't mistaken for drift; proposes a periodic full sweep as a backstop to prove the activity-driven path never silently misses a real drift.

examples.text: There are really two separate bottlenecks stacked on top of each other here, and neither is a query-tuning problem. First, `runReconciliation` calls `accountRepo.find()` with no filter at all, so every one of a billion accounts gets enqueued every single night even if it had zero ledger activity since the last run — that's pure wasted work. Second, the processor is declared with `concurrency: 1`, so it's one worker draining the queue sequentially; even if the SUM query were instant, you're bound by per-job latency times a billion, and no amount of query optimization removes that ceiling — it's architectural. So I'd attack both axes. For throughput, partition the account base — by hash of account id, or by a real boundary like country or product line — and give each partition its own queue and its own scheduled job so partitions reconcile in parallel instead of one giant serial walk. For waste, layer an activity-driven filter on top: stream ledger writes through Debezium CDC, or use Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY, to know which accounts actually moved since the cutoff, and only enqueue those. Those two changes are complementary, not substitutes — partitioning alone still re-sums every untouched account inside each partition, and the CDC filter alone still funnels everything through a single worker per partition, so you need both to actually close the gap. On correctness, I'd keep concurrency=1 per partition queue exactly like the original, so two workers can never race on the same account and double-insert a compensating entry, and I'd keep the single cutoff `Date()` captured at the top of the run so in-flight writes after that instant are never mistaken for drift. I'd also still run a periodic full, unfiltered sweep — say weekly — as a backstop, because trusting a CDC stream to never silently drop an event is a bigger assumption than I want baked into a financial reconciliation job.

The core issue is that `accountRepo.find()` loads every account with no activity filter, and the processor runs at `concurrency: 1`, so you've got both a full unnecessary rescan and a single-threaded bottleneck baked into the same job. I'd fix the throughput side by partitioning accounts — by id hash or by product line — so each partition gets its own queue and can run independently in parallel instead of one worker walking a billion rows. For the waste side, I'd add a change-tracking mechanism, like a CDC stream off the ledger table, so a run only touches accounts that had new entries since the last cutoff instead of re-summing everyone every night. I'd keep the cutoff timestamp captured once at the start of the run, same as the current code does, so it stays consistent and doesn't pick up in-flight transactions. And I'd keep each partition's queue at concurrency=1 so you don't get two workers racing on the same account and double-compensating it. I'd probably want a periodic full sweep too just to sanity-check the filtered path isn't missing anything, though I haven't fully thought through how often that needs to run.

Honestly the main thing that jumps out is the single worker — `concurrency: 1` means everything is serialized, and with a billion accounts that's never going to fit in the window no matter how fast the SUM query is. So I'd shard the account table, maybe by id hash, and spin up multiple queues or workers so you get real parallelism instead of one worker doing everything. That should get you most of the way there in terms of raw throughput. I'd keep the cutoff timestamp as it is, captured once before the scan starts, so it doesn't double-count anything that comes in mid-run. For correctness across the new workers, I'd make sure each account only ever gets processed by one job at a time, otherwise you could end up inserting two compensating entries for the same drift. I didn't dig too deep into whether the full account scan itself is a problem — more workers processing it in parallel should cover most of the scaling need.

I think the fix here is mostly about throughput — a billion accounts through one worker is just too slow, so I'd bump up the concurrency on the Bull processor, maybe run it with several workers instead of one, and possibly add an index on `ledger.account_id` and `created_at` to make the SUM query faster per account. That should help it finish inside the window. I'd probably also batch the accounts into chunks when enqueuing them instead of adding them one by one in the loop, which might cut down some overhead. I didn't really think about the case where two workers touch the same account at once, but I'd guess Bull handles that automatically. The cutoff timestamp logic looks fine as it is, so I wouldn't change that part.

I mean, the logic looks correct to me — it computes the SUM of the ledger and compares it to the stored balance, inserts an adjustment if it's off, that's a pretty standard reconciliation pattern. If it's slow at a billion accounts, I'd probably just look at making the database bigger or giving it more CPU, or maybe caching the account list so `accountRepo.find()` doesn't have to hit the database every time it runs. The cron is only once a day so I don't think timing is that critical — even if it runs a bit long it should still catch up eventually. I don't see anything wrong with using a single worker either, since it makes the code simpler and easier to reason about. Honestly I'm not sure what specifically needs to change here.

checklist: [problemSolving] Diagnoses the ABBA cycle: transfer A→B locks account A then waits on account B, while the concurrent transfer B→A locks account B then waits on account A — each transaction ends up holding exactly what the other one needs, so Postgres detects the cycle and aborts one with a "deadlock detected" error.

[technical] Names the root cause precisely: the handler locks the two accounts in request/argument order (fromAccountId, then toAccountId) instead of a deterministic order, and gives the fix — acquire the row locks in a fixed order independent of transfer direction, e.g. sort the two account ids and lock the lexicographically smaller one first.

[communication] Explains clearly why deterministic ordering breaks the cycle: both transfers now request the same first row regardless of direction, so the second one cleanly waits behind the first instead of forming a cycle — while transfers between disjoint account pairs still run fully in parallel, so no throughput is sacrificed.

[testing] Verifies the fix by firing many concurrent opposite-direction transfers on the same account pair and confirming zero "deadlock detected" errors, correct final balances on both accounts, and an intact SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT) invariant across the ledger.

examples.text: Okay, so this is a classic ABBA deadlock. Look at the lock order in `transfer`: it always does `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on `fromAccountId` first, then `toAccountId` — literally in the order the caller passed the arguments. So if I fire a transfer A→B at the same instant as a transfer B→A, the first transaction locks row A and is about to wait on row B, while the second transaction has already locked row B and is now waiting on row A. Each one is holding exactly what the other needs, that's the cycle, and Postgres's deadlock detector picks one victim and kills it with 'deadlock detected' — which matches exactly what you're seeing: only account pairs that move money in both directions concurrently trip it, single-direction and unrelated pairs never do because there's no cycle possible. The fix is to stop locking in caller-argument order and instead lock in a deterministic order that's independent of transfer direction — e.g. compare `fromAccountId` and `toAccountId` as strings, always `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the lexicographically smaller id first, then the larger one, and just track which balance is 'from' and which is 'to' separately for the actual UPDATE and ledger logic. With that change, an A→B and a B→A transfer both request the same first row, so the second one just queues behind the first and proceeds normally once it commits — no cycle, no deadlock. Transfers between disjoint pairs never contend on the same first row so they stay fully parallel, so there's no throughput cost. To verify, I'd write a load test that spins up dozens of concurrent transfers alternating A→B and B→A on the same pair for a while, assert zero 'deadlock detected' errors and no unexpected 500s, then check the final balances on both accounts add up correctly and that `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)` holds across `ledger_entries` to make sure I didn't break atomicity while adding the ordering fix.

This looks like a deadlock caused by lock ordering. The handler takes `FOR UPDATE` on `fromAccountId` first and `toAccountId` second, in whatever order they're passed in. When two transfers run concurrently in opposite directions on the same pair of accounts, one locks A then wants B, the other locks B then wants A — that's a cycle, and Postgres aborts one of them, which is exactly why only reciprocal pairs fail and one-way transfers are fine. The fix is to always lock the two rows in a fixed order regardless of direction, like sorting the account ids and locking the smaller one first, so both transactions are forced to contend for the same first lock instead of each grabbing a different one and waiting on the other. That breaks the cycle since the second transaction just blocks and waits its turn rather than deadlocking. For verification I'd run a bunch of concurrent A→B/B→A transfers and check we stop seeing 'deadlock detected' in the logs, and confirm the balances end up correct afterward.

So the issue is probably about the order the two `SELECT FOR UPDATE` calls happen in — it locks `fromAccountId` and then `toAccountId`. If two transfers go opposite directions at the same time, they might end up each waiting on the row the other one holds, and that's what triggers the deadlock in Postgres. I think the fix is to lock the accounts in some consistent order instead of just source-then-destination, so it doesn't matter which direction the transfer is going. Maybe sort the ids before locking. I'd test it by running some transfers concurrently and seeing if the deadlock errors go away and the balances still look right.

I think this might be a locking issue since it's using `FOR UPDATE` on both accounts. Maybe when two transfers happen at the same time it causes a conflict because both are trying to lock rows. I'd probably add a retry so that if it fails with a deadlock error we just try the transaction again — that should smooth over the intermittent 500s. I'm not totally sure why it only happens with A→B and B→A specifically though. To check it works I'd just run it a few times and see if it still throws errors.

checklist: [problemSolving] Identifies the exact failure window: a crash between the applied HTTP side effect and the post-hoc audit write loses all evidence the step ran, so recovery cannot tell whether to continue or compensate — money may be moved with no trace.

[technical] Gives the fix: write the saga_step row with status "started" BEFORE the HTTP call leaves the process, then update it to ok/failed after — the same write-ahead-log discipline of recording intent before the side effect.

[communication] Explains why the durable audit table, not the in-memory call stack, must be the source of truth: a "started"-with-no-follow-up row is precisely the signal a recovery scan looks for to find in-doubt steps.

[testing] Verifies by killing the orchestrator mid-saga (after the side effect, before completion) and confirming a recovery scan finds the in-doubt "started" step and can query wallet-service via the sagaId+step idempotency key to resume or compensate.

examples.text: The bug is in executeStep. We call this.walletService.applyStep first, and only after that HTTP call returns do we insert the saga_step row. So the crash window is exactly the gap between the wallet-service call landing and the insert() executing. If the process dies right there, the money has already moved but there's zero durable evidence the step was even attempted, because we only ever write rows with status ok or failed - there's no row for 'in flight'. That's exactly what happened in prod: recoveryScan found nothing, because it just checks recordedKeys.has(idempotencyKey) and treats a missing key as 'never attempted', so it would just re-run executeStep and call wallet-service again for a step that already succeeded. The fix is write-ahead logging: before calling walletService.applyStep, insert a saga_step row with status 'started' using the idempotencyKey. Then after the HTTP call resolves, update that same row to ok or failed. That way the durable table, not the in-memory stack, is the source of truth - a crash after the HTTP call still leaves a 'started' row with no follow-up, and that's precisely the signal recoveryScan should look for. Right now recoveryScan only distinguishes 'recorded' vs 'not recorded'; it needs a third branch for status === 'started' that means 'in-doubt, go query wallet-service by idempotencyKey to find out if it actually applied, then resume or compensate' - since applyStep is presumably idempotent on that key, we can safely query or retry. I'd verify this by writing a test that kills the orchestrator right after the walletService.applyStep call resolves but before the status update, then run recoveryScan and assert it finds the 'started' row and calls into wallet-service with the sagaId+step key to check idempotently rather than blindly re-executing or ignoring it.

If the process crashes between those two lines, the transfer already happened on the wallet-service side but the saga_step table has no row for it at all. That matches the incident: process died right after the HTTP call, and recoveryScan found nothing because it only checks for existing rows and there wasn't one. The fix is to insert a 'started' row before calling walletService.applyStep, then update it to ok or failed afterward. That gives you a trace even if it dies mid-flight. I'd also point out recoveryScan's logic needs to change - right now it only checks recordedKeys.has(...) as true/false, so it can't tell the difference between a step that never ran and one that's stuck in-doubt. It would need to look at the status field and treat 'started' specially, probably by re-checking against wallet-service using the idempotency key before deciding whether to resume or compensate. I'd test this by simulating a crash right after the applyStep call and confirming the recovery scan picks up the started-but-incomplete row.

So there's a window right after applyStep succeeds where if the app crashes, nothing gets saved to saga_step. To test it I'd try crashing the process in the middle and see if the row shows up as pending afterward.

I'd say maybe just wrap the insert and the HTTP call in the same try block differently, or add some retry logic in case the insert fails. Could also add logging so at least we have some server logs of the attempt even if the DB write didn't happen. Might help to add a timeout or health check too so we catch the crash faster next time. I think adding more error handling around the insert call itself would help make it more robust in general.

Honestly this code looks fine to me - it's using try/catch properly and it does log both the ok and failed cases into the audit table, so I'm not sure what's missing. Maybe the issue is that wallet-service itself is unreliable, since it's a separate HTTP service, so the fix would be to add retries on the applyStep call in case the request itself failed silently. Could also be a network timeout issue where the request took too long and got killed by some proxy. The recoveryScan function looks fine too, it loops through active sagas and checks if the step already ran, so I don't see a bug there specifically.

checklist: [technical] Points out that money values in minor units exceed 2^53, so Number/double arithmetic rounds silently — the computed drift and any compensating amount become wrong above that magnitude.

[problemSolving] Prescribes big-integer arithmetic end to end (BigInt / int64 / BigInteger / decimal depending on stack) and serializing amounts as strings in JSON so no downstream consumer re-coerces them to a float.

[communication] Explains the danger is that it is silent: no exception fires, the invariant just quietly breaks — which is far worse than a loud failure — hence the strict "never coerce money to float" rule across all four languages.

[testing] Verifies with a drift value above 2^53 (or a known very large balance) and asserts the computed drift and compensating amount are exact, and that the JSON carries strings rather than numbers.

examples.text: The core problem is that expectedBalance, actualBalance, drift, and compensatingAmount are all typed as `number`, so this reduce over amountMinorUnits and the subsequent subtraction run through IEEE-754 doubles. Doubles only give you exact integer precision up to 2^53 minus one, which is about nine quadrillion cents, or roughly ninety trillion dollars — sounds huge until you sum thousands of ledger entries across a large wallet or a high-volume merchant account, at which point you can cross that threshold and the arithmetic silently starts rounding. And that's the part that scares me the most: there's no exception, no NaN, no crash — the reduce just returns a value that's off by a cent or a dollar and nobody notices until an audit flags it, and by then compensatingAmount has already been posted downstream as a wrong correcting entry, so you're compounding the drift instead of fixing it. Before this merges I'd switch amountMinorUnits, expectedBalance, actualBalance, drift, and compensatingAmount to BigInt end to end — the reduce initial value becomes 0n, the entity column needs a bigint or numeric transformer so TypeORM doesn't hand you a JS number back, and the interface fields all become bigint. The other thing I'd flag is the JSON serialization comment — 'gets serialized straight to JSON for downstream consumers.' JSON.stringify throws on BigInt by default, which is actually good because it forces you to be explicit: convert to a decimal string before returning, e.g. drift: drift.toString(), so the saga orchestrator and audit service receive '123456789012345678' as a string and never get a chance to JSON.parse it back into a lossy float. For testing I'd add a case with a ledger whose entries sum past 2^53 minus one — something like a wallet with a stored balance in the trillions of cents — and assert the computed drift and compensatingAmount are byte-for-byte correct, plus a serialization test asserting the JSON payload has amounts as quoted strings, not bare numbers, so nobody downstream re-coerces them into doubles.

The main correctness issue is around the money types — expectedBalance, actualBalance, drift and compensatingAmount are all plain `number`, and reducing amountMinorUnits with regular addition means you're doing floating point math on money. Once the summed value goes past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER you lose precision and the drift calculation becomes wrong without throwing anything, which for a reconciliation service that's supposed to be the source of truth on discrepancies is pretty bad — you'd be silently trusting a broken number. My fix would be to use BigInt for amountMinorUnits and all the derived fields, so the sum and subtraction stay exact regardless of wallet size. I'd also double check how these values get serialized to JSON for the saga orchestrator, since BigInt doesn't serialize natively — you'd want to convert to strings explicitly rather than letting it error out or get coerced. For tests, I'd add a large-balance case to prove the reconciliation is still exact instead of just testing small round numbers like the current suite probably does.

I'd want to check what the max realistic value is — for most wallets minor units in cents probably never gets anywhere near overflow, but it's still safer to not rely on floating point for financial calculations. I'd suggest maybe using a decimal library or converting to BigInt for the summation part at least. I'd also want to make sure the JSON response doesn't break anything when we return these values to other services. I didn't look too closely at whether drift and compensatingAmount need the same treatment as expectedBalance, but probably yes since they're derived from it, so I'd propagate whatever fix we choose through all four fields to be consistent.

I guess if there are a lot of ledger entries, the reduce could be slow, so maybe we'd want to do the sum in the database with a SQL SUM instead of pulling all rows into memory — that would help with performance for wallets with a huge transaction history. checklist: [technical] Identifies that per-process in-memory state means each replica has an independent breaker — no shared view across replicas.
[problemSolving] Explains the concrete failure: replica A keeps hammering a host that replica B already tripped, and state resets on restart.
[communication] Articulates why circuit state is inherently shared/distributed state, not local worker state.
[testing] Proposes moving state to Redis keys (with TTL/stamp) and verifying by tripping the breaker on one replica and confirming another replica also blocks.

examples.text: So the core issue is that `circuits` is a `private Map` living on each `WebhookDeliveryWorker` instance, and since this service runs as several horizontally-scaled replicas behind a load balancer, every replica boots its own process and constructs its own worker with its own empty Map. There's no shared view of circuit state across replicas at all -- it's purely per-process in-memory state. So concretely: say host X starts failing. Replica A's `recordFailure` increments its own entry, hits `FAILURE_THRESHOLD`, and flips its local circuit to "open" so `canSend` blocks it. But replica B's Map has no entry for that host, or a much lower failure count, so B keeps merrily POSTing to the same dying host through `run()`, completely unaware A already tripped. You've built a breaker that protects one process's view of the world, not the destination host, which is really the whole point of a circuit breaker in a multi-replica deployment. On top of that, this state is gone on every deploy or restart -- a fresh Map means the breaker forgets everything and every replica starts back at "closed" regardless of how hot that host was five seconds before the rollout. The fix is to treat circuit state as genuinely shared, distributed state, not local worker state -- move it into Redis, keyed per host, something like a hash or a couple of keys holding failure count, state, and openedAt timestamp with a TTL around COOLDOWN_MS so it self-expires into half-open. `recordFailure` becomes an atomic INCR (ideally via a Lua script or Redis transaction so concurrent replicas don't race and double-trip or under-count), and `canSend` reads that shared key instead of the local Map. To verify it, I'd spin up two workers pointed at the same Redis instance, hammer failures through worker A until it trips the breaker for a host, then immediately call `canSend` on worker B for that same host and assert it's also blocked -- that's the real proof the fix works, not just that A's own Map updated.

Looking at this, the circuit breaker state -- the `circuits` Map -- is just a private field on the class instance, so it only exists in the memory of whichever process created it. Since this runs as multiple horizontally-scaled replicas, each replica has its own separate breaker with no shared state between them. That means if replica A trips the breaker for a host after five failures, replica B has no idea and keeps sending requests to that same host through its own `canSend`/`recordFailure` pair, so you're not actually protecting the destination the way the breaker is supposed to. It also means a restart wipes the Map clean, so any accumulated failure history for a host just disappears and you start from closed again. I'd fix this by pulling the circuit state out into something shared like Redis -- store the state, failure count, and openedAt per host as a Redis key with a TTL tied to the cooldown, so all replicas read and write the same source of truth instead of each having their own. To test it I'd trip the breaker from one replica's calls and then check that a second replica also sees it as open for that host.

checklist: [problemSolving] Diagnoses that plain `FOR UPDATE` makes the second poller WAIT on the first poller's row locks instead of picking a different batch, so the two pollers serialize instead of scaling out.

[technical] Gives the fix: `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` so each poller skips rows another poller is already holding and claims a disjoint batch — and flips status to `in_flight` inside the SAME transaction as the claim, so a later poller never re-claims an already-claimed row.
[communication] Explains the "SQL table as a work-queue" idea in plain terms, and is careful to frame `SKIP LOCKED` as a concurrency/throughput mechanism, not an exactly-once delivery guarantee.

[testing] Describes a verification: run N poller replicas concurrently against the same table, confirm combined claim throughput scales roughly linearly with N, and confirm no single row is ever claimed by two pollers at once (no double delivery).

examples.text: So looking at claimBatch, every replica runs the exact same query — SELECT ... FROM webhook_deliveries WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE — inside its own transaction. Plain FOR UPDATE takes row locks on whatever rows the query matches, and it doesn't skip rows that are already locked — it blocks until the lock holder commits or rolls back. So if replica A grabs the top 50 pending rows first, replica B's identical query tries to lock those same rows, can't, and just sits there waiting instead of picking a different batch. That's why two replicas together deliver at basically the rate of one: you've accidentally serialized them instead of parallelizing them. The fix is FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — it tells Postgres to skip any row currently locked by another transaction and just grab the next unlocked ones matching the WHERE clause, so each replica ends up claiming a disjoint batch instead of contending for the same rows. I'd also flip status to 'in_flight' inside that same transaction, right alongside the SELECT ... SKIP LOCKED, rather than only setting 'sent' after dispatch like the current code does — that way a row is marked as claimed the instant it's grabbed, so no other replica can ever pick it up again even across retries or crash-recovery sweeps. Conceptually you're treating webhook_deliveries as a SQL-backed work queue, and SKIP LOCKED is the standard multi-consumer pattern for that — but it's important to be clear this only fixes throughput and prevents double-claiming under normal operation, it's not an exactly-once delivery guarantee by itself; if the process dies after claiming but before dispatch completes, you still need something like a lease timeout to reclaim stuck 'in_flight' rows. To verify the fix, I'd run several WebhookPoller replicas concurrently against the same table with a decent backlog of pending rows, and check that combined claim throughput scales roughly linearly as I add replicas instead of flatlining like it does now, and separately I'd assert that no single row ID ever shows up as dispatched by two different replicas in the logs.

The problem is the FOR UPDATE in claimBatch — when replica A locks the top 50 pending rows, replica B running the identical SELECT has to wait for those row locks to release before it can proceed, so the two replicas effectively run one after another instead of in parallel. That's why adding a second replica doesn't move the needle on throughput. The fix is to change FOR UPDATE to FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so a poller skips over rows another transaction already has locked and grabs the next available ones instead of blocking, meaning each replica claims a different, disjoint batch. Basically you're using the table as a queue, and SKIP LOCKED is the go-to pattern in Postgres for letting multiple consumers pull from the same queue table concurrently without stepping on each other. I'd also want the status update to happen as part of the claim, not just at the end after dispatch, so a row is visibly taken as soon as it's selected. To check it works, I'd run a couple of poller instances against the same table and confirm they're not just re-locking the same rows — throughput should go up and I shouldn't see any row dispatched twice.

I think the issue is the FOR UPDATE lock in that query — when two pollers run at the same time, the second one has to wait for the first one's lock on those rows before it can get its own results back, so they end up basically taking turns instead of working at the same time. That would explain why adding a second replica doesn't really speed things up. I'd change FOR UPDATE to FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so the second poller doesn't have to wait — it can just skip past the locked rows and grab a different set instead. That should let both run in parallel and get more throughput. For testing, I'd probably just run two or three pollers at once and see if the total number of webhooks sent per second goes up compared to running just one.

checklist: [problemSolving] Identifies that the HMAC is computed for every request, including out-of-window ones certain to be rejected — wasted crypto CPU under a replay flood.
[technical] Gives the fix: run the cheap window check FIRST and reject stale timestamps before computing the HMAC, keeping constant-time compare for the survivors.
[communication] Explains the reorder also makes the "stale = reject" invariant clearer and that correctness is unchanged — only cost/robustness improves.
[testing] Verifies by flooding out-of-window requests and confirming the HMAC is no longer computed (CPU/latency drop) while valid requests still succeed.

examples.text: Looking at verifyWebhook, the order is the whole story here. Step 1 does createHmac("sha256", WEBHOOK_SECRET).update(rawBody).digest() and a timingSafeEqual compare, and only after that does it look at x-timestamp and check the skew against MAX_SKEW_SECONDS. Under a replay flood, the vast majority of incoming requests are old captured payloads that are guaranteed to fail the freshness check no matter what — but we're still paying for a SHA-256 HMAC computation over the full raw body plus a Buffer.from hex-parse for every single one of them before we ever look at the cheap thing. That's the CPU spike: expensive crypto work spent on requests whose fate was already sealed. The fix is just to reorder — parse and validate x-timestamp first, compute skew with Math.abs(Date.now()/1000 - requestTs), and throw StaleTimestampError immediately if it's outside the window, before touching createHmac at all. For anything that survives that cheap check, keep doing the HMAC computation and timingSafeEqual exactly as-is, so the constant-time property of the actual signature comparison is untouched — we're not weakening security, we're just not wasting cycles proving that already-doomed requests are also doomed on a second axis. It also makes the function read better: 'is this even fresh' is a much more natural first gate than 'let's do crypto and then check the clock.' To verify, I'd load-test with a flood of stale/out-of-window requests and confirm via profiling or a call counter that createHmac/timingSafeEqual are no longer being invoked for those — CPU usage and p99 latency under that flood should drop noticeably — while a control set of valid, fresh requests still gets accepted and forged-signature requests still get rejected, so behavior is unchanged.

The issue is the ordering in verifyWebhook — it computes the HMAC over rawBody and does the timingSafeEqual comparison in Step 1, and only checks the x-timestamp freshness window in Step 2. So every request in the replay flood, even ones that are obviously stale and would get rejected by StaleTimestampError anyway, still pays for a full HMAC computation first. That's wasted crypto CPU on traffic we already know we're going to throw out. The fix is to swap the two checks: validate the timestamp against MAX_SKEW_SECONDS first and bail out early with StaleTimestampError, and only run createHmac plus timingSafeEqual for requests that pass that cheap check. That way we're not changing what gets accepted or rejected, just doing less work to get there, and the timingSafeEqual comparison for real candidates stays exactly as constant-time as before. I'd confirm it by hammering the endpoint with a bunch of out-of-window requests and watching CPU usage go down, and separately making sure valid signed requests within the window still pass.

So the function checks the signature and then checks the timestamp. I think the problem is that when there's a flood of replayed requests, they're all going to fail eventually, but we're doing the HMAC work regardless of whether the timestamp is going to fail too. Maybe we could check the timestamp first since that's a simple math comparison, versus the HMAC which involves actual hashing, so that's more expensive. If we did the timestamp check before computing the hash, we'd skip the hash for anything stale. I'd probably just move the skew calculation up above the HMAC block. I think that would help with the CPU usage under the flood since fewer HMACs get computed. Not 100% sure how much of a difference it makes but it seems like the right direction, and I'd probably just run the endpoint again after and see if CPU looks better.

Maybe the CPU spike is more about there being too many requests overall rather than the order of the checks. I could see adding a rate limiter in front of this so fewer requests even reach verifyWebhook, that would help with the CPU. Or maybe caching valid signatures so we don't recompute them, though I'm not sure that would work for signatures since they're basically all different. I think the timestamp check could maybe move earlier just to fail faster but I'm not sure it changes much since throwing an error happens either way and errors aren't that expensive.

If CPU is spiking it's probably just because there's a lot of traffic hitting the server, so the real fix would be to scale up the server or add more replicas behind a load balancer, or maybe put a WAF or CDN in front of it to absorb the flood before it even reaches the app. I don't think there's anything wrong with verifyWebhook itself — timingSafeEqual is already there for security so that part looks solid. checklist: [problemSolving] Traces that the sender and receiver end up computing the HMAC over two DIFFERENT byte sequences because the JSON payload gets parsed and re-serialized (whitespace, key order can change) somewhere between the moment it is signed and the moment it is sent or verified — not because the secret differs on either side.

[technical] States the fix precisely: sign and verify the SAME raw bytes on both sides — enable raw-body capture on the receiving framework so the handler sees the unmodified body bytes, and stringify the payload exactly once on the sending side; never let a middleware or serializer parse the body into an object and re-stringify it before signing or after receiving.

[communication] Clearly distinguishes "logically equal JSON" (same keys and values) from "byte-identical payload" (the exact same bytes), and explains that HMAC has no concept of JSON semantics — it hashes bytes, so any re-serialization, even one that changes nothing meaningful to a human, produces a different signature.

[testing] Verifies the fix by re-sending a request end-to-end and asserting the receiver now returns 200 instead of 401, and — for a stronger check — diffing the exact bytes signed on the sender against the exact raw bytes the receiver read, confirming they are identical rather than merely "similar".

examples.text: So the secret isn't the problem here, the bytes are. On the sender side, look closely: the code calls JSON.stringify(payload) once to compute the HMAC, but then it passes the raw payload object — not that string — into axios.post. Axios does its own internal serialization of that object to build the actual request body that goes over the wire. Those are two separate JSON.stringify calls, and even though they encode the same logical data, there's no guarantee they produce byte-identical output — key ordering, spacing, even how numbers or Unicode get encoded can differ between them. On the receiver, it's the same class of bug in reverse: express.json() parses the incoming bytes into req.body and throws away the original raw buffer, so verifySignature is forced to call JSON.stringify(req.body) to reconstruct something to hash — but that's a third independent serialization, and there's no reason it matches either of the sender's. HMAC has zero awareness of JSON semantics, it just hashes whatever bytes you feed it, so 'the same JSON' by human eyes is irrelevant — only byte-for-byte identity matters. The fix is to sign and verify the exact same bytes on both ends: on the sender, stringify once, sign that exact string, and send that exact string as the body instead of handing axios the object. On the receiver, configure express.json with the verify option, or use express.raw()/a raw-body middleware, to capture the untouched raw body buffer before it's parsed, and compute the HMAC over that raw buffer, not over a re-stringified req.body. To confirm the fix, I'd resend a real webhook end-to-end and check we get 200 instead of 401, and ideally log the exact bytes signed on the sender against the exact raw bytes read on the receiver and diff them to prove they're identical, not just similar-looking JSON.

Reading through this, the secret matches on both sides so that's ruled out — the issue has to be in how the payload gets turned into bytes. On the sender, they stringify the payload to sign it, but then pass the object itself to axios, which serializes it again separately for the actual HTTP body. That's already two independent stringify calls that could diverge. On the receiver, express.json() parses the body into req.body, and then the middleware stringifies that parsed object again to compute the expected signature — so we're hashing a re-serialized version, not the bytes that actually arrived. Since HMAC just hashes raw bytes and doesn't understand JSON at all, any difference in key order or whitespace between these serializations would produce a totally different signature even if the data is logically equivalent. The fix is to make sure both sides are working off the exact same byte sequence — capture the raw body on the receiver before Express parses it, and on the sender, sign the exact string you're sending, not the object. After deploying that I'd resend a request and confirm it returns 200 now.

Similarly on the receiver, express.json() is parsing the body, and then the code stringifies req.body again for the signature check — so it's re-serializing something that was already parsed, which could come out looking different. Since it's a hash function, even a tiny difference like spacing would break it.
